bio_edx.6.0.summary: The **endocrine system** is made of **glands** that **secrete hormones directly into the bloodstream**. Hormones are **chemical messengers** carried in the **blood plasma** all around the body, but they only affect **target organs** whose cells have the right **receptors**. Edexcel expects you to name and locate six glands (pituitary, thyroid, pancreas, adrenal glands, ovaries, testes), the hormones each releases and their target organs, and to explain why hormonal responses are slower but longer lasting than nervous ones.

core.p: The endocrine system is one of the two ways the body coordinates itself (the other is the nervous system). It is made up of endocrine glands, which are groups of cells that make and release hormones. A hormone is a chemical messenger released into the blood that travels to and changes the activity of a target organ.
bullets: Endocrine glands are **ductless**: they release hormones **straight into the blood**, not through a tube.
Hormones are carried in the **blood plasma**.
Blood goes everywhere, so hormones reach **every organ**, but only **target organs** respond.
Hormones control processes that need **long-lasting** effects: growth, metabolism, reproduction, blood glucose.
Hormones are usually **proteins** or **steroids** (you just need to know they are chemicals).

callouts.p: A chemical messenger secreted by an endocrine gland directly into the bloodstream, which travels to a target organ and causes a response.
An organ that produces hormones and secretes them directly into the blood.

core.p: You must be able to label the six glands named in the spec on a diagram of the body. Learn them top to bottom.
bullets: **Pituitary gland**: at the base of the brain (pea sized).
**Thyroid gland**: in the neck, in front of the windpipe.
**Adrenal glands**: one on top of each kidney.
**Pancreas**: in the abdomen, just below the stomach.
**Ovaries**: in the female pelvis, either side of the uterus.
**Testes**: in the scrotum in males.

callouts.p: Top to bottom: Pituitary, Thyroid, Adrenals, Pancreas, Ovaries or Testes.

core.h: How hormones travel to target organs
core.p: A gland releases its hormone into the blood capillaries running through it. The hormone dissolves in the plasma and is carried by the circulatory system to every part of the body. When it reaches a target organ, it binds to receptors on or in the target cells and changes what those cells do.
bullets: Step 1: stimulus detected; gland **secretes** hormone.
Step 2: hormone enters the **blood** and is carried in **plasma**.
Step 3: hormone is carried around the **whole body**.
Step 4: hormone binds to **receptors** on cells of the **target organ**.
Step 5: target organ produces a **response** (an effector response).
Hormones are eventually broken down (often in the liver) so their effect stops.

callouts.p: Hormones are transported in the blood plasma.

core.p: Every cell is bathed in blood containing hormones, so why do only some respond? Target cells have specific receptor molecules with a shape that is complementary to the hormone. Only cells with those receptors can detect that hormone and respond.
bullets: A **target organ** is an organ whose cells have receptors for a particular hormone.
Cells **without** the receptor are not affected even though the hormone reaches them.
One hormone can have **several** target organs (adrenalin acts on heart, liver, muscles).
One organ can be the target of **several** hormones (the liver responds to insulin, glucagon and adrenalin).

callouts.p: An organ containing cells with receptors for a particular hormone, which responds when the hormone arrives.

core.h: The pituitary gland: the master gland
core.p: The pituitary gland at the base of the brain is often called the master gland because many of its hormones control other endocrine glands. It is controlled by the hypothalamus just above it.
bullets: **FSH** (follicle stimulating hormone): target **ovaries**; causes an egg to mature in a follicle and stimulates oestrogen production.
**LH** (luteinising hormone): target **ovaries**; triggers **ovulation**.
**TSH** (thyroid stimulating hormone): target **thyroid gland**; stimulates thyroxine release.
**ADH** (antidiuretic hormone, triple): target **kidneys**; increases water reabsorption.
**Growth hormone**: targets many tissues such as bones and muscles; controls growth.
FSH and LH also act on the testes in males.

callouts.p: The pituitary releases hormones that stimulate other glands, such as TSH acting on the thyroid and FSH/LH acting on the ovaries.

core.p: The thyroid gland in the neck releases thyroxine. Thyroxine targets most cells of the body and increases the **metabolic rate**: the rate of chemical reactions in cells, such as respiration and protein synthesis.
bullets: Hormone: **thyroxine**.
Target: **most body cells**.
Effect: controls **metabolic rate**, which affects growth, heart rate and body temperature.
Its release is stimulated by **TSH** from the pituitary (details of negative feedback are in 7.3).

core.p: The pancreas releases the hormones that control **blood glucose concentration**. (It also makes digestive enzymes, but that is a separate, non-hormonal role.)
bullets: **Insulin**: released when blood glucose is **too high**; target **liver** (and muscle cells); glucose taken into cells and stored as **glycogen**.
**Glucagon**: released when blood glucose is **too low**; target **liver**; glycogen broken down to glucose.
Main target organ for both: the **liver**.

callouts.p: Spell carefully: glucagon is the hormone, glycogen is the storage carbohydrate and glucose is the sugar.

core.p: The adrenal glands sit on top of the kidneys and release **adrenalin** when you are frightened, stressed or excited. Adrenalin prepares the body for **fight or flight** (detail in 7.2).
bullets: Hormone: **adrenalin**.
Targets include the **heart** (faster beating), **liver** (glycogen to glucose) and **muscles**.
Adrenalin is a good example of a hormone with **many target organs**.

core.p: The sex organs are also endocrine glands. Their hormones control the development of **secondary sexual characteristics** at puberty and the reproductive cycle.
bullets: Ovaries release **oestrogen**: target **uterus** (builds up lining) and the **pituitary**; causes female secondary sexual characteristics.
Ovaries release **progesterone**: target **uterus**; **maintains** the uterus lining.
Testes release **testosterone**: targets reproductive organs and other tissues; controls **sperm production** and male secondary sexual characteristics.
Oestrogen and progesterone are covered in depth in the menstrual cycle (7.4-7.5).

core.h: Summary table: glands, hormones and target organs
core.p: This is the core table for the spec point. Questions often give a gland and ask for the hormone or the target, or give a blank table to complete.
bullets: Learn **gland, hormone, target, effect** for each row.
Higher marks need the effect, not just the name.

head: Gland
Location
Hormone(s)
Target organ(s) and effect
rows: FSH, LH, TSH, ADH, growth hormone
Most body cells: controls metabolic rate
Heart, liver, muscles: fight or flight
Reproductive organs; male characteristics, sperm production

callouts.p: If asked for a target organ, give an organ (for example the liver), not 'the blood'.

core.p: Edexcel questions often ask you to compare the endocrine system with the nervous system. Hormones are slower to act and work over a wider area, but their effects last much longer.
bullets: Nerve impulses are **electrical**; hormones are **chemical**.
Nerve impulses travel along **neurones**; hormones travel in **blood plasma**.
Nervous responses are **very fast**; hormonal responses are **slower**.
Nervous effects are **short lived**; hormonal effects are **long lasting**.
Nervous effects are **localised** (one muscle or gland); hormones can act **widely** on many organs.

callouts.p: Hormones do not travel along nerves, and they travel in the plasma, not inside red blood cells.

core.h: Why the body needs both systems
core.p: Some responses must be instant, such as pulling your hand off a hot plate: the nervous system does this. Others must continue for days, months or years, such as growth, puberty or controlling metabolism: hormones do this. Some situations, like danger, use both: nerves react instantly and adrenalin keeps the body ready.
bullets: Nervous: rapid, precise, short term control.
Hormonal: slower, widespread, long term control.
The hypothalamus and pituitary link the two systems.
Hormones are vital for **homeostasis** (for example blood glucose and water balance).

analogy.p: An endocrine gland is like a radio station broadcasting a message on one frequency. The signal (hormone) spreads everywhere through the air (blood), reaching every house. But only houses with a radio tuned to that frequency (cells with the matching receptor) hear it and act on it; the target organs. The nervous system is more like a phone call along a wire: fast and only to one person. Where it breaks down: radio waves travel almost instantly, but hormones are slow because they are carried by the blood flow, and the hormone is physically used up and broken down, whereas a radio signal is not.

terms.d: The system of glands that produce hormones and secrete them into the blood.
A ductless gland that secretes hormones directly into the bloodstream.
A chemical messenger carried in the blood to a target organ, where it causes a response.
An organ whose cells have receptors for a specific hormone and respond to it.
A molecule on or in a cell with a shape that binds a specific hormone.
The liquid part of the blood, which carries dissolved hormones.
Gland at the base of the brain that releases FSH, LH, TSH, ADH and growth hormone; the master gland.
Gland in the neck that releases thyroxine, which controls metabolic rate.
Organ that releases insulin and glucagon to control blood glucose concentration.
Glands on top of the kidneys that release adrenalin.
Female glands that release oestrogen and progesterone (and eggs).
Male glands that release testosterone (and make sperm).
Hormone from the thyroid that increases metabolic rate.
The rate at which chemical reactions take place in the body's cells.
Male sex hormone from the testes controlling sperm production and male characteristics.
Name for the pituitary, because its hormones control other endocrine glands.

mistakes.w: Hormones travel along nerves.
mistakes.r: Hormones are carried in the blood (plasma).

mistakes.w: Hormones are carried by red blood cells.
mistakes.r: Hormones are dissolved in and carried by the plasma.

mistakes.w: Hormones only travel to their target organ.
mistakes.r: Hormones are carried all around the body but only target organs with receptors respond.

mistakes.w: The target organ of insulin is the blood.
mistakes.r: The main target organ of insulin is the liver (also muscles).

mistakes.w: Adrenalin is made in the kidneys.
mistakes.r: Adrenalin is made in the adrenal glands, which sit on top of the kidneys.

mistakes.w: The pancreas makes glycogen.
mistakes.r: The pancreas secretes insulin and glucagon; glycogen is stored in the liver and muscles.

mistakes.w: The thyroid is in the brain.
mistakes.r: The pituitary is at the base of the brain; the thyroid is in the neck.

mistakes.w: Hormonal responses are faster than nervous responses.
mistakes.r: Hormonal responses are slower but last longer.

exam.q: What is a hormone?
model: A chemical messenger
Secreted by a gland into the blood / carried in the blood to a target organ
exam.tip: Include both 'chemical' and 'carried in blood'.

exam.q: Name the gland that produces thyroxine.
model: Thyroid gland
exam.tip: Learn every gland-hormone pair.

exam.q: Name the hormone released by the adrenal glands.
model: Adrenalin
exam.tip: Spell it adrenalin, as Edexcel does.

exam.q: State how hormones are transported from endocrine glands to target organs.
model: In the blood / in the blood plasma
exam.tip: Plasma is the precise answer.

exam.q: Name two hormones produced by the pituitary gland and give the target organ of each.
model: FSH
target: ovaries
TSH
target: thyroid gland (or LH: ovaries; ADH: kidneys)
exam.tip: Pair each hormone with the correct target.

exam.q: Explain why a hormone in the blood affects only certain organs.
model: Only target organ cells have receptors for that hormone
Hormone binds to receptor (complementary shape) and causes a response
exam.tip: Receptors is the key word.

exam.q: Complete the table: Gland: pancreas. Hormone: ____ . Target organ: ____ .
model: Insulin (or glucagon)
Liver
exam.tip: Liver is the main target for both pancreatic hormones.

exam.q: Give two differences between the way the nervous system and the endocrine system coordinate responses.
model: Nervous uses electrical impulses, endocrine uses chemicals (hormones)
Nervous is faster / short lived / localised; endocrine slower / long lasting / widespread
exam.tip: Compare both sides in each point: use 'whereas'.

exam.q: The pituitary gland is called the master gland. Explain why.
model: It secretes hormones that control other endocrine glands
e.g. TSH stimulates the thyroid / FSH and LH act on the ovaries
exam.tip: Give an example to get the second mark.

exam.q: Describe the role of the endocrine system in the body, naming the glands, hormones and target organs involved.
model: Endocrine glands secrete hormones directly into the blood; carried in plasma to target organs with receptors
Pituitary: FSH and LH to ovaries, TSH to thyroid (ADH to kidneys)
Thyroid: thyroxine to body cells, controls metabolic rate
Pancreas: insulin and glucagon to liver, controls blood glucose
Adrenal glands: adrenalin to heart, liver, muscles for fight or flight
Ovaries: oestrogen and progesterone act on uterus; testes: testosterone controls sperm production and male characteristics
exam.tip: Structure the answer gland by gland; each gland with hormone and target scores credit.

worked.q: A student says: 'Adrenalin reaches the big toe, so the big toe must be a target organ.' Evaluate this statement.
steps: Adrenalin is carried in the blood plasma to all parts of the body, so it does reach the toe
Reaching an organ is not enough: a target organ must have cells with receptors for the hormone
Only organs with adrenalin receptors, such as the heart, liver and muscles, respond
So the statement is wrong unless the toe tissue has the right receptors
worked.ans: Incorrect reasoning: target organs are defined by having receptors, not by receiving the hormone.

worked.q: A patient's thyroid gland is damaged and produces very little thyroxine. Use your knowledge of the endocrine system to predict and explain the effects.
steps: Thyroxine targets most body cells and controls metabolic rate
Less thyroxine means a lower metabolic rate
Slower respiration releases less energy, so the patient may feel tired and cold
Slower metabolism can lead to weight gain
Treatment would be to give thyroxine tablets, which travel in the blood to the target cells
worked.ans: Low thyroxine lowers metabolic rate, causing tiredness, feeling cold and weight gain.

bio_edx.6.1.summary: **Adrenalin** is a hormone secreted by the **adrenal glands** (on top of the kidneys) when the brain detects danger, stress or excitement. Carried in the **blood plasma**, it prepares the body for **fight or flight** by **increasing heart rate**, **increasing blood pressure**, **increasing blood flow to the muscles** and **raising blood glucose** by stimulating the **liver** to convert **glycogen into glucose**. Every effect links to one purpose: delivering more **oxygen and glucose** to muscles for faster **respiration**, releasing more energy for contraction. This is a Higher tier point.

core.h: What adrenalin is and where it comes from
core.p: Adrenalin is a hormone made by the adrenal glands, which sit on top of each kidney. It is released in response to fear, stress, danger or excitement. Like all hormones it is secreted directly into the blood and carried in the plasma to its target organs.
bullets: Gland: **adrenal glands** (one above each kidney).
Trigger: brain detects a **threat, stress or excitement**; nerve impulses stimulate the adrenal glands.
Transport: in the **blood plasma**.
Targets: **heart**, **liver**, **blood vessels** (arterioles) supplying muscles and other organs, plus muscles in airways and the eye.
Spec effects (Higher): heart rate up, blood pressure up, blood flow to muscles up, blood glucose up via the liver.

callouts.p: A hormone secreted by the adrenal glands that prepares the body for fight or flight.
7.2 is a Higher tier point: you must explain each effect of adrenalin, not just list it.

core.p: When you face danger, your body must be ready either to fight the threat or run away (flight). Both need powerful, sustained muscle contraction. Muscle contraction needs energy from respiration, and respiration needs oxygen and glucose. Adrenalin makes sure the muscles get more of both, very quickly.
bullets: The key chain: **more oxygen + more glucose to muscles** to **faster respiration** to **more energy released** to **more muscle contraction**.
Aerobic respiration: glucose + oxygen to carbon dioxide + water (energy released).
Faster blood flow also removes **carbon dioxide** and heat from working muscles.
The response is automatic (you do not choose it).

callouts.p: Grade 9 answers always link each effect back to oxygen and glucose for respiration in muscles.

core.p: Adrenalin binds to receptors in the heart muscle and makes the heart beat faster (and more strongly).
bullets: More beats per minute means **more blood pumped** per minute (higher cardiac output).
So **more oxygen and glucose** are delivered to muscle cells each minute.
Muscles can **respire faster** and release more energy for contraction.
Carbon dioxide is also removed more quickly.

core.p: Because the heart pumps faster and more forcefully, and some blood vessels narrow, the pressure of blood in the arteries rises.
bullets: Higher pressure pushes blood **around the body faster**.
Blood reaches the muscles more quickly with oxygen and glucose.
Caused by stronger, faster heartbeat and **vasoconstriction** of vessels to less important organs.

callouts.p: Do not say adrenalin 'makes more blood'. The volume of blood is the same; it is pumped faster and redirected.

core.h: Effect 3: increased blood flow to the muscles
core.p: Adrenalin causes arterioles supplying skeletal muscles to **widen (dilate)**, while arterioles supplying the gut and skin **narrow**. So blood is diverted from organs that are not needed in an emergency to the muscles that are.
bullets: Vessels to **muscles dilate**: more blood flow there.
Vessels to the **digestive system and skin constrict**: digestion slows (not urgent in an emergency).
This is why people may go **pale** and get 'butterflies' when frightened.
Result: muscles get the largest share of **oxygen and glucose**.

head: Region
Change in blood vessels
Blood flow
Why
rows: Need oxygen and glucose for respiration
Digestion not needed in an emergency

core.p: Adrenalin targets the **liver**. It stimulates liver cells to convert their store of **glycogen into glucose**, which is released into the blood. Blood glucose concentration rises, so more glucose is available for muscle cells to use in respiration.
bullets: Liver stores glucose as the insoluble polymer **glycogen**.
Adrenalin: **glycogen to glucose** in the liver.
Glucose released into the blood: **blood glucose rises**.
Muscles take up glucose for **respiration**, releasing energy for contraction.
(Muscle cells' own glycogen can also be broken down.)

callouts.p: Adrenalin raises blood sugar levels by stimulating the liver to change glycogen into glucose.
Glycogen is the store; glucagon is a different hormone from the pancreas. Do not mix them up.

fig.cap: Adrenalin binds to liver cells, which break down stored glycogen into glucose; glucose enters the blood and is used by muscles for respiration.

core.h: Other effects you may see in questions
core.p: The spec focuses on the four effects above, but questions sometimes describe other fight or flight changes. These all support the same goal.
bullets: **Breathing rate increases** and airways widen: more oxygen absorbed into the blood.
**Pupils dilate**: more light enters the eye, improving vision.
Mental **alertness** increases.
Digestion slows as blood is diverted away from the gut.

core.h: Why a hormone and not just nerves?
core.p: The nervous system gives the instant reaction (for example jumping back), but adrenalin spreads through the blood to many organs at once and its effects last for minutes. This keeps the body ready while the danger lasts.
bullets: Hormone reaches **many target organs** at once via the blood.
Effects are **longer lasting** than a nerve impulse.
Adrenalin is slightly slower to start than a reflex but still acts within seconds.
After the danger, adrenalin is broken down and the effects gradually wear off.

core.h: Adrenalin is not controlled by negative feedback
core.p: Unlike thyroxine (7.3), adrenalin release is not regulated by negative feedback. It is released in response to a stimulus from the brain and actually pushes conditions such as heart rate and blood glucose away from their normal values for a short time.
bullets: Thyroxine: **negative feedback** keeps the level steady.
Adrenalin: released only when the brain detects **stress**; levels rise sharply and then fall when the threat passes.
Good contrast point for comparison questions.

callouts.p: If asked to compare thyroxine and adrenalin, mention that thyroxine is long term and controlled by negative feedback, while adrenalin is short term and triggered by stress.

core.p: Questions often show a graph of heart rate or blood glucose before and after a fright, or after an injection of adrenalin. Describe the pattern using values, then explain it.
bullets: Describe: heart rate **rises rapidly** after the stimulus, peaks, then **falls gradually**.
Explain the rise: adrenalin released, binds to heart receptors.
Explain the slow fall: adrenalin is gradually **broken down** and removed from the blood.
Quote numbers with units (for example 70 to 130 beats per minute).

callouts.p: Percentage change = (change / original value) x 100.

core.h: Summary of the effects of adrenalin
core.p: Use this table as a quick checklist. Each row gives target, effect and why it helps fight or flight.
bullets: Four spec effects, one purpose: more energy for muscles.

head: Target
Effect
Why it helps
rows: More blood (oxygen, glucose) pumped to muscles per minute
More blood flow to muscles, less to gut and skin
Glycogen converted to glucose; blood glucose rises
More glucose for respiration in muscles

analogy.t: Adrenalin as a factory emergency order
analogy.p: Imagine the body as a factory and the muscles as the production line. When an emergency order arrives (danger), the manager (adrenal glands) sends out a memo (adrenalin) by courier to every department. Delivery lorries (the heart) run faster and on higher-pressure schedules; roads to the canteen and offices (gut and skin) are closed so lorries go straight to the production line (more blood to muscles); and the warehouse (liver) unpacks its stored raw materials (glycogen into glucose). Everything gets fuel and oxygen to the line so it can work flat out. Where it breaks down: a memo is read and understood, but adrenalin only works by binding to receptors, and it is broken down within minutes rather than staying on file.

terms.d: Hormone from the adrenal glands that prepares the body for fight or flight.
Endocrine glands found on top of the kidneys that secrete adrenalin.
The body's rapid preparation to confront or escape danger, triggered by adrenalin.
An organ with cells that have receptors for a particular hormone.
The number of heartbeats per minute.
The pressure exerted by blood on the walls of the blood vessels (arteries).
A storage carbohydrate made from glucose, stored in the liver and muscles.
A sugar used by cells as the substrate for respiration.
The amount of glucose dissolved in the blood plasma.
An exothermic reaction in cells that releases energy from glucose.
Widening of arterioles, increasing blood flow through them.
Narrowing of arterioles, reducing blood flow through them.
Organ that stores glycogen and converts it to glucose when stimulated by adrenalin.
A molecule on a target cell that binds a specific hormone.

mistakes.w: Adrenalin is made in the kidneys.
mistakes.r: Adrenalin is made by the adrenal glands, which are on top of the kidneys.

mistakes.w: Adrenalin gives the muscles energy.
mistakes.r: Adrenalin increases the supply of oxygen and glucose to muscles so they can respire faster and release more energy.

mistakes.w: Adrenalin makes the liver turn glucose into glycogen.
mistakes.r: Adrenalin stimulates the liver to convert glycogen into glucose.

mistakes.w: Adrenalin makes energy for the body.
mistakes.r: Energy is not made; it is released by respiration.

mistakes.w: The heart beats faster to pump more blood into the body.
mistakes.r: The heart beats faster to deliver more oxygen and glucose to muscles per minute (same blood volume).

mistakes.w: Adrenalin is carried along nerves to the muscles.
mistakes.r: Adrenalin is carried in the blood plasma.

mistakes.w: Adrenalin is controlled by negative feedback like thyroxine.
mistakes.r: Adrenalin is released in response to stress detected by the brain, not by negative feedback.

mistakes.w: Adrenalin increases blood flow to all organs.
mistakes.r: It increases blood flow to muscles and decreases it to the gut and skin.

exam.q: Name the gland that secretes adrenalin.
model: Adrenal gland(s)
exam.tip: Not kidney.

exam.q: State how adrenalin is transported to its target organs.
model: In the blood (plasma)
exam.tip: Plasma is the precise answer.

exam.q: Give two effects of adrenalin on the body.
model: Any two: increased heart rate; increased blood pressure; increased blood flow to muscles; raised blood glucose / glycogen converted to glucose in liver
exam.tip: Use the spec wording.

exam.q: Explain how adrenalin causes blood glucose concentration to rise.
model: Adrenalin stimulates the liver
To convert glycogen into glucose, released into blood
exam.tip: Name the liver and both molecules.

exam.q: Explain why an increase in heart rate helps the body in the fight or flight response.
model: More blood pumped per minute to muscles
Delivering more oxygen and glucose
For faster respiration, releasing more energy for muscle contraction
exam.tip: Follow the chain all the way to energy for contraction.

exam.q: Explain why adrenalin causes blood flow to the digestive system to decrease.
model: Blood is diverted to the muscles
Digestion is not needed in an emergency / muscles need more oxygen and glucose
exam.tip: State where the blood goes instead.

exam.q: A person's heart rate rose from 72 to 126 beats per minute after a fright. Calculate the percentage increase.
model: Increase = 126 - 72 = 54
exam.tip: Divide by the original value.

exam.q: Explain why the heart rate falls only slowly after the danger has passed.
model: Adrenalin remains in the blood for some time
It is gradually broken down / hormonal effects are long lasting
exam.tip: Contrast hormone duration with nerve impulses.

exam.q: Compare the ways in which thyroxine and adrenalin affect the body.
model: Thyroxine from thyroid; adrenalin from adrenal glands
Thyroxine controls metabolic rate long term; adrenalin acts short term in emergencies
Thyroxine is regulated by negative feedback; adrenalin is released in response to stress
Both are carried in the blood to target organs
exam.tip: Use comparative words such as 'whereas'.

exam.q: Explain how adrenalin prepares the body for fight or flight.
model: Brain detects danger; adrenal glands secrete adrenalin into the blood
Adrenalin increases heart rate
And increases blood pressure, so blood delivered faster
Arterioles to muscles dilate and those to gut and skin constrict, increasing blood flow to muscles
Liver converts glycogen to glucose, raising blood glucose
So muscles receive more oxygen and glucose for faster respiration, releasing more energy for contraction
exam.tip: Give every effect then finish with the respiration link; that link is what separates level 3 answers.

worked.q: A student's blood glucose concentration was 90 mg per 100 cm3 before a scary film and 117 mg per 100 cm3 during it. Calculate the percentage increase and explain the change.
steps: Increase = 117 - 90 = 27 mg per 100 cm3
Percentage increase = (27 / 90) x 100 = 30%
The fear was detected by the brain, causing the adrenal glands to secrete adrenalin
Adrenalin stimulated the liver to convert glycogen to glucose
Glucose was released into the blood, raising its concentration
worked.ans: 30% increase, caused by adrenalin stimulating the liver to break down glycogen into glucose.

worked.q: A sprinter feels nervous on the starting blocks. Explain how adrenalin helps her muscles during the race.
steps: Nerves before the race trigger adrenalin release from the adrenal glands
Heart rate and blood pressure increase so blood reaches muscles faster
Blood vessels to leg muscles dilate, increasing blood flow
Liver converts glycogen to glucose, raising blood glucose
Muscles receive more oxygen and glucose, respire faster and release more energy for contraction
worked.ans: Adrenalin increases delivery of oxygen and glucose to the muscles so more energy is released by respiration for contraction.

bio_edx.6.10.summary: Type 2 diabetes is strongly **correlated** with body mass: the more excess body fat a person carries, especially around the abdomen, the higher their risk. Two simple measures are used to judge this risk: **BMI = mass (kg) / (height (m))^2** and the **waist:hip ratio = waist circumference / hip circumference**. You must be able to calculate both, interpret the values, and **evaluate** their strengths and weaknesses, remembering that a correlation does not prove that obesity causes diabetes in every person.

core.p: Large studies show that as body mass and body fat increase, the proportion of people with **type 2 diabetes** increases. This is a **positive correlation**. Excess fat, particularly **abdominal (visceral) fat**, is linked to body cells becoming **less responsive to insulin**.
bullets: **Obesity** is the biggest single **risk factor** for type 2 diabetes.
A risk factor increases the **chance** of a disease; it does not make it certain.
Other risk factors (age, genetics, inactivity, diet) also contribute, so not every obese person develops type 2 diabetes.
To study the link, doctors need simple, cheap ways of measuring obesity in large numbers of people: **BMI** and **waist:hip ratio**.

callouts.p: A relationship between two variables in which one changes as the other changes; it does not by itself show that one causes the other.

fig.cap: Scatter graph of BMI against relative risk of type 2 diabetes. As BMI increases, risk increases: a positive correlation. The points do not prove obesity causes diabetes, because other factors may be involved.

core.p: BMI compares a person's mass with their height to judge whether they are a healthy weight for their height.
bullets: **BMI = mass (kg) / (height (m))^2**.
Mass must be in **kilograms** and height in **metres**: convert cm to m by dividing by 100 (e.g. 175 cm = 1.75 m).
**Square the height first**, then divide the mass by it.
Units of BMI are **kg/m2** (often left out).
Round sensibly, usually to 1 decimal place.

callouts.p: BMI = mass in kg divided by (height in m) squared.

core.p: The calculated BMI is compared with standard ranges for adults. The exam will usually give you the table, but knowing it helps you interpret answers quickly.
bullets: The higher the category, the higher the risk of type 2 diabetes (and heart disease).
Ranges are for **adults**; children use age-specific charts.
Boundaries are agreed conventions, so a BMI of 24.9 and 25.1 have almost the same real risk.

callouts.p: If the question provides a BMI table, always use its boundaries even if they differ slightly from the ones you learned.

fig.cap: The BMI scale. Values below 18.5 are underweight, 18.5 to 24.9 healthy, 25 to 29.9 overweight, 30 to 39.9 obese and 40 or more severely obese. Risk of type 2 diabetes rises along the scale. Example: 90 / 1.80 squared = 27.8 (overweight).

core.p: Most BMI marks are lost through unit errors or forgetting to square the height.
bullets: Step 1: convert height to metres (e.g. 160 cm = 1.60 m).
Step 2: square the height (1.60 x 1.60 = 2.56).
Step 3: divide mass by this value (e.g. 70 / 2.56 = 27.3).
Step 4: compare with the table (27.3 = overweight).
Rearranging: mass = BMI x height^2, so you can find the mass that would give a target BMI.

callouts.p: 70 / 1.60 / 2 is NOT the same as 70 / 1.60^2. Square the height; do not divide by 2.

core.p: The **waist:hip ratio** measures **where** fat is stored. Fat stored around the **abdomen** (an 'apple' shape) is more strongly linked to type 2 diabetes than fat on the hips and thighs (a 'pear' shape).
bullets: **Waist:hip ratio = waist circumference / hip circumference**.
Measure the waist at its **narrowest** point (around the belly button) and the hips at their **widest** point.
Both must be in the **same units** (both cm or both inches); the ratio has **no units**.
A **higher** ratio means more abdominal fat and a **higher** risk of type 2 diabetes.
Commonly used guide (WHO): a ratio above about **0.90 for men** and **0.85 for women** indicates abdominal obesity and increased risk; use any values given in the question.

callouts.p: Waist circumference divided by hip circumference; a measure of how much fat is stored around the abdomen.

fig.cap: Measuring the waist:hip ratio. Waist circumference is measured at the narrowest point just above the belly button and hip circumference at the widest point around the buttocks, in the same units, then waist is divided by hip.

core.p: This is a simple division but you must interpret the answer.
bullets: Example: waist 96 cm, hips 100 cm: 96 / 100 = **0.96**.
For a man this is above 0.90, so he has abdominal obesity and an increased risk.
Example: waist 70 cm, hips 100 cm: 70 / 100 = **0.70**, low risk.
A ratio of **1.0 or more** means the waist is as wide as or wider than the hips: high risk.
Give the ratio to 2 decimal places.

core.p: 'Evaluate' questions need both **strengths** and **weaknesses**, then a judgement.
bullets: Strength: **quick, cheap and easy**: only scales and a tape measure, no specialist training.
Strength: good for comparing **large populations**; shows clear correlation with diabetes risk.
Weakness: does **not distinguish fat from muscle**: muscular athletes can have a high BMI but little fat (wrongly classed as overweight).
Weakness: does **not show where fat is stored**; abdominal fat is the strongest risk.
Weakness: does not account for **age, sex, ethnicity** or bone density; risk at a given BMI differs between ethnic groups.
Weakness: a person can have a 'healthy' BMI but a lot of abdominal fat and still be at risk.

core.p: The waist:hip ratio gives information that BMI misses.
bullets: Strength: measures **abdominal fat**, which is more closely linked to type 2 diabetes than total body mass.
Strength: quick, cheap, needs only a tape measure; not affected by a muscular build in the same way as BMI.
Weakness: measuring position can vary, so results may be **less reproducible** between people measuring.
Weakness: does not take **height** or total body mass into account.
Weakness: different thresholds needed for **men and women**.
Conclusion: the waist:hip ratio is often a **better indicator** of type 2 diabetes risk than BMI, but using **both** gives the best picture.

head: Feature
BMI
Waist:hip ratio
rows: Yes: muscle counted as excess mass

callouts.p: End an evaluate answer with a conclusion, e.g. waist:hip ratio is a better predictor because abdominal fat is more strongly linked to insulin resistance.

core.p: Data showing that obese people are more likely to have type 2 diabetes show a **correlation**. On its own this does not prove that obesity **causes** diabetes.
bullets: A **third factor** could cause both, such as lack of exercise or a high-sugar diet.
However, there is a **plausible mechanism**: excess abdominal fat is linked to cells becoming less responsive to insulin.
Evidence that losing weight improves blood glucose control supports a causal link.
Look at **sample size**: large studies give more reliable conclusions.
Look for **outliers**: individuals with high BMI but no diabetes show it is a risk, not a certainty.

callouts.p: Say the data show a positive correlation or suggest a link. Do not say they prove that obesity causes diabetes.

core.p: Questions often give a table or graph of BMI or waist:hip ratio against the percentage of people with type 2 diabetes.
bullets: **Describe**: 'as BMI increases, the percentage with type 2 diabetes increases' and quote two values with units.
**Calculate**: how many times greater the risk is (divide the larger by the smaller).
**Explain**: link more abdominal fat to cells not responding to insulin, so glucose stays high.
**Evaluate**: comment on sample size, whether other factors were controlled, and whether the measure fits every person.
Compare groups carefully: men and women, or different ages, may have different patterns.

core.p: Because the link is with body fat, lowering BMI and waist:hip ratio reduces the risk of type 2 diabetes.
bullets: **Balanced diet** with less sugar and fat lowers energy intake.
**Regular exercise** uses energy and helps cells respond to insulin.
Losing abdominal fat lowers the waist:hip ratio.
Monitoring these measures over time shows whether lifestyle changes are working.

analogy.p: BMI is like weighing a suitcase and dividing by its size: it tells you if it is heavy for its size, but not whether the weight is clothes or a brick (fat or muscle). The waist:hip ratio is like checking where the weight is packed: a suitcase that bulges in the middle (abdominal fat) is the one most likely to cause problems. Where it breaks down: a suitcase's contents do not change how it works, whereas fat around the abdomen actively affects the body by making cells less responsive to insulin, and neither measure can tell you about genes or age, which also affect risk.

terms.d: A measure of body mass relative to height: BMI = mass (kg) / (height (m))^2.
Waist circumference divided by hip circumference; indicates how much fat is stored around the abdomen.
Distance around the waist at its narrowest point, around the belly button.
Distance around the hips at their widest point.
Having excess body fat, usually defined as a BMI of 30 or more.
Having a BMI of 25 to 29.9.
Excess fat stored around the abdomen, shown by a high waist:hip ratio.
A condition in which body cells no longer respond to insulin (or not enough insulin is produced), so blood glucose is too high.
Something that increases the chance of developing a disease.
A relationship in which one variable changes as another changes.
As one variable increases, the other also increases.
When a change in one variable directly brings about a change in another.
When body cells do not respond properly to insulin.
Command word: give strengths and weaknesses and reach a supported judgement.

mistakes.w: BMI = mass / height x 2.
mistakes.r: BMI = mass (kg) / (height (m))^2: square the height.

mistakes.w: Using height in cm in the BMI equation.
mistakes.r: Convert height to metres first (e.g. 175 cm = 1.75 m).

mistakes.w: Waist:hip ratio = hip / waist.
mistakes.r: Waist:hip ratio = waist circumference / hip circumference.

mistakes.w: A low waist:hip ratio means high risk.
mistakes.r: A higher waist:hip ratio means more abdominal fat and higher risk.

mistakes.w: The data prove that obesity causes type 2 diabetes.
mistakes.r: The data show a positive correlation; other factors may be involved.

mistakes.w: BMI is accurate for everyone.
mistakes.r: BMI does not distinguish fat from muscle or show where fat is stored.

mistakes.w: Everyone with a high BMI will get type 2 diabetes.
mistakes.r: A high BMI increases the risk; it does not guarantee the disease.

mistakes.w: Giving waist:hip ratio with units (e.g. 0.9 cm).
mistakes.r: It is a ratio of two lengths in the same units, so it has no units.

mistakes.w: Waist:hip ratio is worse than BMI because it ignores weight.
mistakes.r: Waist:hip ratio is often a better indicator because abdominal fat is most strongly linked to type 2 diabetes.

exam.q: Give the equation for calculating BMI.
model: BMI = mass (kg) / (height (m))^2.
exam.tip: Include units to be safe.

exam.q: A woman has a mass of 68 kg and a height of 1.65 m. Calculate her BMI. Give your answer to 1 decimal place.
exam.tip: Show the squared height for a method mark.

exam.q: Calculate the waist:hip ratio of a man with a waist of 102 cm and hips of 98 cm.
exam.tip: Waist on top.

exam.q: Explain why the waist:hip ratio has no units.
model: Both measurements are in the same units, so the units cancel.
exam.tip: A ratio of like quantities has no units.

exam.q: Give one reason why BMI may wrongly suggest that a rugby player is obese.
model: BMI does not distinguish between muscle and fat; muscle is dense/heavy, so the mass is high even with little fat.
exam.tip: Mention muscle versus fat.

exam.q: A table shows the percentage of people with type 2 diabetes rises from 2% at BMI 20 to 20% at BMI 35. Describe the relationship and calculate how many times more common diabetes is at BMI 35.
model: As BMI increases, the percentage with type 2 diabetes increases (positive correlation).
20 / 2 = 10 times more common.
exam.tip: Describe the trend, then do the division.

exam.q: Explain why a high waist:hip ratio is linked to type 2 diabetes.
model: A high ratio shows a lot of fat stored around the abdomen.
Abdominal fat is linked to body cells no longer responding to insulin, so blood glucose stays high.
exam.tip: Link fat location to insulin.

exam.q: Suggest why the data showing a link between BMI and type 2 diabetes do not prove that obesity causes diabetes.
model: It is a correlation only.
Other factors (e.g. lack of exercise, diet, age, genetics) could cause both / may not have been controlled.
exam.tip: Name a third factor.

exam.q: Calculate the maximum mass a man of height 1.80 m can have and still be in the healthy BMI range (BMI below 25).
model: mass = BMI x height^2 = 25 x 1.80^2 = 25 x 3.24
= 81 kg (just under 81 kg)
exam.tip: Rearrange the equation before substituting.

exam.q: Evaluate the use of BMI and waist:hip ratio as indicators of a person's risk of developing type 2 diabetes.
model: Both are quick, cheap and easy to measure with simple equipment, so are useful for large populations.
Both show a positive correlation with type 2 diabetes risk.
BMI does not distinguish between fat and muscle, so muscular people may be wrongly classed as obese.
BMI does not show where fat is stored.
Waist:hip ratio measures abdominal fat, which is more strongly linked to type 2 diabetes/insulin resistance.
Neither accounts for other risk factors (age, genetics, ethnicity); conclusion: waist:hip ratio is often a better indicator, but using both gives the most reliable estimate.
exam.tip: Give strengths and weaknesses of each, then finish with a judgement.

worked.q: A man is 182 cm tall and has a mass of 95 kg. His waist is 104 cm and his hips are 102 cm. Calculate his BMI and waist:hip ratio and comment on his risk of type 2 diabetes.
steps: Convert height: 182 cm = 1.82 m.
Square height: 1.82 x 1.82 = 3.3124.
Waist:hip ratio = 104 / 102 = 1.02.
This is well above 0.90 for men, showing a lot of abdominal fat.
Both measures suggest increased risk; the high waist:hip ratio is the more worrying because abdominal fat is closely linked to insulin resistance.
worked.ans: BMI = 28.7 (overweight); waist:hip ratio = 1.02; increased risk of type 2 diabetes.

worked.q: A woman is 1.60 m tall. Calculate the mass at which she would become obese (BMI 30).
steps: Rearrange: mass = BMI x height^2.

worked.q: Applied example: Two men both have a BMI of 31. Man A is a weightlifter with a waist:hip ratio of 0.82; man B is inactive with a waist:hip ratio of 1.05. Evaluate which man is more at risk of type 2 diabetes.
steps: BMI is the same, so BMI alone suggests equal risk (both obese).
Man A's high BMI is likely due to muscle, which BMI cannot distinguish from fat.
Man A's waist:hip ratio is low (0.82), showing little abdominal fat.
Man B's waist:hip ratio is high (1.05), showing a lot of abdominal fat, and he is inactive (another risk factor).
Abdominal fat is more strongly linked to insulin resistance.
worked.ans: Man B is more at risk; this shows why the waist:hip ratio can be a better indicator than BMI alone.

bio_edx.6.11.summary: The **urinary system** (two kidneys, two ureters, the bladder and the urethra) removes **urea**, excess water and excess mineral ions from the blood as **urine**. Each kidney contains about a million **nephrons**. In each nephron blood is first **filtered** under high pressure from the **glomerulus** into the **Bowman's capsule**, and then useful substances are taken back into the blood by **selective reabsorption**: all of the **glucose** is reabsorbed in the first convoluted tubule, and most of the **water** is reabsorbed along the tubule and collecting duct, so only waste leaves as urine.

core.p: Cells constantly make waste and the amount of water and ions in the blood keeps changing. The kidneys keep the blood's composition steady (part of **homeostasis**) and get rid of waste that would be toxic if it built up.
bullets: **Urea** is made in the **liver** from excess amino acids; it is carried in the blood plasma to the kidneys
Urea is toxic in high concentrations, so it must be **excreted**
The kidneys also remove **excess water** and **excess mineral ions** (salts) to keep the water potential of blood plasma steady
Waste removed by the kidneys leaves the body as **urine** (water + urea + ions)
Excretion = removing waste products made by the body's own metabolism

callouts.p: The removal of waste products of metabolism (such as urea and carbon dioxide) from the body.

core.p: Each organ of the urinary system has one job in the path from blood to toilet. Learn the order: renal artery, kidney, ureter, bladder, urethra.
bullets: **Renal artery**: carries blood containing urea **to** the kidney (branches off the aorta)
**Kidney**: filters the blood and makes urine
**Renal vein**: carries filtered blood with less urea **away** from the kidney to the vena cava
**Ureter**: tube carrying urine from each kidney to the bladder
**Bladder**: muscular bag that **stores** urine
**Urethra**: tube carrying urine from the bladder out of the body; a ring of muscle (sphincter) controls release

callouts.p: There are two ureters (one from each kidney to the bladder) but only one urethra (bladder to outside). Ureter comes first in the body and first in the alphabet order you meet them.

core.p: Each kidney contains about **one million nephrons** (kidney tubules). Having so many gives a huge surface area for filtering and reabsorbing. Every nephron has the same parts in the same order.
bullets: **Glomerulus**: a knot of blood capillaries where blood is filtered
**Bowman's capsule**: cup-shaped start of the nephron that surrounds the glomerulus and collects the filtrate
**First (proximal) convoluted tubule**: coiled tube where **glucose** and some water and ions are **selectively reabsorbed**
**Loop of Henle**: a long loop dipping deep into the kidney; helps the kidney reabsorb **water** and make concentrated urine
**Second (distal) convoluted tubule**: further reabsorption of ions and water
**Collecting duct**: collects fluid from many nephrons; **water** is reabsorbed here (amount controlled by ADH), then urine passes to the ureter
Blood capillaries wrap around the tubules so reabsorbed substances can pass straight back into the blood

callouts.p: Glomerulus and Bowman's capsule, first convoluted tubule, loop of Henle, second convoluted tubule, collecting duct, ureter.

core.p: Filtration (often called **ultrafiltration**) happens because blood in the glomerulus is under **high pressure**. The blood vessel taking blood into the glomerulus is wider than the vessel taking blood out, so blood is squeezed and small molecules are forced out through the capillary wall into the Bowman's capsule.
bullets: High pressure forces **small molecules** out of the blood: **water, glucose, urea and mineral ions**
The liquid in the Bowman's capsule is called the **filtrate**
**Large molecules** (plasma **proteins**) and **blood cells** are too big to pass through, so they **stay in the blood**
Filtration is **not selective**: useful glucose is filtered out along with waste urea, which is why reabsorption is needed next
Thin capillary walls and the thin wall of the capsule give a short distance for filtration

callouts.p: The fluid that passes from the blood in the glomerulus into the Bowman's capsule: water, glucose, urea and mineral ions, but no proteins or blood cells.
For the mark say proteins and blood cells are too large to be filtered, not just that they are not filtered.

core.h: Why filtration depends on molecule size
core.p: The filter acts like a sieve with tiny gaps. Only molecules smaller than the gaps can be pushed through by the pressure.
bullets: Small: water, glucose, urea, ions, so they **pass into the filtrate**
Large: proteins, red and white blood cells, platelets, so they **remain in the blood**
Protein in urine is a sign that the glomerulus is **damaged** (the filter has holes that are too big)
Blood leaving the glomerulus is more concentrated in proteins because water has been removed

fig.cap: Filtration in the glomerulus: high blood pressure pushes small molecules (water, glucose, urea, ions) through the filtration barrier into the Bowman's capsule, while red blood cells and proteins are too large and stay in the blood.

core.p: The body cannot afford to lose glucose, which is needed for respiration. So in the **first convoluted tubule** **all of the glucose** is taken back into the blood. This is **selective** because only useful substances are reabsorbed, and urea is left behind.
bullets: **All glucose** is reabsorbed in the first convoluted tubule (in a healthy person)
Glucose is reabsorbed by **active transport**, which moves it **against a concentration gradient**
Active transport needs **energy from respiration**, so tubule cells contain **many mitochondria**
Tubule cells have **microvilli** (folded membranes) giving a **large surface area** for reabsorption
The tubule is close to blood capillaries, giving a short distance back into the blood
Healthy urine contains **no glucose**

callouts.p: The reabsorption of useful substances (all the glucose, and some water and mineral ions) from the filtrate back into the blood, while waste such as urea is left to form urine.
As glucose is reabsorbed its concentration in the filtrate falls below that in the blood, so to take back the last of it the cells must pump it against the concentration gradient using energy.

core.h: Stage 3: Reabsorption of water and ions
core.p: Around 99% of the water filtered is reabsorbed. Water moves back into the blood by **osmosis**, along the tubule, the loop of Henle and the **collecting duct**. Mineral ions are reabsorbed according to what the body needs.
bullets: **Water** is reabsorbed by **osmosis** in the first convoluted tubule, loop of Henle and collecting duct
The **loop of Henle** makes the tissue around the collecting duct very salty (low water potential), so water is drawn out of the collecting duct by osmosis
The amount of water reabsorbed in the **collecting duct** depends on the body's needs (controlled by the hormone ADH, see 7.20B)
**Mineral ions** (e.g. sodium) are reabsorbed as needed, partly by active transport; excess ions stay in the urine
Reabsorbing water means the body does not dehydrate even though about 180 litres of filtrate are made each day

callouts.p: Glucose: active transport. Water: osmosis. Do not swap them.

core.p: Urea is filtered out of the blood in the glomerulus, but it is **not selectively reabsorbed**. As water is reabsorbed, the urea left in the tubule becomes **more concentrated**.
bullets: Urea passes into the filtrate because it is a small molecule
There is no active transport system to take urea back, so most of it stays in the tubule
Urea concentration in urine is much higher than in blood plasma because water has been removed
Blood in the renal vein has a lower urea concentration than blood in the renal artery

core.p: A favourite exam question gives a table of concentrations and asks you to explain the differences. Use the two processes: filtration (size decides) and reabsorption (usefulness decides).
bullets: Protein: in plasma, **not** in filtrate (too large to be filtered)
Glucose: in plasma and filtrate at the **same concentration** (small, filtered freely), **none in urine** (all reabsorbed)
Urea: in filtrate at same concentration as plasma; **much higher in urine** (water reabsorbed, urea not)
Water and ions: filtered, then **some** reabsorbed depending on the body's needs

core.p: Grade 9 answers link each feature to the job it does.
bullets: **Glomerulus** has many capillaries and blood under **high pressure**, so filtration is fast
**Bowman's capsule** is cup-shaped and surrounds the glomerulus, so all filtrate is collected
**Convoluted** (coiled) tubules are long, giving more **time and surface area** for reabsorption
Tubule cells have **microvilli** (large surface area) and **many mitochondria** (energy for active transport of glucose)
Dense **capillary network** around the tubule keeps a concentration gradient and carries reabsorbed substances away
**Loop of Henle** is long in animals that need to save water (e.g. desert mammals), allowing more water reabsorption
**Collecting duct** passes through salty tissue, so water can be drawn out by osmosis

callouts.p: Always pair the feature with its consequence: many mitochondria (1) to release energy for active transport of glucose (1).

core.h: Signs in urine and what they mean
core.p: Testing urine tells doctors whether the nephrons are working properly.
bullets: **Glucose in urine**: blood glucose is so high that the reabsorption carriers cannot take it all back, a sign of **diabetes**
**Protein in urine**: the glomerulus filter is damaged (kidney disease)
**Dark, concentrated urine**: the body is short of water so more is reabsorbed
**Pale, dilute urine**: excess water is being removed

core.h: Putting it together: the journey of a urea molecule
core.p: Following one molecule through the system is a great way to plan a 6-mark answer.
bullets: Made in the liver from excess amino acids
Carried in blood plasma to the kidney in the **renal artery**
Forced out of the glomerulus into the **Bowman's capsule** by high pressure (filtration)
Passes along the convoluted tubules and loop of Henle without being reabsorbed
Becomes concentrated as water is reabsorbed in the **collecting duct**
Leaves in urine via the **ureter** to the **bladder**, where it is stored, then out through the **urethra**

fig.cap: The urinary system. Blood with urea arrives in the renal artery, is filtered in the kidney and leaves in the renal vein. Urine flows down each ureter to the bladder, where it is stored, and leaves through the urethra.

analogy.t: Clearing out your bedroom by emptying everything onto the landing
analogy.p: Imagine tipping every small item from your room into a box on the landing (filtration: everything small enough goes, useful or not; the furniture is too big to move and stays put, like proteins and blood cells). You then go through the box and carry back everything you want, especially your phone (glucose, all of it reclaimed, with effort, like active transport). What is left in the box (rubbish, like urea) goes to the bin (urine). Where it breaks down: the kidney does not decide item by item what it wants; reabsorption depends on carrier proteins and osmosis, and the amount of water taken back is set by hormones, not by choice. Also filtration happens continuously, not in one go.

terms.d: Waste product made in the liver from excess amino acids; removed by the kidneys in urine.
Removal of waste products of metabolism from the body.
Organ that filters blood, removing urea, excess water and excess ions to form urine.
Blood vessel carrying blood containing urea to the kidney.
Blood vessel carrying filtered blood away from the kidney.
Tube carrying urine from a kidney to the bladder.
Muscular organ that stores urine.
Tube carrying urine from the bladder to outside the body.
Kidney tubule; the functional unit of the kidney where blood is filtered and urine is made.
Knot of capillaries in the Bowman's capsule where blood is filtered under high pressure.
Cup-shaped start of the nephron surrounding the glomerulus that collects the filtrate.
Small molecules (water, glucose, urea, ions) forced out of the blood into the Bowman's capsule by high pressure.
Fluid in the nephron formed by filtration; contains no proteins or blood cells.
Taking useful substances (all glucose, some water and ions) from the filtrate back into the blood.
Coiled part of the nephron where reabsorption takes place; the first one reabsorbs all the glucose.
Loop of the nephron that helps reabsorb water so that concentrated urine can be produced.
Final tube of the nephron where water is reabsorbed by osmosis and urine passes to the ureter.
Movement of substances against a concentration gradient using energy from respiration.

mistakes.w: The kidney filters out the glucose and it leaves in urine.
mistakes.r: Glucose is filtered but all of it is reabsorbed in the first convoluted tubule, so healthy urine has no glucose.

mistakes.w: Proteins are filtered then reabsorbed.
mistakes.r: Proteins are too large to be filtered, so they never enter the filtrate.

mistakes.w: Glucose is reabsorbed by diffusion.
mistakes.r: Glucose is reabsorbed by active transport, against a concentration gradient, using energy from respiration.

mistakes.w: Water is reabsorbed by active transport.
mistakes.r: Water is reabsorbed by osmosis.

mistakes.w: Urine travels from the kidney to the bladder in the urethra.
mistakes.r: The ureter carries urine from kidney to bladder; the urethra carries it from the bladder out of the body.

mistakes.w: The kidneys make urea.
mistakes.r: Urea is made in the liver; the kidneys remove it from the blood.

mistakes.w: Filtration is selective.
mistakes.r: Filtration depends only on size; selective reabsorption is the step that picks out useful substances.

mistakes.w: Urea is reabsorbed along with glucose.
mistakes.r: Urea is not reabsorbed (selectively); it becomes more concentrated as water is reabsorbed.

mistakes.w: Blood is filtered in the collecting duct.
mistakes.r: Filtration happens in the glomerulus into the Bowman's capsule; the collecting duct reabsorbs water.

exam.q: Name the tube that carries urine from the kidney to the bladder.
model: Ureter
exam.tip: Spell it clearly: ureter, not urethra.

exam.q: Name the part of the nephron where blood is filtered.
model: Glomerulus (and Bowman's capsule)
exam.tip: Glomerulus is the capillary knot; the capsule collects the filtrate.

exam.q: Explain why protein is not found in the filtrate in the Bowman's capsule.
model: Protein molecules are too large
so cannot pass through the capillary wall / filter into the Bowman's capsule
exam.tip: Size is the key idea for filtration.

exam.q: Name one substance found in the glomerular filtrate that is not found in the urine of a healthy person.
model: Glucose (accept amino acids)
exam.tip: Protein is wrong: it is never in the filtrate in the first place.

exam.q: Explain how glucose is reabsorbed in the nephron.
model: In the first / proximal convoluted tubule
by active transport
against a concentration gradient, using energy (from respiration)
exam.tip: Location, method and energy: one mark each.

exam.q: Cells lining the first convoluted tubule contain many mitochondria. Explain why.
model: Mitochondria carry out (aerobic) respiration to release energy
energy is needed for active transport of glucose back into the blood
exam.tip: Link mitochondria to energy, then energy to active transport.

exam.q: The concentration of urea in urine is much higher than in the filtrate. Explain why.
model: Water is reabsorbed (from the tubule / collecting duct) by osmosis
urea is not reabsorbed, so the same amount of urea is in less water
exam.tip: You need both halves: water out, urea stays.

exam.q: A urine test shows glucose in a person's urine. Suggest what this indicates and explain why.
model: The person may have diabetes / high blood glucose
too much glucose is filtered for all of it to be reabsorbed (carriers saturated)
exam.tip: Suggest = apply knowledge to a new situation.

exam.q: Describe the role of the bladder and urethra.
model: Bladder stores urine
urethra carries urine out of the body
exam.tip: One function for each structure.

exam.q: Explain how the structure of the nephron is related to its function in filtering the blood and forming urine.
model: Blood enters the glomerulus under high pressure
small molecules such as water, glucose, urea and ions are forced into the Bowman's capsule (filtration)
proteins and blood cells are too large and remain in the blood
in the first convoluted tubule all glucose is reabsorbed by active transport
tubule cells have many mitochondria / microvilli for energy / large surface area
water is reabsorbed by osmosis in the loop of Henle and collecting duct
urea is not reabsorbed so it stays in the urine, which passes to the ureter
exam.tip: Work through the nephron in order and give a structure-function link at each stage.

worked.q: The kidneys produce 180 dm3 of filtrate a day and 1.5 dm3 of urine. Calculate the percentage of filtered water that is reabsorbed (assume filtrate and urine are almost all water).
steps: Volume reabsorbed = 180 - 1.5 = 178.5 dm3
Percentage reabsorbed = (178.5 / 180) x 100
worked.ans: About 99.2% of the filtered water is reabsorbed.

worked.q: Glucose concentration is 1.0 g/dm3 in blood plasma, 1.0 g/dm3 in the filtrate and 0 g/dm3 in urine. Urea is 0.3 g/dm3 in plasma, 0.3 g/dm3 in filtrate and 20 g/dm3 in urine. Explain these figures.
steps: Glucose and urea are small molecules, so they are filtered freely: concentration in filtrate equals plasma
All glucose is reabsorbed by active transport in the first convoluted tubule, so urine has 0 g/dm3
Urea is not reabsorbed while about 99% of water is, so urea becomes concentrated
Concentration factor for urea = 20 / 0.3 = about 67 times
worked.ans: Filtration is by size, so filtrate matches plasma; selective reabsorption removes all glucose, while removal of water concentrates urea about 67 times.

worked.q: Suggest why desert mammals such as kangaroo rats have very long loops of Henle.
steps: A longer loop of Henle makes the tissue around the collecting duct saltier
This gives a steeper water potential gradient
So more water is reabsorbed from the collecting duct by osmosis
Very concentrated urine is produced and water is conserved
worked.ans: A long loop of Henle allows more water to be reabsorbed, producing small volumes of concentrated urine so the animal conserves water in a dry habitat.

svg.cap: Structure of a nephron. Blood is filtered from the glomerulus into the Bowman's capsule; glucose is reabsorbed in the first convoluted tubule; the loop of Henle and second convoluted tubule follow; water is reabsorbed from the collecting duct, which carries urine to the ureter.

bio_edx.6.12.summary: The water content of the blood is kept within a narrow range by **negative feedback** using the hormone **ADH (antidiuretic hormone)**. The **hypothalamus** detects the water level of the blood and the **pituitary gland** releases ADH into the blood. ADH makes the **collecting ducts** of the kidney nephrons **more permeable to water**, so more water is reabsorbed into the blood by **osmosis** and a **smaller volume of more concentrated urine** is produced; when there is too much water, less ADH is released and lots of dilute urine is made.

core.h: Why water content must be controlled
core.p: Controlling blood water is part of **homeostasis**. If the blood plasma becomes too concentrated or too dilute, water moves into or out of cells by **osmosis** and cells stop working properly.
bullets: Blood too **dilute** (too much water): water enters cells by osmosis, cells **swell** and may burst (animal cells have no cell wall)
Blood too **concentrated** (too little water): water leaves cells by osmosis, cells **shrink** and their reactions slow
Enzymes and cell processes need a steady concentration of water and ions
The **kidneys** are the effectors that adjust how much water is lost in urine

callouts.p: Every explanation of why water balance matters comes back to osmosis: net movement of water from a dilute solution to a more concentrated solution across a partially permeable membrane.

core.p: The body is always gaining and losing water. The kidneys are the only route that the body can adjust precisely to balance the books.
bullets: Water gained: **drinks**, **food**, and water made by **respiration**
Water lost: **urine**, **sweat**, **breathing out** (exhaled air) and **faeces**
We cannot control water lost in breath, and sweating is controlled for temperature, not water balance
So the volume and concentration of **urine** is altered to keep blood water constant

core.p: **ADH** stands for **antidiuretic hormone**. Diuresis means producing lots of urine, so an antidiuretic hormone **reduces** urine volume.
bullets: Made in the **hypothalamus** and released by the **pituitary gland** in the brain
Travels in the **blood plasma** (like all hormones) to its target organ
Target organ: the **kidneys**; target tissue: the **collecting ducts** of the nephrons
Effect: increases the **permeability** of the collecting duct to **water**
More ADH means less urine; less ADH means more urine

callouts.p: Antidiuretic hormone, released by the pituitary gland, which increases the permeability of the collecting duct to water so that more water is reabsorbed into the blood.

fig.cap: The pathway of control: the hypothalamus detects the water content of the blood, the pituitary gland releases ADH into the blood, and the ADH travels to its target, the collecting ducts in the kidneys.

core.p: The **hypothalamus** in the brain contains receptors that monitor the **water content (concentration)** of the blood flowing through it. It is the same control centre that controls body temperature.
bullets: Receptor and coordinator: hypothalamus
If blood water content is **too low** it signals the pituitary to release **more ADH**
If blood water content is **too high** it signals the pituitary to release **less ADH**
The pituitary gland sits just below the hypothalamus

core.h: How ADH acts on the collecting duct
core.p: The collecting duct passes through very salty tissue deep in the kidney, so the fluid around it has a lower water concentration than the urine inside. Water will leave the duct by **osmosis** only if the duct wall lets it through. **ADH controls how permeable that wall is.**
bullets: **High ADH**: collecting duct walls become **more permeable** to water
More water moves **out of the collecting duct by osmosis** and back into the blood
Result: **small volume** of **concentrated** urine
**Low ADH**: collecting duct walls are **less permeable**
Less water is reabsorbed, so a **large volume** of **dilute** urine is produced
ADH does not change filtration or glucose reabsorption; it only affects water reabsorption in the collecting duct

callouts.p: Mark schemes reward 'makes the collecting duct more permeable to water'. Writing 'ADH absorbs water' or 'ADH reabsorbs water' scores nothing.
ADH is a chemical messenger; water is reabsorbed by osmosis. ADH only opens the door.

fig.cap: Effect of ADH on the collecting duct. With low ADH the duct wall is less permeable, little water moves into the blood by osmosis and a large volume of dilute urine is made. With high ADH the wall is more permeable, much more water is reabsorbed and a small volume of concentrated urine is made.

core.p: After exercise, on a hot day, after salty food or when you have not drunk enough, the blood water content falls.
bullets: Blood water content **falls** (blood becomes more concentrated)
Detected by the **hypothalamus**
**Pituitary gland releases more ADH** into the blood
ADH travels to the kidneys and makes the **collecting ducts more permeable** to water
**More water is reabsorbed** into the blood by osmosis
**Small volume of concentrated** (dark) urine
Blood water content **rises back to normal**; you may also feel thirsty

fig.cap: The negative feedback loop for dehydration. A fall in blood water content is detected by the hypothalamus, more ADH is released by the pituitary, the collecting ducts become more permeable, more water is reabsorbed and the blood water content returns to normal, which then reduces ADH release.

core.h: When you have drunk too much water
core.p: The opposite chain of events happens when the blood has too much water.
bullets: Blood water content **rises** (blood becomes more dilute)
Detected by the **hypothalamus**
**Pituitary gland releases less ADH**
**Collecting ducts become less permeable** to water
**Less water is reabsorbed** into the blood
**Large volume of dilute** (pale) urine
Blood water content **falls back to normal**

core.p: Water control is a classic example of **negative feedback**: a change away from the normal level causes a response that **reverses** the change.
bullets: The response is proportional to the change: the further from normal, the more (or less) ADH
Once blood water is back to normal, the hypothalamus **reduces the change** in ADH release
This stops the system overshooting
Parts: stimulus (change in water content), receptor (hypothalamus), gland (pituitary), hormone (ADH), effector (collecting ducts of kidney), response (change in water reabsorbed)

callouts.p: A control mechanism in which a change from the normal level triggers a response that brings the level back towards normal.

core.p: Exam questions often show urine flow after a person drinks a large volume of water.
bullets: Urine flow rises after about 30 minutes as water is absorbed from the gut into the blood
Blood becomes more dilute, so **less ADH** is released
Collecting ducts become less permeable, so **more, dilute urine** is produced: the peak
As excess water is removed, blood water returns to normal, ADH rises again and urine flow falls back
Drinking a salty solution would cause **more ADH** and little change in urine volume

fig.cap: Typical results for urine flow after drinking 1 dm3 of water compared with no drink. Urine flow peaks about an hour after drinking, when ADH release is lowest, then returns to normal by negative feedback.
