core.p: Many everyday situations alter how much ADH the pituitary releases.
bullets: **Exercise and hot weather**: water lost in sweat, so more ADH
**Salty food**: blood becomes more concentrated, so more ADH
**Drinking lots of water**: blood more dilute, so less ADH
**Alcohol** reduces ADH release, so more dilute urine is made, which can cause dehydration
If the pituitary cannot make enough ADH, a person produces very large volumes of dilute urine and becomes dehydrated easily

callouts.p: For any 'suggest' question, first decide whether the blood will become more or less concentrated, then follow the chain: ADH, permeability, water reabsorbed, urine.

core.p: Volume and concentration change in opposite directions.
bullets: The kidneys still have to remove the same amount of **urea**
If less water is lost, the same urea is in less water, so urine is **more concentrated**
If more water is lost, urine is **more dilute**
Colour is a quick clue: dark yellow urine means high ADH; pale urine means low ADH

analogy.t: ADH is the key to a leaky hosepipe
analogy.p: Picture the collecting duct as a hosepipe running through a dry garden (the salty tissue). The garden would love to soak up water. ADH is like a key that unlocks small holes along the hose: more ADH, more holes open, more water soaks into the garden (blood) and only a little trickles out of the end (concentrated urine). Little ADH, the holes stay shut and most water gushes out of the end (dilute urine). Where it breaks down: the holes are not physical punctures; the duct wall becomes more permeable, and water still moves only because of osmosis, never by being pushed.

terms.d: Maintaining a constant internal environment, such as blood water content.
Antidiuretic hormone: increases the permeability of the collecting duct to water.
Reducing the volume of urine produced.
Part of the brain that detects the water content of the blood.
Gland at the base of the brain that releases ADH into the blood.
Organ a hormone acts on; for ADH, the kidneys.
Last part of the nephron, where the amount of water reabsorbed is controlled by ADH.
How easily a substance, such as water, can pass through a membrane or wall.
Net movement of water from a dilute solution to a more concentrated solution through a partially permeable membrane.
Taking substances from the fluid in the nephron back into the blood.
A change from normal triggers a response that returns conditions to normal.
Condition in which the body has lost too much water and blood water content is too low.
Small volume of urine with a high concentration of urea and ions, made when ADH is high.
Large volume of urine with a low concentration of solutes, made when ADH is low.
Organ that brings about a response; for water balance, the kidneys.

mistakes.w: ADH absorbs water from the urine.
mistakes.r: ADH makes the collecting duct more permeable to water, so more water is reabsorbed by osmosis.

mistakes.w: When dehydrated, less ADH is released.
mistakes.r: When dehydrated, more ADH is released so more water is reabsorbed.

mistakes.w: ADH is released by the kidneys.
mistakes.r: ADH is released by the pituitary gland; the kidneys are its target organ.

mistakes.w: ADH makes the kidney filter less blood.
mistakes.r: ADH acts on the collecting duct and changes water reabsorption, not filtration.

mistakes.w: ADH travels along nerves to the kidney.
mistakes.r: ADH is a hormone carried in the blood plasma.

mistakes.w: The brain detects it.
mistakes.r: Name the hypothalamus as the part that detects the blood water content.

mistakes.w: More ADH makes a large volume of concentrated urine.
mistakes.r: More ADH makes a small volume of concentrated urine.

mistakes.w: Water is actively transported out of the collecting duct.
mistakes.r: Water moves out by osmosis.

exam.q: Name the gland that releases ADH.
model: Pituitary gland
exam.tip: Not the hypothalamus, which detects the change.

exam.q: Name the part of the nephron that ADH acts on.
model: Collecting duct
exam.tip: Be precise: 'kidney' alone may not score when the nephron part is asked for.

exam.q: State how ADH travels from the gland to its target organ.
model: In the blood (plasma)
exam.tip: All hormones travel in the blood.

exam.q: Describe the effect of ADH on the collecting duct.
model: Makes the collecting duct more permeable to water
so more water is reabsorbed (into the blood)
exam.tip: Permeability first, then consequence.

exam.q: Explain why a person's urine is darker in colour after running a marathon on a hot day.
model: Water lost in sweat so blood water content falls
detected by the hypothalamus; pituitary releases more ADH
collecting ducts become more permeable so more water reabsorbed by osmosis
small volume of concentrated urine (more concentrated urea gives darker colour)
exam.tip: Follow the whole chain from stimulus to urine.

exam.q: A student drinks 1 dm3 of water. Explain the change in the volume of urine produced over the next hour.
model: Blood water content rises / blood more dilute
hypothalamus detects; less ADH released by the pituitary
collecting ducts less permeable to water so less water reabsorbed
large volume of dilute urine produced
exam.tip: Mirror image of the dehydration answer.

exam.q: Explain why the control of water content of the blood is an example of negative feedback.
model: A change in blood water content from normal
causes a response that reverses the change / returns it to normal
exam.tip: Say what is reversed.

exam.q: Alcohol reduces the release of ADH. Suggest why drinking alcohol can lead to dehydration.
model: Less ADH in the blood
collecting ducts less permeable so less water reabsorbed
large volume of dilute urine; more water lost from the body
exam.tip: Suggest questions reward applying the ADH chain to a new situation.

exam.q: Explain why it is important to control the water content of the blood.
model: If blood too dilute water enters cells by osmosis and they swell / burst
if blood too concentrated water leaves cells by osmosis and they shrink
exam.tip: Mention osmosis and the effect on cells.

exam.q: Explain how the body responds when the water content of the blood is too low, and how this response is controlled.
model: Hypothalamus detects low water content
pituitary gland releases more ADH
ADH carried in the blood to the kidneys
collecting ducts become more permeable to water
more water reabsorbed into the blood by osmosis
small volume of concentrated urine
water content returns to normal; ADH release reduced (negative feedback)
exam.tip: Use the full sequence and finish with the feedback step for top marks.

worked.q: A person's urine output was 1.8 dm3 per day in cool weather and 0.9 dm3 per day during a heatwave. Calculate the percentage decrease and explain it.
steps: Decrease = 1.8 - 0.9 = 0.9 dm3
Percentage decrease = (0.9 / 1.8) x 100 = 50%
In the heatwave more water is lost in sweat, so blood water content falls
More ADH is released, collecting ducts become more permeable and more water is reabsorbed
worked.ans: Urine output fell by 50% because more ADH was released, so more water was reabsorbed from the collecting ducts.

worked.q: Use the urine flow graph: flow is 1 cm3 per min at 0 min and 9 cm3 per min at 60 min after drinking 1 dm3 of water. Calculate the increase and explain the shape of the curve.
steps: Increase = 9 - 1 = 8 cm3 per min (9 times the starting rate)
Water absorbed from gut makes the blood more dilute
Hypothalamus detects this; less ADH released; collecting ducts less permeable
More, dilute urine produced, so flow peaks
Excess water removed, ADH returns to normal and flow falls back to about 1 cm3 per min by 180 min
worked.ans: Flow rose by 8 cm3 per min because low ADH reduced water reabsorption; it fell again as negative feedback restored normal ADH levels.

worked.q: Model answer: compare the urine of a person who has eaten a very salty meal with that of a person who has drunk a lot of water.
steps: Salty meal: blood more concentrated, so more ADH released
Collecting ducts more permeable, more water reabsorbed
Small volume, concentrated urine
Lots of water: blood more dilute, less ADH, ducts less permeable
Large volume, dilute urine
worked.ans: The salty-meal person makes a small volume of concentrated urine (high ADH); the water drinker makes a large volume of dilute urine (low ADH).

bio_edx.6.13.summary: When the kidneys fail, urea, excess water and excess ions build up in the blood and the person will die without treatment. There are two main treatments: **kidney dialysis**, where blood passes over a **partially permeable membrane** and urea and excess ions **diffuse** into **dialysis fluid**, and a **kidney transplant** from an organ donor. Dialysis must be repeated several times a week, while a transplant can give a near-normal life but carries the risk of **rejection**, so the patient must take **immunosuppressant drugs**.

core.p: Kidney failure means the kidneys can no longer filter the blood properly. Waste and water are not removed, so the composition of the blood is no longer controlled.
bullets: **Urea** builds up in the blood and becomes toxic
**Excess water** is not removed, so body fluids build up (swelling) and blood pressure can rise
**Mineral ion** concentrations go out of balance, which affects the heart and cells
Water moves into or out of cells by osmosis, damaging them
Causes include infection, damage from diabetes or high blood pressure, and inherited conditions
Without treatment, total kidney failure leads to death

callouts.p: Edexcel requires you to describe both: kidney dialysis and a kidney transplant (organ donation).

core.p: In **haemodialysis** the patient's blood is taken from a blood vessel in the arm, pumped through a dialysis machine and returned to a vein. The machine does the kidney's job of removing urea and balancing water and ions.
bullets: Blood flows through very thin tubes made of a **partially permeable membrane**
The tubes are surrounded by **dialysis fluid**
**Urea** and excess **mineral ions** **diffuse** out of the blood, through the membrane, into the dialysis fluid
Excess **water** is also removed
**Blood cells and proteins** are **too large** to cross the membrane, so they stay in the blood
A **bubble trap** removes air bubbles before the blood returns to the body
**Heparin** (an anticoagulant) is added to stop the blood clotting in the machine
Fluid is kept at body temperature (about 37 C) so the blood is not cooled

callouts.p: A treatment for kidney failure in which blood flows past a partially permeable membrane so that urea and excess substances diffuse out of the blood into dialysis fluid.

fig.cap: A dialysis machine. Blood is pumped from the arm through partially permeable tubing in the dialyser, where urea diffuses into the dialysis fluid. Fresh fluid flows in the opposite direction to the blood, used fluid is removed, and a bubble trap removes air before the blood returns to a vein.

core.h: What is in dialysis fluid and why
core.p: The dialysis fluid is carefully made so that only the right substances leave the blood. The key is to compare its concentration with normal blood plasma.
bullets: It contains **glucose** at the **same concentration** as normal blood plasma, so there is **no net diffusion** of glucose and none is lost
It contains **mineral ions** at the **same concentration as normal blood**, so only **excess** ions diffuse out of the patient's blood
It contains **no urea**, so there is a steep **concentration gradient** and urea diffuses out of the blood
It contains no blood cells or proteins (these cannot cross the membrane anyway)

head: Substance
In dialysis fluid
Result
rows: Too large to cross; stay in blood

callouts.p: Explaining why glucose is not lost is a common 2 mark question: it is at the same concentration on both sides, so there is no concentration gradient.

core.p: Diffusion only continues while there is a difference in concentration. The machine is designed to keep the gradient as steep as possible.
bullets: Dialysis fluid flows in the **opposite direction** to the blood (**countercurrent flow**)
This keeps a concentration gradient for urea along the **whole length** of the membrane
Used fluid is constantly removed and replaced with **fresh fluid**, so urea does not build up in the fluid
Long, thin, coiled tubes give a **large surface area** and a **thin membrane** gives a short diffusion distance

callouts.p: If fluid and blood flowed the same way, their urea concentrations would soon become equal and diffusion would stop part way along.

fig.cap: Close-up of the membrane in a dialysis machine. Urea diffuses from the blood, which has a high urea concentration, through the partially permeable membrane into dialysis fluid that contains no urea. Cells and proteins are too large to cross. Glucose and ions are at normal blood levels in the fluid so there is no net loss of them.

core.p: Dialysis keeps a person alive, but it is not a cure and it has big effects on daily life.
bullets: Sessions last about **3 to 4 hours**, usually **three times a week**
Often done in hospital, though some patients have a machine at home
Between sessions urea and fluid **build up** again, so patients must **control their diet**: limit salt, protein and fluid intake
Patients may feel unwell as waste builds up before each session
Risks include **infection** at the needle site and **blood clots**
Dialysis is **expensive** for the health service over many years
It is often used while a patient **waits for a transplant**

fig.cap: Typical blood urea concentration for a patient having dialysis on Monday, Wednesday and Friday. Urea rises steadily between sessions and falls sharply during each dialysis session; it reaches its highest level after the longer gap over the weekend.

core.p: A second type of dialysis uses the lining of the patient's own abdomen as the partially permeable membrane.
bullets: Dialysis fluid is put into the abdomen through a tube
Urea and excess ions diffuse from blood capillaries into the fluid
The used fluid is drained and replaced several times a day
It can be done at home and lets the patient move around, but carries a risk of infection

core.p: A **kidney transplant** replaces the failed kidneys with a healthy kidney from a **donor**. A person needs only **one** working kidney to live normally.
bullets: Donors may be **living** (often a close relative, who can give one of their two kidneys) or people who have **died**, such as after an accident
The donor kidney is placed in the patient's lower abdomen and joined to an **artery**, a **vein** and the **bladder**
The patient's own failed kidneys are often left in place
If successful, the new kidney filters blood **all the time**, so the patient no longer needs dialysis
Patients can lead a more normal life with fewer diet restrictions

callouts.p: Giving an organ, such as a kidney, to be transplanted into another person who needs it.

core.h: Rejection and how it is prevented
core.p: The main problem with a transplant is **rejection**. Cells of the donor kidney have **antigens** on their surface that differ from the patient's own, so the patient's **immune system** recognises the kidney as foreign.
bullets: **White blood cells** (lymphocytes) attack the foreign kidney, which can make it fail
To reduce rejection, the donor's **tissue type** (antigens) and **blood group** are **matched** as closely as possible to the patient's
Close relatives are more likely to be a good tissue match
The patient must take **immunosuppressant drugs** for the rest of their life
Immunosuppressants **suppress the immune system**, so the patient is more likely to get **infections**
Even with matching and drugs, a transplanted kidney may eventually fail and need replacing

callouts.p: Rejection is reduced by immunosuppressant drugs, not antibiotics. Antibiotics kill bacteria.

core.p: There are far more people needing kidneys than there are donor kidneys available.
bullets: Patients may wait **years** on a waiting list, needing dialysis meanwhile
A kidney must be a **good tissue match**, which limits which donors can be used
Many people have not registered their wishes about donation
England, Wales and Scotland now use an **opt-out** system: adults are considered donors unless they have said they do not want to donate
Living donors face the risks of a major operation

core.p: Evaluation questions ask you to weigh up the two treatments. Give advantages and disadvantages of each, then reach a judgement.
bullets: Transplant is usually the **better long-term** option if a matched kidney is available
Dialysis is available **straight away** and does not need a donor
Dialysis is more **expensive over time**; a transplant has a high one-off cost plus drugs
A judgement should consider the patient's health, availability of a donor and quality of life

head: Dialysis
Transplant
rows: About 3 sessions a week, 3 to 4 hours
Strict control of salt, protein, fluid
Infection, blood clots, urea build-up between sessions

callouts.p: A 6 mark evaluate answer needs points for both sides and a justified conclusion, for example: a transplant is better because it removes the need for regular dialysis, provided a matched kidney is available.

core.h: Linking back to the healthy kidney
core.p: Dialysis copies only part of what a nephron does, which helps explain its limits.
bullets: A nephron **filters** blood then **selectively reabsorbs** useful substances; dialysis instead stops useful substances leaving by having them in the fluid at normal concentrations
A healthy kidney works **continuously**; dialysis is intermittent, so urea levels rise and fall
A healthy kidney responds to **ADH** to fine-tune water balance; dialysis cannot respond to hormones in the same way
A transplanted kidney restores all of these functions

analogy.t: Dialysis is like a tea bag in reverse
analogy.p: A tea bag is a partially permeable bag: small flavour molecules diffuse out into the water but the tea leaves stay inside. In dialysis, the blood is in the bag (tubing) and small urea molecules diffuse out into the surrounding fluid while big blood cells and proteins stay in. Keep pouring away the tea and adding fresh water, and flavour keeps leaving: that is like replacing the dialysis fluid to keep the concentration gradient. Where it breaks down: in tea everything small leaves, but in dialysis the fluid already contains glucose and ions at normal blood levels so those are kept, and the blood keeps moving rather than sitting still.

terms.d: When the kidneys cannot filter the blood, so urea, water and ions build up.
Treatment where blood passes over a partially permeable membrane so urea and excess substances diffuse into dialysis fluid.
Liquid with the same glucose and ion concentrations as normal blood plasma but no urea.
Membrane that lets small molecules such as urea through but not large ones such as proteins.
Net movement of particles from an area of higher concentration to an area of lower concentration.
Difference in concentration between two areas; needed for diffusion.
Blood and dialysis fluid flowing in opposite directions to keep a gradient along the whole membrane.
Anticoagulant added to blood during dialysis to stop it clotting.
Surgery to replace failed kidneys with a healthy donor kidney.
Living or dead person who provides an organ for transplant.
Molecule on the surface of cells that the immune system recognises.
The recipient's immune system attacking a transplanted organ because it has foreign antigens.
Choosing a donor whose antigens and blood group are as similar as possible to the recipient's.
Drugs that suppress the immune system to reduce the risk of rejection.
System where people are treated as organ donors unless they have recorded that they do not wish to be.

mistakes.w: Dialysis fluid contains no glucose.
mistakes.r: Dialysis fluid contains glucose at the same concentration as normal blood, so no glucose is lost.

mistakes.w: Urea moves into the fluid by osmosis.
mistakes.r: Urea moves by diffusion down a concentration gradient; osmosis is only for water.

mistakes.w: Proteins and blood cells diffuse into the fluid.
mistakes.r: They are too large to pass through the partially permeable membrane.

mistakes.w: The patient takes antibiotics to stop rejection.
mistakes.r: Immunosuppressant drugs are taken to stop rejection.

mistakes.w: Immunosuppressants kill the antigens.
mistakes.r: They suppress the immune system so white blood cells are less likely to attack the donor kidney.

mistakes.w: The body rejects the kidney because it is too big.
mistakes.r: Rejection happens because the donor cells have different antigens, recognised as foreign by the immune system.

mistakes.w: Dialysis cures kidney failure.
mistakes.r: Dialysis must be repeated regularly; it does not cure the kidneys.

mistakes.w: You need two kidneys from a donor.
mistakes.r: One working kidney is enough, which is why living donors can give one.

mistakes.w: The fluid flows the same way to mix better.
mistakes.r: Fluid flows in the opposite direction (countercurrent) to maintain a concentration gradient.

exam.q: Name the process by which urea passes from the blood into the dialysis fluid.
model: Diffusion
exam.tip: Not osmosis and not active transport.

exam.q: Give one reason why the patient's blood proteins are not lost during dialysis.
model: Proteins are too large to pass through the (partially permeable) membrane
exam.tip: Size is the reason.

exam.q: Explain why the dialysis fluid contains glucose at the same concentration as normal blood plasma.
model: No concentration gradient for glucose
so no (net) glucose diffuses out of the blood / glucose is not lost
exam.tip: Use 'no net movement'.

exam.q: Explain why the dialysis fluid contains no urea.
model: Creates a (steep) concentration gradient
so urea diffuses from the blood into the fluid
exam.tip: Gradient then direction.

exam.q: Explain why the dialysis fluid flows in the opposite direction to the blood.
model: Maintains a concentration gradient (for urea)
along the whole length of the membrane / so more urea diffuses out
exam.tip: Countercurrent is the key word.

exam.q: State why a patient having a kidney transplant must take drugs for the rest of their life, and one disadvantage of these drugs.
model: Immunosuppressant drugs to stop the immune system rejecting the kidney
patient more likely to get infections
exam.tip: Name the drug type and its side effect.

exam.q: Explain why doctors try to use a kidney from a close relative for a transplant.
model: Relative's tissue type / antigens are more likely to be similar
so less risk of rejection by the immune system
exam.tip: Link similarity of antigens to rejection.

exam.q: Describe how a dialysis machine removes urea from the blood.
model: Blood taken from the patient and passed through the machine
blood flows through partially permeable tubing / membrane surrounded by dialysis fluid
fluid contains no urea, so urea diffuses from blood into the fluid
fluid is replaced / flows countercurrent to maintain the concentration gradient; blood returned to the body
exam.tip: Describe the route and the diffusion.

exam.q: Suggest why a patient on dialysis must limit the amount of protein and salt in their diet.
model: Excess protein / amino acids are converted to urea, which builds up between sessions
excess salt (ions) cannot be removed between sessions and affects water balance
exam.tip: Link to build-up between sessions.

exam.q: Evaluate the use of a kidney transplant rather than dialysis to treat kidney failure.
model: Transplant: no need for regular dialysis sessions / more normal life
transplant: fewer diet restrictions
transplant: cheaper in the long term
transplant: shortage of donors / long waiting lists; needs tissue match
transplant: risk of rejection; lifelong immunosuppressants increase infection risk; major surgery
dialysis: available without a donor / no rejection, but time consuming, restrictive and costly
conclusion: transplant is better long term if a matched kidney is available, dialysis used while waiting
exam.tip: Both sides plus a justified conclusion for level 3.

worked.q: A patient has 3 dialysis sessions a week, each lasting 4 hours. Calculate the total time spent on dialysis in a year (52 weeks).
steps: Time per week = 3 x 4 = 12 hours
Time per year = 12 x 52 = 624 hours
In days: 624 / 24 = 26 days
worked.ans: 624 hours, which is 26 whole days a year attached to the machine.

worked.q: The urea concentration in a patient's blood is 30 units before dialysis and 9 units after. Calculate the percentage decrease and explain why it rises again before the next session.
steps: Decrease = 30 - 9 = 21 units
Percentage decrease = (21 / 30) x 100 = 70%
Between sessions the liver keeps making urea from excess amino acids
With no working kidneys, the urea is not removed, so it builds up again
worked.ans: Urea falls by 70% during dialysis, then rises again because it is still produced but not excreted between sessions.

worked.q: Model answer: explain why a transplant patient is told to avoid people with infections.
steps: The patient takes immunosuppressant drugs to prevent rejection
These suppress the immune system / white blood cells
So the patient cannot fight pathogens as well
They are more likely to catch infections, which could be serious
worked.ans: Immunosuppressants weaken the immune system, so the patient is more vulnerable to infections.

bio_edx.6.2.summary: Thyroxine is a hormone made by the **thyroid gland** in the neck that raises the **metabolic rate** (the rate of the chemical reactions in cells, such as respiration). Its level is kept steady by **negative feedback**: when thyroxine is low the **hypothalamus** releases **TRH**, which makes the **pituitary gland** release **TSH**, which makes the thyroid release more thyroxine; when thyroxine is back to normal (or high) it **inhibits** the release of TRH and TSH. This point is **Higher tier only** (spec 7.3H) and is the classic Edexcel example of negative feedback.

core.p: You must be able to **explain how thyroxine controls metabolic rate as an example of negative feedback**. Edexcel spells out the chain you must give: low thyroxine stimulates **TRH** production in the **hypothalamus**, TRH causes release of **TSH** from the **pituitary gland**, TSH acts on the **thyroid** to produce **thyroxine**, and when thyroxine levels are normal thyroxine **inhibits the release of TRH and the production of TSH**.
bullets: This is **Higher tier only** content, on Paper 2 (Topic 7).
Two hormones are made by the brain (TRH and TSH) and one by the thyroid (thyroxine).
Most marks come from putting the **gland, hormone and effect in the right order**.
The word **negative feedback** must appear in a good answer, with what it means: a change triggers a response that **reverses** the change.
Links to 7.1 (endocrine glands), 7.9 (homeostasis) and 7.13 (insulin and glucagon, another negative feedback system).

callouts.p: Low thyroxine -> hypothalamus releases TRH -> pituitary releases TSH -> thyroid releases thyroxine -> thyroxine back to normal -> TRH and TSH inhibited.

core.p: **Thyroxine** is a hormone secreted by the **thyroid gland** into the **blood**. It travels to almost every cell in the body and **increases the metabolic rate**. Metabolic rate is the rate at which energy is transferred by the chemical reactions in cells, especially **respiration**.
bullets: A higher metabolic rate means cells **respire faster**, using more glucose and oxygen and releasing more energy (some as heat).
Thyroxine is important for **growth and development**, including normal development of the brain and nervous system in children.
It also helps control body **heat production**, so it links to body temperature.
Thyroxine contains **iodine**, so the diet must provide iodine for the thyroid to make it.
Thyroxine acts over a **long time** (hours to days) unlike adrenalin, which works in seconds.

callouts.p: The rate at which the energy stored in food is transferred by all the reactions that take place in the body (chemical reactions in cells) to keep you alive.

core.h: The three glands and where they are
core.p: Three endocrine glands are involved. The **hypothalamus** is a small region at the base of the brain. The **pituitary gland** hangs just below the hypothalamus. The **thyroid gland** is a butterfly shaped gland in the **neck**, in front of the windpipe.
bullets: **Hypothalamus**: monitors the level of thyroxine in the blood and releases **TRH**.
**Pituitary gland**: the 'master gland'; releases **TSH** when stimulated by TRH.
**Thyroid gland**: releases **thyroxine** when stimulated by TSH.
All three hormones travel in the **blood plasma** to reach their target organ.

fig.cap: Position of the glands. The hypothalamus is part of the brain, the pituitary gland hangs just below it, and the thyroid gland sits in the front of the neck.

core.h: TRH and TSH: the two 'messenger' hormones
core.p: The full names help you remember what each one does. **TRH** is **thyrotropin releasing hormone**: it tells the pituitary to release a thyroid stimulating hormone. **TSH** is **thyroid stimulating hormone**: it stimulates the thyroid to release thyroxine.
bullets: TRH: made in the **hypothalamus**, target organ = **pituitary gland**.
TSH: made in the **pituitary gland**, target organ = **thyroid gland**.
Thyroxine: made in the **thyroid gland**, targets = **body cells** (and it also acts back on the hypothalamus and pituitary).
Using the abbreviations TRH and TSH is fine in the exam, but do not swap them.
Memory aid: **R** comes before **S** in the alphabet, and TRH comes before TSH in the chain.

callouts.t: Do not mix up the glands
callouts.p: TRH comes from the hypothalamus, NOT the pituitary. TSH comes from the pituitary, NOT the thyroid. The thyroid only makes thyroxine.

core.p: **Negative feedback** is a control mechanism where a **change** away from the normal level is **detected** and a response is triggered that **reverses the change**, bringing the level back to normal. It keeps conditions in the body **fairly constant**, which is part of **homeostasis**.
bullets: If a level **rises**, the response makes it **fall**.
If a level **falls**, the response makes it **rise**.
The response is switched off (or turned down) once the level is back to normal, so the level does not overshoot too far.
The result is a level that **fluctuates slightly around a set point** rather than staying perfectly flat.
Other examples in Topic 7: blood glucose (insulin and glucagon), body temperature (triple), water content via ADH (triple).

callouts.p: When a change in a level in the body triggers a response that reverses the change, returning the level to normal.

core.p: If the level of thyroxine in the blood **falls below normal** (for example in a cold environment or when the body needs more energy), the low level is detected and the system switches the thyroid **on**.
bullets: Low thyroxine **stimulates** the **hypothalamus** to produce and release **TRH**.
TRH travels in the blood to the **pituitary gland**, causing it to **release TSH**.
TSH travels in the blood to the **thyroid gland**, which then **produces and releases more thyroxine**.
Blood thyroxine level **rises**, so **metabolic rate increases**.
Each step needs the one before it: no TRH means no extra TSH, which means no extra thyroxine.

core.h: When thyroxine returns to normal or is too high
core.p: Once the thyroxine level is **back to normal** (or goes above normal), thyroxine itself acts on the hypothalamus and pituitary gland to **inhibit** them. This is the 'feedback' part: the product of the chain switches the chain off.
bullets: Thyroxine **inhibits the release of TRH** from the hypothalamus.
Thyroxine **inhibits the production/release of TSH** from the pituitary gland.
With less TSH, the thyroid is stimulated less and **releases less thyroxine**.
Thyroxine level **falls** back towards normal and **metabolic rate decreases**.
When it dips below normal again, inhibition is lifted and the cycle repeats, so the level **oscillates around normal**.

callouts.p: A high thyroxine level leads to LESS thyroxine being made, and a low level leads to MORE. The response is always opposite to the change.

core.h: The whole loop as a diagram
core.p: Put the two halves together and you get a **closed loop**. Solid arrows show stimulation (a hormone travelling in the blood to its target). Dashed arrows show **inhibition** by thyroxine.
bullets: Stimulating arm: hypothalamus -> TRH -> pituitary -> TSH -> thyroid -> thyroxine.
Inhibiting arm: thyroxine -> hypothalamus (less TRH) and pituitary (less TSH).
In a 6 mark answer, describe **both** arms and finish with how the level returns to normal.

callouts.p: If a question gives you a blank flow diagram, fill in gland names, hormone names and arrow directions carefully. Each correct label is usually a mark.

core.h: Why the level fluctuates around normal
core.p: Negative feedback does not hold a level perfectly still. There is a short **delay** between a change being detected and the hormones taking effect, because hormones must be made and must travel in the blood. So the level **overshoots slightly** each way and wobbles around the normal value.
bullets: Above normal: TRH and TSH are inhibited, thyroxine falls.
Below normal: TRH and TSH are released, thyroxine rises.
The wobble stays small because the correction starts as soon as the change is detected.
On a graph question, the peaks are where inhibition kicks in and the troughs are where stimulation kicks in.

core.p: Keeping thyroxine within narrow limits keeps metabolic rate suitable for the body's needs. Too much or too little thyroxine causes problems, which shows why the feedback system is needed.
bullets: **Too little thyroxine** (an underactive thyroid): low metabolic rate, so tiredness, weight gain, feeling cold.
**Too much thyroxine** (an overactive thyroid): high metabolic rate, so weight loss, feeling hot, fast heart rate, anxiety.
A diet lacking **iodine** means the thyroid cannot make enough thyroxine; TSH stays high and the thyroid can swell (a **goitre**).
These examples are for understanding; the spec focuses on the feedback loop itself.

core.h: Summary flow chart of both responses
core.p: Many exam questions start with 'the thyroxine level falls' or 'the thyroxine level rises' and ask what happens next. Practise both directions.
bullets: Always name the **gland** AND the **hormone** at each step.
Say what happens to **metabolic rate** at the end.
Use the words **stimulates**, **releases**, **inhibits**, **negative feedback**.

core.p: Questions sometimes ask you to compare the two hormones in this part of the topic. Adrenalin is a fast, short-lived emergency hormone; thyroxine is a slow, long-term controller of metabolism kept steady by negative feedback.
bullets: Adrenalin is not controlled by a negative feedback loop of releasing hormones in the way thyroxine is.
Both increase energy release, but adrenalin acts in seconds and thyroxine over days.

head: Feature
Thyroxine
Adrenalin
rows: Negative feedback via TRH and TSH

callouts.p: 'Explain' needs a reason at each step (because, so, which causes). 'Describe' just needs the steps in order.

analogy.p: Think of the hypothalamus as a **manager** watching a thermometer (the thyroxine level). When it is too cold (low thyroxine), the manager phones the supervisor (TRH to the pituitary), who switches on the boiler (TSH to the thyroid), which pumps out heat (thyroxine). When the room is warm enough, the heat itself makes the manager and supervisor stop phoning, so the boiler is turned down. Where it breaks down: a real thermostat is usually just on or off, but hormone release is **graded** (more or less), and hormones are chemicals carried in the blood to many cells, not signals down a single wire. Also, thyroxine acts on the hypothalamus and pituitary directly, not through a separate sensor.

terms.d: A hormone produced by the thyroid gland that increases the metabolic rate of body cells; it contains iodine.
An endocrine gland in the neck that produces and releases thyroxine when stimulated by TSH.
A region at the base of the brain that monitors thyroxine level and releases TRH when it is low.
An endocrine gland below the hypothalamus that releases TSH (and many other hormones); often called the master gland.
Thyrotropin releasing hormone: released by the hypothalamus, it causes the pituitary gland to release TSH.
Thyroid stimulating hormone: released by the pituitary gland, it stimulates the thyroid gland to produce thyroxine.
The rate at which energy is transferred by the chemical reactions in the body's cells, such as respiration.
A mechanism in which a change in a level triggers a response that reverses the change, returning the level to normal.
To reduce or stop a process; normal thyroxine levels inhibit the release of TRH and TSH.
A chemical messenger secreted by an endocrine gland into the blood, which carries it to a target organ.
The organ whose cells respond to a particular hormone, e.g. the thyroid is the target organ of TSH.
A gland that secretes hormones directly into the bloodstream.
The maintenance of a constant internal environment despite changes inside or outside the body.
A mineral needed in the diet because it is part of the thyroxine molecule.

mistakes.w: The pituitary gland releases TRH.
mistakes.r: The hypothalamus releases TRH; the pituitary gland releases TSH.

mistakes.w: TSH is made by the thyroid gland.
mistakes.r: TSH is made by the pituitary gland and acts on the thyroid gland, which makes thyroxine.

mistakes.w: Thyroxine controls blood sugar.
mistakes.r: Thyroxine controls metabolic rate; blood glucose is controlled by insulin and glucagon.

mistakes.w: When thyroxine is high, the thyroid stops working by itself.
mistakes.r: High (normal) thyroxine inhibits the release of TRH from the hypothalamus and TSH from the pituitary, so the thyroid is stimulated less.

mistakes.w: Negative feedback means the level goes down.
mistakes.r: Negative feedback means the response reverses the change: a fall leads to a rise and a rise leads to a fall.

mistakes.w: Hormones are carried by nerves to the thyroid.
mistakes.r: TRH, TSH and thyroxine are all carried in the blood (plasma) to their target organs.

mistakes.w: Thyroxine makes the heart beat faster for fight or flight.
mistakes.r: That is adrenalin. Thyroxine increases the metabolic rate over a longer period.

mistakes.w: Low thyroxine stimulates the pituitary to make thyroxine.
mistakes.r: Low thyroxine stimulates the hypothalamus to release TRH, then the pituitary releases TSH, then the thyroid makes thyroxine.

mistakes.w: Metabolic rate is how fast you digest food.
mistakes.r: Metabolic rate is the rate of the chemical reactions in cells, such as respiration, that transfer energy.

exam.q: Name the gland that produces thyroxine.
model: Thyroid (gland)
exam.tip: Spell it thyroid, not thyroxine gland.

exam.q: State the effect of thyroxine on the body.
model: Increases metabolic rate / increases rate of respiration in cells
exam.tip: 'Increases' must be stated; 'controls metabolism' alone may not score.

exam.q: Name the hormone released by the pituitary gland that acts on the thyroid gland.
model: TSH / thyroid stimulating hormone
exam.tip: Do not write TRH; that comes from the hypothalamus.

exam.q: Name the hormone released by the hypothalamus in response to a low level of thyroxine, and state its target organ.
model: TRH / thyrotropin releasing hormone
Pituitary gland
exam.tip: Two marks, two separate facts: hormone and target.

exam.q: Explain what is meant by negative feedback.
model: A change in a level (from normal) is detected
and causes a response that reverses the change / returns the level to normal
exam.tip: Mention reversing the change, not just 'keeping it constant'.

exam.q: The level of thyroxine in a person's blood increases above normal. Describe how this level is returned to normal.
model: Thyroxine inhibits release of TRH from the hypothalamus
Thyroxine inhibits release/production of TSH from the pituitary gland
So less thyroxine is released by the thyroid (level falls back to normal)
exam.tip: Name both glands that are inhibited.

exam.q: Explain why the control of thyroxine is described as negative feedback.
model: High thyroxine reduces/inhibits release of TRH/TSH, so less thyroxine made
Low thyroxine leads to more TRH/TSH, so more thyroxine made; the response is opposite to the change
exam.tip: Link a change to an opposite response.

exam.q: A person has a diet lacking in iodine. Suggest why this person may have a low metabolic rate.
model: Iodine is needed to make thyroxine
Less thyroxine, so metabolic rate is not increased / lower rate of respiration
exam.tip: 'Suggest' means apply your knowledge to a new situation.

exam.q: Compare the effects and control of thyroxine and adrenalin.
model: Thyroxine from thyroid; adrenalin from adrenal glands
Thyroxine increases metabolic rate; adrenalin prepares the body for fight or flight
Thyroxine acts slowly/long term; adrenalin acts quickly/short term
Thyroxine controlled by negative feedback (TRH/TSH); adrenalin released in response to stress/fear
exam.tip: 'Compare' needs points about both hormones in each sentence.

exam.q: Explain how the body maintains a normal level of thyroxine in the blood. (6 marks)
model: When thyroxine level is low, the hypothalamus is stimulated
Hypothalamus releases TRH (into the blood)
TRH causes the pituitary gland to release TSH
TSH travels in the blood to the thyroid gland, which releases thyroxine
When thyroxine level returns to normal, it inhibits release of TRH and TSH
So less thyroxine is made; this is negative feedback, keeping the level (and metabolic rate) within narrow limits
exam.tip: Give the full chain in order and use the phrase negative feedback; each gland plus hormone is a marking point.

exam.q: The pituitary gland of a patient stops producing TSH. Predict and explain the effect on the patient's metabolic rate.
model: Thyroid is not stimulated
Little/no thyroxine released
Metabolic rate decreases / is low
exam.tip: Follow the chain downstream from the broken step.

worked.q: A person moves to a very cold climate and their thyroxine level starts to fall. Describe the sequence of events that returns their thyroxine level to normal.
steps: Step 1: the low thyroxine level stimulates the hypothalamus.
Step 2: the hypothalamus releases TRH into the blood.
Step 3: TRH reaches the pituitary gland, which releases TSH into the blood.
Step 4: TSH reaches the thyroid gland, which produces and releases more thyroxine.
Step 5: metabolic rate increases (more respiration, more heat released).
Step 6: once thyroxine is back to normal, it inhibits release of TRH and TSH, so production slows (negative feedback).
worked.ans: Low thyroxine -> TRH from hypothalamus -> TSH from pituitary -> more thyroxine from thyroid -> metabolic rate rises; normal thyroxine then inhibits TRH and TSH.

worked.q: A graph shows a patient's blood TSH level is very high but their thyroxine level is very low. Suggest an explanation.
steps: Normally low thyroxine causes TRH and TSH release, so TSH being high makes sense if thyroxine is low.
But high TSH should make the thyroid release more thyroxine, bringing the level up.
Thyroxine stays low, so the thyroid gland is not responding to TSH (or cannot make thyroxine, e.g. lack of iodine).
Because thyroxine stays low, there is no inhibition of TRH and TSH, so TSH stays high.
worked.ans: The thyroid gland is not producing thyroxine (e.g. damaged or lacking iodine); thyroxine stays low so it never inhibits TRH/TSH release, so TSH remains high.

worked.q: Model answer: why is it important that thyroxine inhibits both the hypothalamus and the pituitary gland, rather than only stimulating them when low?
steps: Without inhibition, TRH and TSH would keep being released.
The thyroid would keep producing thyroxine, so the level would keep rising.
Metabolic rate would become too high (weight loss, overheating).
Inhibition switches the chain off once the level is normal, keeping it within narrow limits.
worked.ans: Inhibition is the feedback that stops overproduction; it reverses a rise, so thyroxine and metabolic rate stay close to normal (homeostasis).

bio_edx.6.3.summary: The **menstrual cycle** is a roughly **28 day** cycle that prepares the uterus to receive a fertilised egg. Four hormones control it: **FSH** and **LH** from the **pituitary gland**, and **oestrogen** and **progesterone** from the **ovaries**. Oestrogen builds the **uterus lining**, an **LH surge** triggers **ovulation** around day 14, and progesterone **maintains** the lining; if no egg is fertilised, progesterone falls and the lining breaks down (**menstruation**). Spec 7.4 covers the stages and the roles of oestrogen and progesterone; 7.5 (**Higher tier**) covers how all four hormones interact.

core.p: **7.4**: describe the **stages of the menstrual cycle**, including the roles of **oestrogen and progesterone** in its control. **7.5 (Higher only)**: explain the **interactions of oestrogen, progesterone, FSH and LH** in the control of the menstrual cycle, including **repair and maintenance of the uterus wall, ovulation and menstruation**.
bullets: Foundation students must know the stages and what oestrogen and progesterone do.
Higher students must also explain how the four hormones **stimulate or inhibit** each other.
Expect a hormone level graph in almost every question on this point.
This point leads into 7.6 to 7.8: contraception and fertility treatments work by changing these hormones.

callouts.p: Pituitary gland: FSH and LH. Ovaries: oestrogen and progesterone.

core.h: The four stages of the cycle
core.p: The cycle starts on the **first day of bleeding** (day 1). A typical cycle lasts about **28 days**, but lengths vary between people and from month to month.
bullets: **Stage 1, days 1 to 4 (about)**: **menstruation**. The thick uterus lining breaks down and is lost through the vagina, with some blood.
**Stage 2, days 5 to 14**: the **uterus lining is repaired and thickens** again, becoming spongy and full of blood vessels. An egg matures in a follicle in the ovary.
**Stage 3, about day 14**: **ovulation**, the release of a mature egg from the ovary into the oviduct.
**Stage 4, days 14 to 28**: the uterus lining is **maintained**, ready for a fertilised egg to implant. If no fertilised egg implants, the lining breaks down and the cycle starts again.

callouts.p: The release of a mature egg (ovum) from an ovary.
The breakdown and loss of the uterus lining (with blood) through the vagina, at the start of each cycle.

core.p: Two of the hormones are made by the **pituitary gland** at the base of the brain, and two are made by the **ovaries**. They all travel in the **blood** to their target organs.
bullets: **FSH** (follicle stimulating hormone): pituitary gland -> targets the **ovaries**.
**LH** (luteinising hormone): pituitary gland -> targets the **ovaries**.
**Oestrogen**: ovaries (made by the developing follicle) -> targets the **uterus** and the **pituitary gland**.
**Progesterone**: ovaries (made by the **corpus luteum**, the empty follicle left after ovulation) -> targets the **uterus** and the **pituitary gland**.

head: Hormone
Made in
Main roles
rows: Causes an egg (follicle) to mature in the ovary; stimulates the ovary to produce oestrogen
Surge triggers ovulation; causes the follicle to become the corpus luteum
Repairs and thickens uterus lining; inhibits FSH; high level stimulates LH surge
Maintains uterus lining; inhibits FSH and LH

callouts.p: FSH and LH are NOT made by the ovaries. They are made by the pituitary gland and act ON the ovaries.

core.p: **Oestrogen** is made by the ovary, mainly by the developing **follicle**, so its level **rises during the first half of the cycle** as the follicle grows.
bullets: Causes the **uterus lining to repair and thicken** after menstruation (days 5 to 14).
**Inhibits the release of FSH** from the pituitary gland, so that no more eggs start to mature.
When it reaches a **high level** (around day 12 to 13), it **stimulates the release of LH**, causing the **LH surge**.
Oestrogen is also the main female sex hormone for secondary sexual characteristics (from puberty).

callouts.t: Oestrogen does two jobs at the pituitary
callouts.p: It inhibits FSH, and at a high level it stimulates LH. Higher tier answers must state both.

core.p: **Progesterone** is released by the **corpus luteum** in the ovary after ovulation, so its level **rises in the second half of the cycle** (days 14 to 28).
bullets: **Maintains the uterus lining**, keeping it thick and full of blood vessels ready for a fertilised egg to implant.
**Inhibits the release of FSH and LH** from the pituitary gland, so no new egg matures and no further ovulation happens.
If the egg is **not fertilised**, the corpus luteum breaks down, **progesterone level falls**, and the lining is no longer maintained, so **menstruation** begins.
The fall in progesterone also removes the inhibition of FSH, so FSH rises and a new cycle starts.
If the egg **is fertilised** and implants, progesterone stays high, the lining is kept and periods stop during pregnancy.

callouts.p: The trigger for menstruation is the FALL in progesterone. Say 'progesterone level falls so the uterus lining is no longer maintained and breaks down'.

core.p: **FSH, follicle stimulating hormone**, is released by the pituitary gland at the start of the cycle. Its name tells you its job: it **stimulates a follicle** in the ovary.
bullets: Causes an **egg to mature** inside a **follicle** in the ovary.
Stimulates the ovary (the follicle) to **produce oestrogen**.
Its release is then **inhibited by oestrogen** (negative feedback) and later by **progesterone**.
FSH is high at the start of the cycle because progesterone has just fallen.

callouts.p: A small fluid filled structure in the ovary in which an egg matures.

core.p: **LH, luteinising hormone**, is also made by the pituitary gland. Its level stays low until about day 12 to 14, when the **high level of oestrogen** triggers a sudden **LH surge**.
bullets: The **LH surge stimulates ovulation**: the mature follicle bursts and releases the egg (about day 14).
LH causes the empty follicle to develop into the **corpus luteum**, which then secretes **progesterone**.
LH release is **inhibited by progesterone** in the second half of the cycle.

callouts.p: The structure that forms from the empty follicle after ovulation; it secretes progesterone.

fig.cap: What happens in the ovary. FSH makes a follicle grow and mature (it releases oestrogen); the LH surge triggers ovulation, releasing the egg; the empty follicle becomes the corpus luteum, which releases progesterone.

core.p: The hormones form a chain in which each one **switches the next on or off**. The pituitary hormones act on the ovary, and the ovary hormones act back on the pituitary (and on the uterus).
bullets: **1. FSH** (pituitary) -> egg matures in a follicle and the ovary makes **oestrogen**.
**2. Oestrogen** -> uterus lining thickens; **FSH inhibited**; when high, **LH stimulated**.
**3. LH surge** -> **ovulation** (about day 14); follicle becomes **corpus luteum**.
**4. Corpus luteum** -> **progesterone** -> lining **maintained**; **FSH and LH inhibited**.
**5. No fertilisation** -> corpus luteum breaks down -> **progesterone falls** -> **menstruation**; FSH no longer inhibited, so FSH rises and the cycle restarts.

callouts.p: Oestrogen inhibits FSH. Progesterone inhibits FSH and LH. The only stimulation from the ovary to the pituitary is: high oestrogen stimulates LH.

fig.cap: Interactions between the pituitary gland and the ovary. FSH and LH travel in the blood to the ovary. Oestrogen inhibits FSH and, at a high level, stimulates the LH surge. Progesterone (dashed) inhibits both FSH and LH.

core.p: Exam questions nearly always show the four hormone levels plotted against day of cycle. Learn the **shape and timing** of each curve and link each peak to an event.
bullets: **FSH**: rises at the start, small peak around day 13 to 14, then falls (inhibited by progesterone).
**Oestrogen**: rises through days 5 to 13 as the follicle grows, peaks **just before** ovulation.
**LH**: low, then a **sharp peak (surge) just before day 14**, which causes ovulation.
**Progesterone**: low in the first half, rises after ovulation, peaks around day 21, then falls before day 28.
Ovulation happens just **after** the LH peak; menstruation starts when progesterone has fallen.

callouts.p: The curve with the tallest, narrowest peak at day 14 is LH. The curve that is high only in the second half is progesterone.

core.h: Repair and maintenance of the uterus wall
core.p: Both ovary hormones act on the **uterus lining (endometrium)** but at different times and in different ways.
bullets: **Repair and thickening** (days 5 to 14): **oestrogen**. The lining regrows and becomes thicker with more blood vessels.
**Maintenance** (days 14 to 28): **progesterone**. It keeps the thick lining in place so it can receive an embryo.
A thick lining with a good blood supply allows a fertilised egg (embryo) to **implant** and receive nutrients and oxygen.
If the lining were not maintained, any embryo could not implant, which is why progesterone is essential in early pregnancy.

head: Oestrogen
Progesterone
rows: Inhibits FSH; high level stimulates LH

core.h: What happens if the egg is fertilised
core.p: Not directly a spec bullet, but understanding it helps you explain the role of progesterone and links to contraception.
bullets: The egg is fertilised in the **oviduct** and the embryo implants in the thick uterus lining.
The **corpus luteum does not break down**, so progesterone stays **high**.
High progesterone keeps the lining in place and keeps FSH and LH inhibited, so **no new eggs mature** and **no menstruation** happens.
This is why the contraceptive pill (7.6) uses progesterone and oestrogen: they inhibit FSH and LH.

core.h: Negative and positive effects in the cycle
core.p: Much of the cycle works by **negative feedback**: the ovary hormones reduce the release of the pituitary hormones that caused them to be made. This stops more than one egg maturing at a time.
bullets: FSH causes oestrogen production, and oestrogen **inhibits FSH**: negative feedback.
LH causes the corpus luteum to form, and its progesterone **inhibits LH** (and FSH): negative feedback.
High oestrogen **stimulating** the LH surge is the exception, and it is what times ovulation.
Grade 9 link: changing these hormones artificially (pills, implants, clomifene, IVF drugs) controls fertility.

callouts.p: Work in time order: FSH, oestrogen, LH, progesterone, then what happens with no fertilisation. Name the gland, hormone and effect at each step.

analogy.t: A relay race with a team captain
analogy.p: The pituitary gland is the **team captain** who starts the race by handing the baton (FSH) to the ovary. The ovary's first runner (oestrogen) builds the track (the uterus lining) and tells the captain to stop sending FSH. When oestrogen is running at full speed, it signals the captain to fire the starting pistol for the main event (the LH surge: ovulation). The second runner (progesterone) guards the track, keeping it ready, and tells the captain to stay quiet (inhibits FSH and LH). If no one arrives (no fertilisation), the guard leaves, the track is dismantled (menstruation) and the captain starts again. Where it breaks down: hormones are chemicals in the blood acting on many cells at once, not single batons passed hand to hand, and their levels change gradually rather than switching on and off.

terms.d: A cycle of about 28 days in which an egg matures and is released and the uterus lining is built up, maintained and then shed.
The breakdown and loss of the uterus lining, with blood, through the vagina (days 1 to 4 approximately).
The release of a mature egg from the ovary, about day 14, triggered by a surge of LH.
Follicle stimulating hormone, from the pituitary gland; causes an egg to mature in a follicle and stimulates the ovary to make oestrogen.
Luteinising hormone, from the pituitary gland; a surge causes ovulation and the follicle to become the corpus luteum.
Hormone made by the ovaries; repairs and thickens the uterus lining, inhibits FSH and at high levels stimulates LH release.
Hormone made by the corpus luteum in the ovary; maintains the uterus lining and inhibits FSH and LH.
Endocrine gland at the base of the brain that releases FSH and LH.
Female reproductive organ that contains eggs and produces oestrogen and progesterone.
A fluid filled structure in the ovary in which an egg develops; it produces oestrogen.
Structure formed from the empty follicle after ovulation; it secretes progesterone.
The inner layer of the uterus (endometrium); becomes thick and rich in blood vessels so an embryo can implant.
When an embryo (fertilised egg) embeds in the thick uterus lining.
A sharp rise in LH level just before day 14, stimulated by high oestrogen, that causes ovulation.
To reduce or stop the release of a hormone, e.g. progesterone inhibits FSH and LH.

mistakes.w: FSH and LH are made in the ovaries.
mistakes.r: FSH and LH are made in the pituitary gland and act on the ovaries.

mistakes.w: Progesterone builds up the uterus lining.
mistakes.r: Oestrogen repairs and thickens the lining; progesterone maintains it.

mistakes.w: Oestrogen causes ovulation.
mistakes.r: The LH surge causes ovulation; high oestrogen stimulates the release of LH.

mistakes.w: Menstruation happens because oestrogen rises.
mistakes.r: Menstruation happens when progesterone levels fall, so the lining is no longer maintained.

mistakes.w: Ovulation is the egg being fertilised.
mistakes.r: Ovulation is the release of a mature egg from the ovary; fertilisation is fusion with a sperm.

mistakes.w: Oestrogen stimulates FSH.
mistakes.r: Oestrogen inhibits FSH (and a high level stimulates LH).

mistakes.w: The cycle starts at ovulation.
mistakes.r: Day 1 of the cycle is the first day of menstruation; ovulation is at about day 14.

mistakes.w: Progesterone is made by the pituitary gland.
mistakes.r: Progesterone is made by the ovary (the corpus luteum).

mistakes.w: Menstruation is the release of the egg.
mistakes.r: Menstruation is the shedding of the uterus lining with blood.

exam.q: State what is meant by ovulation.
model: Release of an egg (ovum) from the ovary
exam.tip: Say 'from the ovary'.

exam.q: Name the gland that produces FSH.
model: Pituitary (gland)
exam.tip: Not the ovary.

exam.q: State the role of oestrogen in the menstrual cycle.
model: Causes the uterus lining to (repair and) thicken / build up
exam.tip: Higher papers may also want 'inhibits FSH'.

exam.q: Describe the role of progesterone in the menstrual cycle.
model: Maintains the uterus lining
Inhibits (release of) FSH and LH
exam.tip: Maintains, not builds.

exam.q: Using the hormone graph, identify the day on which ovulation occurs and give a reason for your answer.
model: About day 14
Just after the peak/surge in LH
exam.tip: Always link the answer to a feature of the graph.

exam.q: Explain why the uterus lining breaks down at the end of the cycle if the egg is not fertilised.
model: Corpus luteum breaks down so progesterone level falls
So the lining is no longer maintained (and is shed)
exam.tip: The fall in progesterone is the key idea.

exam.q: Describe the stages of the menstrual cycle.
model: Days 1 to 4: menstruation, uterus lining breaks down and is lost
Days 5 to 14: lining repairs/thickens (oestrogen)
Day 14: ovulation, egg released from ovary
Days 14 to 28: lining maintained (progesterone); breaks down if no fertilisation
exam.tip: Give approximate day numbers for each stage.

exam.q: Explain the role of LH in the menstrual cycle.
model: (Surge of) LH stimulates/causes ovulation
Causes follicle to develop into corpus luteum (which makes progesterone)
exam.tip: Higher tier: say what triggers it too (high oestrogen).

exam.q: Explain why only one egg usually matures in each cycle.
model: Oestrogen inhibits FSH release
So no further follicles/eggs are stimulated to mature (progesterone also inhibits FSH later)
exam.tip: Link the inhibition to the role of FSH.

exam.q: Explain how the hormones oestrogen, progesterone, FSH and LH interact to control the menstrual cycle. (6 marks)
model: FSH from the pituitary causes an egg to mature in the ovary and stimulates oestrogen production
Oestrogen causes the uterus lining to repair/thicken
Oestrogen inhibits FSH; high oestrogen stimulates LH release
LH surge causes ovulation (about day 14) and formation of corpus luteum
Corpus luteum produces progesterone, which maintains the uterus lining and inhibits FSH and LH
If no fertilisation, progesterone falls, lining breaks down (menstruation) and FSH is no longer inhibited so the cycle restarts
exam.tip: Higher tier only. Go in time order and include stimulate/inhibit at each step.

exam.q: Suggest why the progesterone level stays high during pregnancy, and why this is important.
model: Corpus luteum (and later placenta) keeps producing progesterone
Uterus lining is maintained so embryo stays implanted / no menstruation / FSH and LH inhibited so no new eggs mature
exam.tip: 'Suggest' lets you use reasoning beyond the spec as long as it is sensible.

worked.q: A woman's cycle is 32 days long. Ovulation usually occurs about 14 days before the start of the next period. On which day of her cycle would you expect ovulation?
steps: Next period starts on day 33 (day 1 of the next cycle).
Ovulation is about 14 days before this.
worked.ans: About day 19 of her cycle (not day 14, because her cycle is longer than 28 days).

worked.q: A blood test on day 21 shows high progesterone and low FSH and LH. Explain these results.
steps: Day 21 is after ovulation, so the corpus luteum has formed.
The corpus luteum releases progesterone, so progesterone is high.
Progesterone inhibits the release of FSH and LH from the pituitary gland.
So FSH and LH are low, and the uterus lining is being maintained.
worked.ans: High progesterone from the corpus luteum after ovulation is maintaining the lining and inhibiting FSH and LH release, so both are low.

worked.q: Model answer: describe the roles of oestrogen and progesterone in the menstrual cycle (Foundation, 4 marks).
steps: Oestrogen is made by the ovaries in the first half of the cycle.
Oestrogen causes the uterus lining to repair and thicken after menstruation.
Progesterone is made by the ovary after ovulation.
Progesterone maintains the thick lining; when progesterone falls the lining breaks down (menstruation).
worked.ans: Oestrogen thickens the uterus lining (days 5 to 14); progesterone maintains it (days 14 to 28) and when it falls menstruation begins.

bio_edx.6.4.summary: Contraception is any method that **prevents pregnancy**. **Hormonal methods** (the **pill**, **skin patch**, **injection** and **implant**) contain **oestrogen and/or progesterone**: these **inhibit FSH and LH**, so **eggs do not mature and ovulation does not happen**, and progesterone also **thickens cervical mucus** so sperm cannot get through. **Barrier methods** (the **condom** and **diaphragm**) physically **stop sperm reaching the egg**. Spec 7.6 asks how hormonal contraception affects the menstrual cycle and 7.7 asks you to **evaluate** hormonal and barrier methods, weighing effectiveness, side effects, convenience and protection against **sexually transmitted infections (STIs)**.

core.p: **7.6**: explain how **hormonal contraception** works by influencing the **menstrual cycle** and preventing pregnancy. **7.7**: **evaluate hormonal and barrier methods** of contraception. Evaluate means give **advantages and disadvantages** and come to a **judgement**.
bullets: Builds directly on 7.4 to 7.5: you must know what FSH, LH, oestrogen and progesterone normally do.
Both points are for **all students** (not Higher only), though Higher answers name FSH and LH more precisely.
Common question styles: explain how the pill works, compare two methods, evaluate a method using data in a table.
Barrier methods covered: **condoms** (male and female) and the **diaphragm** (cap), usually used with spermicide.

callouts.p: Any method used to prevent pregnancy, either by stopping eggs being released or by stopping sperm reaching an egg.

core.p: Pregnancy needs a **sperm to fertilise an egg** in the oviduct, and the embryo to **implant** in the uterus lining. Contraception breaks this chain.
bullets: **Hormonal methods**: change hormone levels so **no egg is released** (and sperm find it hard to pass the cervix).
**Barrier methods**: put a **physical barrier** between sperm and egg.
Other methods exist (e.g. intrauterine devices, sterilisation, abstinence) but the spec focuses on hormonal and barrier methods.

head: Type
Examples
How it works
rows: Combined pill, progesterone-only pill, patch, injection, implant
Hormones inhibit FSH/LH so no ovulation; thicken cervical mucus
Physically stop sperm reaching the egg

core.h: How hormonal contraception affects the cycle
core.p: In a normal cycle, **oestrogen inhibits FSH** and **progesterone inhibits FSH and LH**. Hormonal contraceptives copy this. By keeping oestrogen and/or progesterone **constantly high**, they keep **FSH and LH low**.
bullets: Low **FSH** means **no egg matures** in the ovary.
Low **LH** means there is **no LH surge**, so **no ovulation**.
No egg released means no egg can be fertilised.
**Progesterone** also makes the **mucus in the cervix thick and sticky**, so sperm cannot swim through to the uterus.
Some progesterone methods also **thin the uterus lining**, making implantation less likely.

callouts.p: Hormonal contraceptives work like a fake pregnancy signal: high oestrogen/progesterone inhibit FSH and LH, so no egg matures and no ovulation occurs.

core.p: The **combined pill** contains **oestrogen and progesterone** and is taken by mouth **every day** (often for 21 days, then a 7 day break during which a bleed happens).
bullets: Oestrogen and progesterone **inhibit FSH and LH**, so **eggs do not mature and are not released**.
Progesterone also **thickens cervical mucus**.
More than **99% effective** if taken correctly; less effective if pills are missed or the user vomits.
Advantages: very effective, reversible, can make periods lighter and more regular.
Disadvantages: must be **remembered daily**; possible **side effects** such as mood changes, headaches, breast tenderness, and an increased risk of **blood clots**; **no protection against STIs**.

callouts.p: The pill does NOT 'stop the ovaries working' by damaging them. It keeps FSH and LH low so no egg matures. Fertility returns when the pill is stopped.

core.p: Some people cannot take oestrogen (for example because of a higher risk of blood clots), so there are methods that contain **progesterone only**.
bullets: **Progesterone-only pill (mini pill)**: taken every day; mainly works by **thickening cervical mucus**, and can stop ovulation.
**Contraceptive injection**: progesterone injected; **lasts for several weeks to months** (often about 8 to 13 weeks) depending on the type.
**Contraceptive implant**: a small flexible rod placed **under the skin** of the upper arm; releases progesterone slowly and **lasts up to 3 years**.
Fewer side effects linked to oestrogen, but may cause irregular bleeding.
Implant and injection mean the user does **not have to remember daily**, so **typical use is more effective**.

core.p: The **patch** is stuck onto the skin and releases **oestrogen and progesterone** into the blood through the skin. It works in the same way as the combined pill.
bullets: A new patch is applied **once a week** (usually for 3 weeks, then a patch-free week).
Easier to remember than a daily pill.
Still works if the user vomits, unlike the pill.
Same possible side effects as the combined pill; no protection against STIs.

core.p: **Condoms** are thin sheaths, usually made of latex. A **male condom** is worn over the erect penis; a **female condom** is worn inside the vagina. Both **trap sperm** so they cannot reach the egg.
bullets: **Male condom**: about **98% effective** if used correctly.
**Only condoms protect against STIs** (such as HIV, chlamydia and gonorrhoea) because they stop contact between body fluids.
No hormones, so **no hormonal side effects**.
Easy to buy and used only when needed.
Disadvantages: can **split or slip off**; must be put on correctly every time; some people are allergic to latex.

callouts.p: Condoms are the only contraceptive method that protects against sexually transmitted infections. Hormonal methods and the diaphragm do not.

core.p: The **diaphragm** (or cap) is a shallow dome of thin rubber or silicone that is placed in the vagina **over the cervix** before sex, so sperm cannot enter the uterus.
bullets: Must be used with **spermicide**, a chemical that kills or disables sperm.
About **92 to 96% effective** with spermicide if used correctly.
Must be left in for several hours after sex.
Must be fitted correctly (the right size); no hormonal side effects.
**Does not protect against STIs**.

callouts.p: A chemical that kills or disables sperm; used with a diaphragm to increase effectiveness.

core.p: **Effectiveness** is usually given as the **percentage of users who do not get pregnant in a year**. Figures for **correct (perfect) use** are higher than for **typical use**, because people forget pills or use condoms incorrectly.
bullets: Hormonal methods are **more effective** than barrier methods when used correctly.
Long-acting methods (implant, injection) have **typical use close to perfect use**, because there is nothing to remember daily.
Barrier methods depend on being used **correctly every time**.
In data questions, **compare numbers** and say which method is most effective, then give a reason.
