core.p: To **evaluate** you must weigh up **advantages and disadvantages** of both types and reach a **conclusion** that depends on the person's needs.
bullets: **Hormonal**: more effective; does not interrupt sex; but possible side effects; no STI protection; requires medical prescription (pill, injection, implant).
**Barrier**: protects against STIs (condoms); no side effects from hormones; easy to get; but less effective; can fail if torn or misused; must be used every time.
Best protection overall: a hormonal method **plus** a condom (pregnancy and STI protection).
A judgement could be: 'For someone in a new relationship, condoms are better because they protect against STIs, even though they are less effective at preventing pregnancy'.

head: Factor
Hormonal methods
Barrier methods
rows: Possible: mood changes, headaches, blood clot risk
Yes (fertility returns, may take time after injection)

core.h: Side effects and risks of hormonal methods
core.p: Because hormonal methods change hormone levels in the whole body, they can have **side effects**. These are a key part of any evaluation.
bullets: Possible side effects include **mood changes**, **headaches**, **nausea**, **breast tenderness**, weight change and irregular bleeding.
Methods containing oestrogen slightly **increase the risk of blood clots** (and high blood pressure in some people).
An implant needs a small procedure to fit and remove; an injection cannot be removed once given.
Fertility may take some months to return after the injection.

callouts.p: No method is 100% effective (except abstinence). Avoid writing that the pill 'always' prevents pregnancy.

core.p: Six mark evaluation questions reward a **balanced** answer with **reasons** and a **justified conclusion**.
bullets: Explain **how** each method works (hormones inhibit FSH/LH; barrier blocks sperm).
Give at least two **advantages** and two **disadvantages** for each.
Use **data** if provided (effectiveness percentages).
Finish with a **judgement**: which is better for the situation given, and why.
Use precise words: **ovulation**, **inhibits FSH and LH**, **cervical mucus**, **STIs**, **side effects**.

callouts.p: How it works -> advantages -> disadvantages -> comparison -> conclusion.

analogy.t: Locking the gate or guarding the road
analogy.p: Think of pregnancy as a **delivery**: an egg must leave the warehouse (ovary) and a courier (sperm) must reach it. **Hormonal methods** are like **switching off the warehouse's order system** (FSH and LH): no package is ever prepared or sent out, and the road is also made muddy (thick cervical mucus). **Barrier methods** are like a **locked gate on the road**: the courier is physically blocked, but if the gate is left open or damaged (condom splits) the delivery can still happen. Only the condom gate also keeps out unwanted visitors (STIs). Where it breaks down: hormones affect the whole body, which is why side effects happen, and a warehouse switch-off is never perfectly 100% reliable.

terms.d: Methods used to prevent pregnancy.
Methods that use oestrogen and/or progesterone to inhibit FSH and LH, preventing egg maturation and ovulation.
A contraceptive method that physically prevents sperm from reaching the egg, e.g. condom or diaphragm.
An oral contraceptive containing oestrogen and progesterone, taken daily.
An oral contraceptive containing only progesterone; mainly thickens cervical mucus.
A small rod placed under the skin that slowly releases progesterone for up to 3 years.
An injection of progesterone that prevents pregnancy for several weeks to months.
A patch on the skin that releases oestrogen and progesterone into the blood; replaced weekly.
A thin latex sheath worn on the penis (male) or in the vagina (female) that traps sperm; protects against STIs.
A dome shaped barrier placed over the cervix, used with spermicide, to stop sperm entering the uterus.
A chemical that kills or disables sperm.
Mucus at the cervix; progesterone makes it thick and sticky so sperm cannot pass through.
Sexually transmitted infection, such as HIV or chlamydia, passed on during sexual contact.
The release of a mature egg from an ovary; prevented by hormonal contraception.
The percentage of people using a method who do not become pregnant in a year.

mistakes.w: The pill kills sperm.
mistakes.r: The pill contains hormones that inhibit FSH and LH so no egg matures or is released; spermicide kills sperm.

mistakes.w: The pill protects against STIs.
mistakes.r: Only condoms protect against STIs; hormonal methods do not.

mistakes.w: Hormonal contraceptives stimulate FSH.
mistakes.r: They inhibit FSH (and LH), so eggs do not mature.

mistakes.w: The diaphragm protects against STIs like a condom.
mistakes.r: The diaphragm does not protect against STIs.

mistakes.w: The implant contains oestrogen.
mistakes.r: The implant (and injection) contain progesterone only.

mistakes.w: Barrier methods are more effective than hormonal ones.
mistakes.r: Hormonal methods are generally more effective (over 99% with correct use) than barrier methods.

mistakes.w: The pill stops the uterus lining forming so the egg cannot be fertilised.
mistakes.r: The main effect is preventing egg maturation and ovulation, plus thickening cervical mucus.

mistakes.w: Evaluate means list the advantages.
mistakes.r: Evaluate means give advantages and disadvantages and come to a justified conclusion.

exam.q: Name one barrier method of contraception.
model: Condom (male or female) / diaphragm / cap
exam.tip: Pill is not a barrier method.

exam.q: Name the two hormones in the combined contraceptive pill.
model: Oestrogen
Progesterone
exam.tip: Spelling of oestrogen matters on some papers.

exam.q: Give one reason why someone might choose a condom rather than the pill.
model: Protects against STIs / no hormonal side effects / no need to remember daily
exam.tip: STIs is the strongest answer.

exam.q: Explain how the combined pill prevents pregnancy.
model: Oestrogen/progesterone inhibit FSH (and LH) release
So no egg matures / no ovulation
Progesterone thickens cervical mucus so sperm cannot reach the egg
exam.tip: Link each hormone to its effect.

exam.q: Explain how a diaphragm prevents pregnancy.
model: Covers the cervix / acts as a physical barrier
So sperm cannot enter the uterus/reach the egg (spermicide kills sperm)
exam.tip: Mention the cervix.

exam.q: Suggest why the contraceptive implant is more effective in typical use than the pill.
model: Implant lasts for years / releases hormone continuously
No need to remember to take it daily, so no missed doses
exam.tip: Think about human error.

exam.q: Explain why progesterone-only methods may be prescribed instead of the combined pill.
model: Some people cannot take oestrogen
Because of risk of side effects such as blood clots
exam.tip: Link the alternative to a side effect.

exam.q: A table shows the male condom is 98% effective and the combined pill 99% effective with correct use. Calculate how many more pregnancies per 1000 users in a year would be expected with the condom.
model: Condom: 2% of 1000 = 20; pill: 1% of 1000 = 10
Difference = 10 more pregnancies
exam.tip: Convert effectiveness to failure rate first.

exam.q: Compare how hormonal and barrier methods of contraception prevent pregnancy.
model: Hormonal methods use oestrogen/progesterone
which inhibit FSH/LH so no egg matures/ovulation
Barrier methods physically stop sperm reaching the egg
Hormonal acts on the body's cycle; barrier does not affect hormones/cycle
exam.tip: Say something about both in each comparison.

exam.q: Evaluate the use of hormonal and barrier methods of contraception. (6 marks)
model: Hormonal methods inhibit FSH/LH so prevent ovulation; barrier methods block sperm
Hormonal more effective (over 99%) than barrier (around 92 to 98%)
Hormonal: possible side effects e.g. mood changes, blood clots; must remember (pill)
Barrier (condom) protects against STIs; hormonal does not
Barrier: can split/be used incorrectly; no hormonal side effects
Conclusion: depends on needs, e.g. hormonal plus condom gives best protection against pregnancy and STIs
exam.tip: Balanced points plus a justified conclusion are needed for the top band.

worked.q: Data: in one year, 0.3% of combined pill users with perfect use and 9% with typical use became pregnant. Calculate how many of 2000 typical users would become pregnant, and explain the difference from perfect use.
steps: Typical use: 9% of 2000 = 0.09 x 2000 = 180 pregnancies.
Perfect use: 0.3% of 2000 = 0.003 x 2000 = 6 pregnancies.
Difference: 180 - 6 = 174.
Typical use includes missed pills, late pills, or vomiting, so hormone levels drop and FSH and LH are no longer inhibited; ovulation can happen.
worked.ans: 180 typical users would become pregnant (174 more than with perfect use), because in real life pills are missed so ovulation is not always prevented.

worked.q: A couple want contraception. They are in a new relationship and do not know each other's sexual health. Recommend a method and justify it.
steps: Identify the needs: prevent pregnancy AND avoid STIs.
Hormonal methods are very effective against pregnancy (over 99%) but give no STI protection.
Condoms protect against STIs and are about 98% effective with correct use.
Combining a condom with a hormonal method gives both high effectiveness and STI protection.
worked.ans: Use a condom (for STI protection), ideally with a hormonal method such as the pill or implant for maximum protection against pregnancy.

worked.q: Model answer: explain why a woman taking the combined pill does not ovulate.
steps: The pill keeps blood oestrogen and progesterone levels high.
These hormones inhibit the release of FSH and LH from the pituitary gland.
Without FSH, no egg matures in a follicle.
Without an LH surge, no egg is released, so there is no ovulation.
worked.ans: High oestrogen and progesterone from the pill inhibit FSH and LH, so no egg matures and there is no LH surge to trigger ovulation.

bio_edx.6.5.summary: Some couples are infertile because the woman does not ovulate or because eggs and sperm cannot meet naturally. **Assisted reproductive technology (ART)** uses the same hormones that control the menstrual cycle to help. **Clomifene therapy** is a drug that makes the pituitary release more **FSH and LH**, so an egg matures and is released. In **IVF (in vitro fertilisation)** the woman is given FSH and LH so several eggs mature, the eggs are collected and fertilised outside the body, and an embryo is placed into the uterus.

core.p: The menstrual cycle is controlled by four hormones. **FSH** (follicle stimulating hormone) from the pituitary gland makes a follicle containing an egg mature in the ovary. **LH** (luteinising hormone) from the pituitary triggers **ovulation**, the release of the egg. **Oestrogen** and **progesterone** from the ovaries build up and maintain the uterus lining. If any of these is missing or too low, a woman may not ovulate, so she cannot become pregnant. Doctors can give hormones (or drugs that change hormone levels) to fix this.
bullets: **Infertility** means a couple cannot conceive after trying for a long time (usually a year or more).
A common cause in women is **not ovulating** (no egg is released), often because too little FSH or LH is made.
Other causes: blocked oviducts (egg and sperm cannot meet), low sperm count, or unknown causes.
ART is the name for medical treatments that help people have a baby; Edexcel names **IVF** and **clomifene therapy**.
Both treatments work by raising **FSH and LH** at the right time, because these are the hormones that make eggs mature and be released.

callouts.p: Medical treatments, often using hormones, that help infertile couples to have children, such as clomifene therapy and IVF.

core.h: Reminder: what FSH and LH do
core.p: You must link each treatment to the job each hormone does. Examiners give marks for naming the hormone **and** its effect.
bullets: **FSH**: secreted by the **pituitary gland**; causes a **follicle to mature** (develop) in the ovary; also stimulates the ovary to make oestrogen.
**LH**: secreted by the **pituitary gland**; a surge of LH around day 14 causes **ovulation** (egg released from the follicle).
**Oestrogen**: secreted by the ovaries; thickens the uterus lining; at low levels it **inhibits** FSH and LH release (negative feedback).
**Progesterone**: secreted by the corpus luteum; **maintains** the thick uterus lining so an embryo can implant.

head: Hormone
Made in
Effect used in ART
rows: Its negative feedback on FSH and LH is blocked by clomifene
Given after IVF to maintain the uterus lining

callouts.p: Clomifene therapy and IVF both increase FSH and LH so that eggs mature and are released.

core.p: **Clomifene** is a drug, usually taken as tablets for a few days early in the menstrual cycle. It is used for women who **do not ovulate regularly** because they make too little FSH and LH. It does not contain FSH or LH itself: it makes the woman's own pituitary gland release more of them.
bullets: Given to women who **do not release eggs** (do not ovulate) or ovulate irregularly.
Taken as tablets near the **start of the cycle**, when follicles are beginning to develop.
Result: **more FSH and LH** are secreted by the pituitary gland.
More FSH makes a **follicle mature**; more LH causes **ovulation**.
The couple then try to conceive naturally (fertilisation happens inside the body), so the timing of sex around ovulation matters.
It is cheaper and less invasive than IVF, so it is often tried first.

callouts.p: A fertility treatment in which the drug clomifene is given to a woman who does not ovulate; it causes more FSH and LH to be released, so eggs mature and are released.

core.p: Normally **oestrogen** from the ovary feeds back to the hypothalamus and pituitary and **inhibits** the release of FSH and LH. Clomifene **blocks oestrogen receptors** in the brain, so the brain behaves as if oestrogen is low. The **negative feedback is removed**, and the pituitary releases **more FSH and LH**. This extra FSH makes a follicle mature, and extra LH triggers ovulation.
bullets: Oestrogen normally **inhibits** FSH (and LH) release: this is negative feedback.
Clomifene stops oestrogen having this effect on the hypothalamus and pituitary.
So the pituitary **increases** its secretion of FSH and LH.
**FSH rises** so a follicle (egg) matures; **LH rises** so ovulation occurs.
For most mark schemes, the key line is simply: clomifene **causes more FSH and LH to be released**, so **ovulation** happens.

callouts.p: At GCSE you get the marks for: increases FSH and LH, stimulates egg maturation (FSH) and ovulation (LH). The receptor-blocking detail is extra grade 9 explanation.
Clomifene is not FSH or LH. It is a drug that makes the woman's own pituitary gland release more of them.

core.h: Effect of clomifene on hormone levels
core.p: If you are shown a graph, clomifene therapy shows up as **higher FSH (and LH) levels** in the first part of the cycle than without treatment, followed by ovulation. Without treatment, FSH stays too low for a follicle to mature, so there is no LH surge and no ovulation.
bullets: Without treatment: FSH stays low, follicles do not mature fully, no LH surge, no egg released.
With clomifene: FSH rises higher, a follicle matures, oestrogen rises, an **LH surge** follows and the egg is released.
When describing a graph, quote the trend and give the link: higher FSH, so follicle matures.

core.p: **IVF** stands for **in vitro fertilisation**. In vitro means 'in glass': the egg is fertilised **outside the body**, in a dish in the laboratory, and the embryo is then put into the woman's uterus. IVF is used when the oviducts are blocked, sperm cannot reach the egg, when clomifene has not worked, or for unexplained infertility.
bullets: Fertilisation happens **outside the body** (in a Petri dish).
Hormones are used to make **several eggs mature at once**, so there are several eggs to collect.
Eggs are **collected** from the ovaries, mixed with the father's **sperm**, and fertilised.
The fertilised eggs develop into **embryos** (small balls of cells).
One or two embryos are **inserted into the uterus**, where one may implant and develop into a baby.
If sperm are poor swimmers, a single sperm can be injected straight into the egg.

callouts.p: Eggs are collected from a woman, fertilised by sperm outside the body in a laboratory, and the resulting embryos are placed in the woman's uterus.

core.h: The hormones used in IVF, step by step
core.p: Hormones are used at several stages of IVF. Learn the order and the reason for each one.
bullets: **Step 1: FSH injections** (often given with LH) for about 10 to 12 days, so that **many follicles mature** at the same time instead of just one.
**Step 2: an injection of LH** (or a hormone that acts like LH) to cause **final maturation** of the eggs just before collection.
**Step 3: eggs collected** from the ovaries with a fine needle, guided by ultrasound.
**Step 4: eggs mixed with sperm** in a dish so fertilisation happens.
**Step 5: embryos grow** for a few days and are checked to see they are developing normally.
**Step 6: one or two embryos inserted** into the uterus through the cervix.
**Progesterone** (sometimes with oestrogen) may be given to **keep the uterus lining thick** so the embryo can implant.
Some clinics first give a drug to switch off the woman's natural cycle so that eggs are not released before collection.

callouts.p: So that several eggs mature at once, giving more eggs to collect and fertilise, which raises the chance of at least one healthy embryo.

fig.cap: The main stages of IVF, in order 1 to 6. FSH and LH injections make several eggs mature, the eggs are collected and fertilised with sperm in a dish, and an embryo is placed into the uterus. Progesterone helps keep the lining ready for implantation.

core.p: Both treatments use hormones to increase FSH and LH, but they are used for different problems and differ in cost and risk.
bullets: Clomifene: fertilisation **inside the body**; IVF: fertilisation **outside the body**.
Clomifene: tablets; IVF: injections, egg collection and embryo transfer.
Clomifene helps only if the problem is **not ovulating**; IVF can also help with blocked oviducts or low sperm count.

head: Feature
Clomifene therapy
IVF
rows: FSH and LH injections, then progesterone
Pituitary releases more FSH and LH
Extra FSH and LH given directly
In a dish in a laboratory
Blocked oviducts, low sperm count, failed clomifene

core.p: When evaluating, give benefits and drawbacks and finish with a judgement.
bullets: Allows infertile couples to have their **own biological child**.
Clomifene is **simple and cheap** and avoids surgery.
IVF can work when the oviducts are blocked, because fertilisation happens outside the body.
In IVF, embryos can be **checked** before transfer, so only healthy-looking embryos are used.
Spare embryos can be frozen and used later without repeating the hormone treatment.

core.p: Hormone treatments can make **more than one egg** mature, and IVF may involve transferring more than one embryo. This is the biggest risk examiners ask about.
bullets: **Multiple births** (twins, triplets): risky for the mother and babies, for example premature birth and low birth weight.
**Low success rate**: many IVF cycles do not lead to a baby, and success falls as the woman gets older.
IVF is **expensive** and may need to be repeated.
It is **emotionally and physically stressful** for the couple.
Side effects of the hormones, and in a few cases the ovaries over-react to the fertility drugs and swell (overstimulation).
**Ethical issues** with IVF: unused embryos may be destroyed; some people object to this.

callouts.p: Fertility hormones can cause several eggs to mature and be released (or several embryos to be transferred in IVF), so more than one baby may develop.

core.p: Doctors use the biology of the treatment to lower the risks.
bullets: Hormone levels and follicle growth are **monitored** (blood tests and ultrasound) so the dose can be adjusted.
Transferring **only one embryo** greatly reduces the chance of twins or triplets.
Clomifene is given for a **limited number of cycles** at the lowest dose that works.

core.h: Linking ART to the menstrual cycle and contraception
core.p: This point uses the same hormones as contraception but in the opposite direction. The contraceptive pill gives oestrogen and progesterone to **inhibit FSH and LH**, so no egg matures or is released. Fertility treatment does the reverse: it **increases FSH and LH** so eggs do mature and are released.
bullets: Contraception: **lower** FSH and LH, so no ovulation.
Fertility treatment: **raise** FSH and LH, so ovulation (or many eggs for IVF).
Seeing this link helps with 6 mark questions that compare uses of hormones.

callouts.p: For each treatment: name the hormone or drug, say what it does to FSH/LH, say what that does to the egg, then add one evaluation point.

analogy.t: A thermostat with its sensor covered
analogy.p: Oestrogen acts like a thermostat sensor telling the pituitary 'enough, turn the FSH down'. Clomifene is like putting a cloth over the sensor: the pituitary thinks oestrogen is low and turns the FSH and LH up, so an egg matures and is released. IVF is different: it is like bypassing the thermostat and turning the heater up directly, by injecting FSH and LH. Where it breaks down: a real thermostat controls one output, but the pituitary makes two hormones with different jobs, and the body's response to the hormones is not exactly predictable, so several eggs may be released.

terms.d: Being unable to conceive a child naturally.
Medical treatments that help infertile couples have children, including clomifene therapy and IVF.
Follicle stimulating hormone, secreted by the pituitary gland; causes a follicle (egg) to mature in the ovary.
Luteinising hormone, secreted by the pituitary gland; a surge of LH causes ovulation.
The release of a mature egg from a follicle in the ovary.
A fluid-filled structure in the ovary in which an egg matures.
A fertility drug that causes the pituitary gland to release more FSH and LH, so ovulation occurs.
Treatment of women who do not ovulate with the drug clomifene to stimulate egg maturation and ovulation.
In vitro fertilisation: fertilising eggs with sperm outside the body in a laboratory, then putting an embryo into the uterus.
Taking place outside a living organism, for example in a dish in a laboratory.
The ball of cells that develops from a fertilised egg by mitosis.
When an embryo attaches to and embeds in the thick lining of the uterus.
A change causes a response that reverses the change; here oestrogen inhibits FSH and LH release.
Hormone that maintains the thick uterus lining; may be given after embryo transfer in IVF.
More than one baby born from one pregnancy, a risk of fertility treatment.

mistakes.w: Clomifene is a hormone that releases eggs.
mistakes.r: Clomifene is a drug that causes more FSH and LH to be released by the pituitary gland; FSH matures the egg and LH causes ovulation.

mistakes.w: In IVF the egg is fertilised in the uterus.
mistakes.r: In IVF fertilisation happens outside the body (in vitro), in a dish; the embryo is then inserted into the uterus.

mistakes.w: IVF women are given oestrogen to make eggs mature.
mistakes.r: They are given FSH (and LH) to make several eggs mature.

mistakes.w: FSH causes ovulation.
mistakes.r: FSH causes follicles/eggs to mature; LH causes ovulation.

mistakes.w: The eggs are injected back into the woman.
mistakes.r: Embryos (fertilised eggs that have divided) are inserted into the uterus.

mistakes.w: FSH and LH are made in the ovaries.
mistakes.r: FSH and LH are secreted by the pituitary gland.

mistakes.w: A disadvantage is that the baby might be ill.
mistakes.r: Name a specific risk: multiple births (twins/triplets) with risks of premature birth, low success rate, cost, or ethical issues over unused embryos.

mistakes.w: Clomifene and IVF both put more sperm in.
mistakes.r: Both treatments act on the woman's hormones (FSH and LH) to make eggs mature and be released.

exam.q: Name the gland that secretes FSH and LH.
model: Pituitary gland
exam.tip: Not hypothalamus and not ovary.

exam.q: State what IVF stands for.
model: In vitro fertilisation
exam.tip: Spell 'vitro' correctly; 'in vitro' means outside the body.

exam.q: Explain how clomifene therapy can help a woman who does not ovulate to become pregnant.
model: Clomifene causes more FSH and LH to be released (from the pituitary)
FSH causes an egg/follicle to mature
LH causes ovulation / release of the egg, so it can be fertilised
exam.tip: Name both hormones and give the job of each.

exam.q: Explain why a woman having IVF is given injections of FSH.
model: FSH stimulates follicles / eggs to mature
so several eggs mature at once to be collected (increasing chance of success)
exam.tip: The word 'several' or 'many' earns the second mark.

exam.q: Give one reason why a woman having IVF may be given progesterone after embryo transfer.
model: To maintain the (thick) uterus lining so the embryo can implant
exam.tip: Maintain, not build up from nothing.

exam.q: Describe the stages of IVF.
model: Woman given FSH (and LH) to make several eggs mature
Eggs collected from the ovaries
Eggs fertilised by sperm outside the body / in a dish
Embryo(s) inserted into the uterus
exam.tip: Keep the stages in order; one mark per correct stage.

exam.q: State one risk to the mother and babies of fertility treatment with hormones.
model: Multiple births / twins or triplets (with risk of premature birth or low birth weight)
exam.tip: Multiple births is the answer examiners look for first.

exam.q: Explain why clomifene would not help a woman whose oviducts are blocked, but IVF could.
model: Clomifene only causes ovulation; the egg still cannot travel down the oviduct to meet sperm
In IVF eggs are collected from the ovary and fertilised outside the body, so the oviduct is bypassed
exam.tip: Link to where fertilisation normally happens: the oviduct.

exam.q: Clomifene affects the negative feedback of oestrogen on the pituitary gland. Explain how this increases the chance of ovulation.
model: Normally oestrogen inhibits FSH and LH release
clomifene stops/blocks this inhibition so more FSH and LH are released
more FSH so egg matures and more LH so ovulation occurs
exam.tip: Higher-level answers mention negative feedback by name.

exam.q: Evaluate the use of hormones in assisted reproductive technology to treat infertility.
model: Clomifene increases FSH and LH so ovulation occurs in women who do not ovulate
In IVF, FSH and LH injections make several eggs mature for collection
Eggs fertilised outside the body and embryo inserted into the uterus
Advantage: couples can have their own biological child; clomifene is cheap and non-invasive
Disadvantages: risk of multiple births, low success rate, IVF expensive and stressful, ethical issues over unused embryos
Conclusion: a justified judgement, for example worthwhile if only one embryo is transferred to reduce multiple births
exam.tip: 6 markers need both treatments, both sides, and a conclusion.

worked.q: A woman has very low FSH levels and does not ovulate. Explain which treatment a doctor would try first and why.
steps: Identify the problem: low FSH means follicles do not mature, so there is no LH surge and no egg is released.
Clomifene causes the pituitary to release more FSH and LH.
More FSH makes a follicle mature; more LH causes ovulation.
Clomifene is tablets, cheaper and less invasive than IVF, so it is tried first.
worked.ans: Clomifene therapy first, because it raises FSH and LH so she ovulates, and it is cheaper and simpler than IVF; IVF would be used if clomifene fails.

worked.q: An IVF clinic transfers two embryos into each patient. Of 200 patients, 60 become pregnant and 12 of these have twins. Calculate the percentage of patients who became pregnant, and the percentage of pregnancies that were twins. Suggest how the clinic could reduce twin births.
steps: Percentage pregnant = 60 / 200 x 100 = 30%.
Percentage of pregnancies that were twins = 12 / 60 x 100 = 20%.
Twins happen because both embryos implant.
Transferring only one embryo would reduce twin pregnancies (although the success rate per cycle may fall).
worked.ans: 30% became pregnant; 20% of pregnancies were twins; transfer only one embryo per cycle.

worked.q: Model answer: Describe the roles of FSH and LH in IVF treatment. (3 marks)
steps: FSH is injected to stimulate several follicles / eggs to mature.
LH is injected to cause final maturation of the eggs (just before collection).
The mature eggs are then collected and fertilised outside the body.
worked.ans: FSH makes several eggs mature; LH completes egg maturation; the eggs are collected and fertilised in a dish.

bio_edx.6.6.summary: **Homeostasis** is the maintenance of a **constant internal environment** in the body, even when conditions inside or outside the body change. The body keeps **body temperature**, **blood glucose concentration** and **water content** (the concentration of body fluids) within narrow limits. This matters because **enzymes** and **cells** only work properly in a narrow range of conditions. Control systems use **receptors**, **coordination centres** and **effectors**, usually linked by **negative feedback**, through the nervous system and hormones.

core.p: Your cells sit in tissue fluid, and the conditions in that fluid (temperature, glucose concentration, water and ion concentration) make up the **internal environment**. Homeostasis is keeping these conditions **constant**, or more exactly within a narrow range around a normal value, no matter what changes happen.
bullets: **Internal environment**: the conditions inside the body that surround the cells, such as blood and tissue fluid.
**Constant** really means kept **within narrow limits**: values move up and down a little around a normal level (the set point).
Homeostasis responds to **internal changes** (e.g. heat from exercise, glucose absorbed after a meal) and **external changes** (e.g. a cold day, a hot drink, losing water on a hot day).
It is **automatic**: you do not have to think about it.
Homeostasis is controlled by the **nervous system** and the **endocrine (hormone) system**.

callouts.p: The maintenance of a constant internal environment in the body, in response to internal and external changes.

core.p: Edexcel expects you to know the three conditions controlled by homeostasis in humans.
bullets: **Body temperature**: kept at about **37 °C**.
**Blood glucose concentration**: kept within narrow limits by the hormones **insulin** and **glucagon** from the pancreas.
**Water content of the body** (concentration of blood and body fluids, osmoregulation): controlled by the kidneys (and, in triple biology, the hormone ADH).
Each one has its own spec point; here you need the **big idea**: why keeping them constant matters and how control systems work.

head: Condition
Normal value
Main organs involved
Danger if not controlled
rows: Enzymes work too slowly or denature
Narrow range (about 4 to 7 mmol per dm3)
Cells lack glucose for respiration, or water leaves cells
Cells swell or shrink by osmosis

callouts.p: Temperature, blood glucose and water levels are the three homeostatic conditions.

core.p: Almost every reaction in cells, including respiration, is controlled by **enzymes**. Enzymes have an **optimum temperature** and **optimum pH**. In humans the optimum temperature is about 37 °C. If the body gets too cold, enzyme-controlled reactions become **too slow** to keep cells alive. If it gets too hot, the enzymes' **active sites change shape** (they **denature**), so substrates no longer fit and reactions stop.
bullets: Too cold: molecules have less kinetic energy, fewer successful collisions, reactions (e.g. respiration) slow down: risk of **hypothermia**.
Too hot: bonds holding the enzyme in shape break, the **active site changes shape**, enzyme denatures: risk of **heat stroke**.
Keeping temperature constant keeps enzymes working at or near their **optimum rate**.
This is the reason examiners most often want: **enzymes need a constant temperature (and pH) to work efficiently**.

callouts.p: Enzymes are not 'killed' by heat. They are denatured: the active site changes shape so the substrate no longer fits.

fig.cap: Enzyme activity against temperature. Human enzymes work fastest at about 37 °C. Below this reactions are slow; above it the enzymes denature. This is why body temperature must be kept constant.

core.h: Why constant conditions matter: water and cells
core.p: Water moves into and out of cells by **osmosis**, from a dilute solution to a more concentrated solution across the partially permeable cell membrane. If body fluids become too concentrated or too dilute, the cells are damaged.
bullets: Body fluid **too dilute** (too much water): water moves **into** cells by osmosis, cells **swell** and may burst (animal cells have no cell wall).
Body fluid **too concentrated** (too little water): water moves **out of** cells by osmosis, cells **shrink** and stop working properly.
Keeping the water content and ion concentration constant keeps cells the right size and shape, so they function normally.
We gain water from food, drink and respiration; we lose it in urine, sweat, faeces and breath, so control is always needed.

core.h: Why constant conditions matter: blood glucose
core.p: Cells need **glucose** for **respiration** to release energy. The brain in particular relies on a steady supply of glucose.
bullets: **Too low** blood glucose: cells do not get enough glucose for respiration, so they cannot release enough energy; the person may feel weak, faint or become unconscious.
**Too high** blood glucose: the blood becomes more concentrated, so water moves **out of** cells by osmosis; over time high glucose damages blood vessels and organs.
Insulin lowers blood glucose; glucagon raises it. Together they keep it in a narrow range (see the blood glucose spec point).

core.p: The question wording 'in response to internal and external change' is from the spec, so be ready to give examples of both.
bullets: **External** changes: hot or cold weather, a hot bath, swimming in cold water, a hot dry day that makes you sweat.
**Internal** changes: heat released by muscles during exercise, glucose absorbed after a meal, glucose used up during exercise or fasting, water lost in sweat, salty food raising ion concentration.
Homeostasis responds to the **effect** of these changes on the internal environment and reverses it.

head: Change
Internal or external
Condition affected
rows: Body temperature rises, blood glucose falls, water lost in sweat
Temperature rises and water is lost in sweat

core.p: All homeostatic control systems have the same three parts. Learn them in order.
bullets: **Receptors** (sensors): cells that **detect a change** (stimulus) in the internal environment, e.g. temperature receptors in the skin and brain.
**Coordination centre**: receives and **processes information** from receptors and decides on the response, e.g. the **brain** (hypothalamus), spinal cord or the **pancreas**.
**Effectors**: **muscles or glands** that carry out the response to **restore** the normal level, e.g. sweat glands, muscles that shiver, the liver storing glucose.
Information travels by **nerve impulses** (fast, short-lived) or **hormones** in the blood (slower, longer-lasting).

callouts.p: A muscle or gland that brings about a response to a stimulus.

core.p: Homeostasis works by **negative feedback**. If a level **rises above** normal, the response makes it **fall**; if it **falls below** normal, the response makes it **rise**. The response always **opposes (reverses) the change**, so the level returns to normal. The level then keeps being monitored, so the loop repeats.
bullets: Step 1: a change from the normal level happens.
Step 2: **receptors detect** the change.
Step 3: the **coordination centre** processes the information.
Step 4: **effectors** respond.
Step 5: the change is **reversed** and the level returns to normal.
Because the loop repeats, levels **fluctuate slightly** around the normal value rather than staying perfectly still.
Often there are **two opposing** effectors or hormones (e.g. insulin and glucagon; sweating and shivering), giving finer control.

callouts.p: A control mechanism in which a change from the normal level causes a response that reverses the change, returning the level to normal.
Use the phrase 'returns to normal' or 'reverses the change'. Just saying 'the body responds' gets no mark.

core.h: What negative feedback looks like on a graph
core.p: On a graph of a homeostatic variable against time you see the level **oscillating** in small swings around the normal value. Each time it moves too far one way, a response brings it back.
bullets: Rise above normal, then a fall back (e.g. sweating cools the body).
Fall below normal, then a rise back (e.g. shivering warms the body).
When describing a graph, give the direction of change, the response and the result: 'temperature rose above 37 °C, so sweating increased and temperature fell back to 37 °C'.

fig.cap: Body temperature over time, kept near 37 °C by negative feedback. When it rises, sweating brings it down; when it falls, shivering brings it up, so it fluctuates in small swings around the normal value.

core.h: Nervous and hormonal control in homeostasis
core.p: Both coordination systems are used. Nerves give fast responses; hormones give slower but longer-lasting ones.
bullets: **Temperature**: mainly nervous: the hypothalamus sends nerve impulses to sweat glands, blood vessels in the skin and muscles.
**Blood glucose**: hormonal: the pancreas releases insulin or glucagon into the blood.
**Water content**: the kidneys adjust how much water is lost in urine (controlled by the hormone ADH, triple only).

core.p: When a control system fails or is overwhelmed, conditions move outside safe limits and the person becomes ill. These examples show why homeostasis is important.
bullets: **Type 1 diabetes**: the pancreas does not make enough insulin, so blood glucose can rise too high.
**Hypothermia**: core temperature falls too low; enzyme reactions slow and organs fail.
**Heat stroke**: core temperature rises too high; enzymes denature.
**Dehydration** or drinking far too much water: cells shrink or swell by osmosis.
**Kidney failure** (triple): water and ion balance cannot be controlled and urea builds up.

callouts.p: Homeostasis keeps conditions optimal for enzyme action and cell function.

analogy.p: A house thermostat is set to 20 °C (the set point). A temperature sensor (receptor) detects the room getting colder, the control box (coordination centre) switches the boiler (effector) on, the room warms up, and the boiler switches off again: negative feedback. An air conditioner would be the opposing effector that cools the room. Where it breaks down: the body controls many conditions at once, uses both nerves and hormones, and many effectors are living cells that can also be damaged by the very conditions they control; a thermostat also only switches on or off, while body responses can be graded.

terms.d: Maintaining a constant internal environment in response to internal and external changes.
The conditions surrounding the body's cells, such as blood and tissue fluid.
The value the body tries to keep a condition at, e.g. 37 °C for body temperature.
A change in the environment (internal or external) that can be detected.
A cell or group of cells that detects a stimulus.
An organ such as the brain, spinal cord or pancreas that receives information and coordinates a response.
A muscle or gland that carries out a response.
A response that reverses a change from the normal level, returning conditions to normal.
A biological catalyst; a protein that speeds up reactions and works best at an optimum temperature and pH.
When an enzyme's active site changes shape (e.g. by high temperature) so the substrate no longer fits.
The net movement of water from a dilute solution to a more concentrated solution through a partially permeable membrane.
Control of the water content and concentration of body fluids.
Control of body temperature.
A chemical messenger secreted by a gland into the blood that acts on target organs.

mistakes.w: Homeostasis keeps the body exactly the same all the time.
mistakes.r: Homeostasis keeps conditions within narrow limits around a normal level; values fluctuate slightly.

mistakes.w: If the body is too hot, enzymes die.
mistakes.r: Enzymes are denatured: the active site changes shape so the substrate no longer fits.

mistakes.w: Negative feedback means something bad happens.
mistakes.r: Negative feedback means the response reverses the change, returning the level to normal.

mistakes.w: Homeostasis controls the external environment.
mistakes.r: It controls the internal environment of the body in response to internal and external changes.

mistakes.w: Too much water in the blood makes cells shrink.
mistakes.r: Too dilute: water enters cells by osmosis and they swell; too concentrated: water leaves and they shrink.

mistakes.w: Effectors detect changes.
mistakes.r: Receptors detect changes; effectors (muscles or glands) carry out the response.

mistakes.w: Cells need constant glucose to make energy.
mistakes.r: Cells need glucose for respiration, which releases (transfers) energy; energy is not made.

mistakes.w: Homeostasis is controlled only by hormones.
mistakes.r: It involves both the nervous system and the endocrine (hormone) system.

exam.q: Define the term homeostasis.
model: Maintaining a constant internal environment (in response to internal and external changes)
exam.tip: Say internal environment, not just 'the body'.

exam.q: Name two conditions in the human body controlled by homeostasis.
model: Body temperature
Blood glucose concentration / water content (of the blood or body)
exam.tip: Be specific: blood glucose, not just sugar.

exam.q: Explain why it is important that body temperature is kept at about 37 °C.
model: 37 °C is the optimum temperature for enzymes
too high: enzymes denature / active site changes shape; too low: reactions are too slow
exam.tip: Always link temperature to enzymes.

exam.q: State the name of the type of control mechanism used in homeostasis.
model: Negative feedback
exam.tip: Not positive feedback.

exam.q: Describe what is meant by negative feedback.
model: A change from the normal level is detected
a response reverses the change / returns the level to normal
exam.tip: Include both the detection and the reversal.

exam.q: Explain why the water content of the blood must be kept constant.
model: Water moves into or out of cells by osmosis
if blood is too dilute, water enters cells and they swell / burst
if blood is too concentrated, water leaves cells and they shrink, so cells do not function properly
exam.tip: Use the word osmosis and give direction of water movement.

exam.q: Give one internal change and one external change that could affect body temperature.
model: Internal: heat released by muscles during exercise / respiration
External: cold weather / hot environment / swimming in cold water
exam.tip: Label which is which.

exam.q: Describe the roles of receptors, the coordination centre and effectors in a homeostatic control system.
model: Receptors detect a change (stimulus)
Coordination centre (e.g. brain / pancreas) processes information and coordinates response
Effectors (muscles or glands) bring about a response that restores the normal level
exam.tip: One clear job for each part.

exam.q: A graph shows a person's body temperature rising during exercise and then falling back to 37 °C. Explain how this shows negative feedback.
model: The rise in temperature is detected / causes a response such as sweating
which reverses the change so temperature returns to 37 °C
exam.tip: Quote the graph and name a response.

exam.q: Explain the importance of maintaining a constant internal environment in response to internal and external change.
model: Homeostasis keeps conditions within narrow limits despite internal and external changes
Constant temperature (about 37 °C) keeps enzymes at their optimum; too hot denatures, too cold slows reactions
Constant water content prevents cells swelling or shrinking by osmosis
Constant blood glucose provides glucose for respiration / prevents water leaving cells
Changes detected by receptors, coordinated by brain / pancreas, effectors respond
Negative feedback reverses changes using nervous and hormonal responses, so cells and enzymes function properly
exam.tip: Cover all three conditions with a reason for each, plus how control works.

worked.q: A student's blood glucose was 5.0 mmol per dm3 before lunch and 7.5 mmol per dm3 one hour after lunch. Calculate the percentage increase, then describe how homeostasis responds.
steps: Increase = 7.5 - 5.0 = 2.5 mmol per dm3.
Percentage increase = 2.5 / 5.0 x 100 = 50%.
The rise is an internal change (glucose absorbed from the meal).
It is detected by the pancreas, which releases insulin; the liver and muscles take up glucose and store it as glycogen.
Blood glucose falls back to normal: negative feedback.
worked.ans: 50% increase; insulin is released, reversing the change so blood glucose returns to normal.

worked.q: Model answer: A climber is on a mountain in freezing weather. Explain why her body must keep her core temperature constant and how this is achieved. (4 marks)
steps: The cold air is an external change that lowers body temperature.
Temperature receptors detect the fall; the brain (hypothalamus) coordinates a response.
Effectors respond, e.g. muscles shiver to release heat by respiration, which raises temperature back towards 37 °C (negative feedback).
This keeps enzymes at their optimum temperature so reactions such as respiration do not slow down too much.
worked.ans: Receptors detect the fall, the brain coordinates, effectors such as shivering muscles warm the body, keeping enzymes near their 37 °C optimum.

worked.q: Applied example: A runner loses 1.5 dm3 of water in sweat during a race and drinks nothing. Explain the effect on her cells and the homeostatic response.
steps: Water loss makes the blood more concentrated.
Water moves out of cells by osmosis, so cells shrink and work less well.
The change is detected and the kidneys respond by producing a smaller volume of more concentrated urine, conserving water.
Drinking (thirst) also restores water content.
worked.ans: Cells lose water by osmosis and shrink; the kidneys conserve water so the water content returns towards normal.

bio_edx.6.7.summary: **Thermoregulation** is the homeostatic control of body temperature at about **37 °C**, the optimum for human enzymes. The **thermoregulatory centre in the hypothalamus** detects the temperature of the blood and receives nerve impulses from temperature receptors in the **skin**. It then sends impulses to effectors in the skin and muscles. When too hot: **vasodilation** and more **sweating** increase heat loss. When too cold: **vasoconstriction**, less sweating and **shivering** reduce heat loss and release more heat.

core.p: Thermoregulation is part of homeostasis. The body keeps its **core temperature** at about **37 °C** because this is the **optimum temperature for enzymes**. Heat is constantly released by **respiration** (especially in muscles and the liver) and constantly lost to, or gained from, the surroundings. The body balances heat gain against heat loss.
bullets: Too hot (above about 37 °C): enzymes **denature** as their active sites change shape; serious overheating is **heat stroke**.
Too cold: enzyme-controlled reactions such as respiration become **too slow**; serious cooling is **hypothermia**.
Heat is **gained** from respiration and from hot surroundings.
Heat is **lost** mainly through the **skin** by radiation, conduction, convection and **evaporation of sweat**.
Control is by **negative feedback**: any change from 37 °C triggers responses that reverse it.

callouts.p: The control of body temperature, keeping it at about 37 °C by balancing heat gain and heat loss.

core.p: The skin is the main organ for exchanging heat with the surroundings. Edexcel names the **dermis**, **sweat glands** and **blood vessels** as the parts you must explain.
bullets: **Epidermis**: the thin outer layer of skin cells; sweat pores open onto its surface.

**Dermis**: the thicker layer below the epidermis; it contains **sweat glands**, **blood vessels** (arterioles and capillaries), **hair follicles**, **erector muscles** and **temperature receptors** (nerve endings).
**Sweat glands**: coiled glands in the dermis that secrete sweat through a duct to a pore on the skin surface.
**Blood vessels**: arterioles carry blood to **capillaries near the skin surface**; shunt vessels can carry blood deeper, bypassing the surface capillaries.
**Fat layer** (below the dermis): insulates the body and reduces heat loss.

head: Part of skin
Role in thermoregulation
rows: Contains the sweat glands, blood vessels and temperature receptors
Detect skin (external) temperature; send impulses to the hypothalamus
Secrete sweat; evaporation transfers heat away from the skin
Widen or narrow to change how much blood flows near the surface
Raise hairs to trap an insulating layer of air (more useful in furry mammals)

core.p: The **hypothalamus** is a small region at the base of the brain. It contains the **thermoregulatory centre**, which acts as the **coordination centre** for temperature control.
bullets: It contains **receptors that monitor the temperature of the blood** flowing through the brain (this is the **core** body temperature).
It also **receives nerve impulses** from **temperature receptors in the skin**, which detect external temperature changes early.
It **compares** the temperature with the normal value of about 37 °C.
It **sends nerve impulses** to **effectors**: sweat glands, muscles in the walls of arterioles in the skin, skeletal muscles (shivering) and erector muscles.
This control is mainly **nervous**, so responses are **fast**.

callouts.p: Hypothalamus = thermoregulatory centre. It monitors blood temperature and receives impulses from skin receptors, then sends impulses to effectors.
The hypothalamus is in the brain. It is not the pituitary gland and it does not release a hormone to control temperature at GCSE.

core.h: Responses when the body is too hot
core.p: If core temperature rises above 37 °C (e.g. during exercise or on a hot day), the hypothalamus triggers responses that **increase heat loss**.
bullets: **Vasodilation**: arterioles supplying the skin capillaries **widen (dilate)**, so **more blood flows near the skin surface** and **more heat is lost by radiation**.
**Sweating**: sweat glands **secrete more sweat**; the water in sweat **evaporates** from the skin and evaporation **transfers heat energy** away from the skin, cooling it.
**Hairs lie flat** (erector muscles relax), so less air is trapped and heat escapes more easily.
**No shivering**: muscles do not contract to release extra heat.
Result: heat loss is greater than heat gain, so temperature **falls back to 37 °C** (negative feedback).

callouts.p: Say sweat cools the skin when it evaporates. Sweat on its own does not cool you; it is the evaporation that transfers heat.

core.h: Responses when the body is too cold
core.p: If core temperature falls below 37 °C, the hypothalamus triggers responses that **reduce heat loss** and **increase heat release**.
bullets: **Vasoconstriction**: arterioles supplying the skin capillaries **narrow (constrict)**, so **less blood flows near the skin surface** and **less heat is lost by radiation**; blood goes through deeper shunt vessels instead.
**Less sweat** (or none) is secreted, so less heat is lost by evaporation.
**Shivering**: skeletal muscles **contract and relax rapidly**; this needs more **respiration**, which **releases heat**, warming the body.
**Hairs stand up** (erector muscles contract), trapping a layer of air that **insulates** the skin.
Result: heat is conserved and produced, so temperature **rises back to 37 °C**.

callouts.p: Rapid, involuntary contraction and relaxation of skeletal muscles, which increases respiration and so releases heat.

fig.cap: Summary of how the hypothalamus responds. Above 37 °C it causes vasodilation and sweating so more heat is lost. Below 37 °C it causes vasoconstriction, less sweating and shivering so less heat is lost and more is released.

core.p: These are the two responses most often tested. Both involve the **arterioles** (small arteries) that supply blood to the **capillaries near the skin surface**. The arteriole walls contain muscle, which contracts or relaxes under control of nerve impulses from the hypothalamus.
bullets: **Vasodilation**: muscle in arteriole walls **relaxes**, the arteriole **widens**, more blood flows through surface capillaries, skin looks red/flushed, **more heat lost**.
**Vasoconstriction**: muscle in arteriole walls **contracts**, the arteriole **narrows**, less blood flows through surface capillaries, skin looks pale, **less heat lost**.
The **blood vessels do not move** up or down in the skin; only their width (and so the blood flow through them) changes.
Shunt vessels let blood bypass the surface capillaries during vasoconstriction.

callouts.p: Never write 'capillaries move closer to the skin'. Write 'arterioles dilate so more blood flows through capillaries near the skin surface'.

fig.cap: Vasodilation (left) and vasoconstriction (right). When hot, the arteriole widens so lots of blood flows through capillaries near the surface and much heat is radiated. When cold, the arteriole narrows and blood is diverted through the deeper shunt vessel, so little heat is lost.

core.p: Sweat glands in the dermis secrete **sweat** (mainly water, plus salts and a little urea) onto the skin surface. When the water **evaporates**, it takes heat energy from the skin, which cools it.
bullets: Sweat production **increases** when hot and **decreases** when cold.
Sweating cools you only if the sweat can **evaporate**; in very humid air evaporation is slow, so cooling is less effective.
Sweating loses **water and salts**, so a person must drink to avoid dehydration (links to osmoregulation).
Sweat glands are **effectors**, controlled by nerve impulses from the hypothalamus.

core.p: Shivering links thermoregulation to **respiration**. Muscle contraction uses energy from respiration, and respiration is not 100% efficient: some energy is transferred to the surroundings as **heat**.
bullets: Shivering = rapid involuntary muscle contractions.
The muscles need more ATP, so the **rate of respiration increases**.
Respiration **releases heat**, which warms the blood flowing through the muscles.
Exercise warms you up for the same reason.

core.p: Put the whole thermoregulation system into the receptor, coordination centre, effector framework.
bullets: **Stimulus**: change in body temperature (internal, e.g. exercise; external, e.g. cold weather).
**Receptors**: temperature receptors in the **skin** and in the **hypothalamus** (monitoring blood).
**Coordination centre**: **thermoregulatory centre in the hypothalamus**.
**Effectors**: sweat glands, muscles in arteriole walls, skeletal muscles, erector muscles.
**Response**: changes in heat loss and heat release that bring temperature back to 37 °C.
As temperature returns to normal, the response is reduced: this is **negative feedback**.

callouts.p: Name the receptors, the hypothalamus, then each effector with its effect on heat loss, then say temperature returns to 37 °C by negative feedback.

core.h: Applying it: exercise and cold water
core.p: Exam questions often set the scene and ask you to apply the ideas.
bullets: **Running a race**: muscles respire faster, releasing heat; blood temperature rises; hypothalamus detects this; vasodilation and sweating increase; face looks red and sweaty.
**Swimming in cold water**: skin receptors detect cold; vasoconstriction makes skin pale; shivering starts; heat is lost faster in water than in air, so the risk of hypothermia is higher.
**Hot, humid day**: sweat evaporates slowly, so cooling is less effective and overheating is more likely.
**Small babies and elderly people** are more at risk of temperature problems as their control is less effective.

analogy.t: Car radiator with a smart thermostat
analogy.p: The hypothalamus is like a car's engine thermostat. The engine (your muscles and liver) makes heat. When it gets hot, the thermostat opens valves to send more coolant through the radiator at the front (vasodilation sends more blood to the skin), and a water spray on the radiator would cool it by evaporation (sweating). When it is cold, the valves close so coolant stays deep in the engine (vasoconstriction), and the engine can be revved (shivering) to make more heat. Where it breaks down: the 'pipes' near the skin are always there; only their width changes, and sweat cooling depends on how humid the air is, which a radiator does not care about.

terms.d: The control of body temperature at about 37 °C.
Part of the brain containing the thermoregulatory centre, which monitors blood temperature and coordinates responses.
The coordination centre in the hypothalamus that controls body temperature.
A nerve ending (in the skin or hypothalamus) that detects temperature changes.
The thin outer layer of the skin.
The layer of skin below the epidermis containing sweat glands, blood vessels, hair follicles and receptors.
A gland in the dermis that secretes sweat onto the skin surface; evaporation of sweat cools the body.
A small artery; arterioles supplying the skin can widen or narrow to control blood flow to surface capillaries.
A tiny blood vessel with walls one cell thick; capillaries near the skin surface lose heat to the surroundings.
Widening of arterioles supplying skin capillaries, increasing blood flow near the surface so more heat is lost.
Narrowing of arterioles supplying skin capillaries, reducing blood flow near the surface so less heat is lost.
A blood vessel that lets blood bypass the surface capillaries, used during vasoconstriction.
Rapid involuntary muscle contraction that increases respiration and releases heat.
Liquid water turning to vapour; it transfers heat energy away from the skin.
Dangerously low body temperature.
Dangerously high body temperature.

mistakes.w: Capillaries move closer to the surface of the skin.
mistakes.r: Arterioles dilate so more blood flows through the capillaries near the skin surface; blood vessels do not move.

mistakes.w: Sweat cools the body down.
mistakes.r: Evaporation of sweat (water) from the skin transfers heat energy away, cooling the body.

mistakes.w: Shivering makes energy.
mistakes.r: Shivering increases respiration in muscles, which releases heat (energy is transferred, not made).

mistakes.w: The skin controls body temperature.
mistakes.r: The thermoregulatory centre in the hypothalamus is the coordination centre; the skin contains receptors and effectors.

mistakes.w: Vasoconstriction happens when you are hot.
mistakes.r: Vasoconstriction happens when too cold, reducing heat loss; vasodilation happens when too hot.

mistakes.w: The hypothalamus detects the temperature of the air.
mistakes.r: It monitors the temperature of the blood (core temperature); skin receptors detect external temperature and send impulses to it.

mistakes.w: Blood vessels contract to make the blood colder.
mistakes.r: Arterioles constrict to reduce blood flow near the skin surface, so less heat is lost by radiation.

mistakes.w: The pituitary gland controls body temperature.
mistakes.r: The hypothalamus controls body temperature, mainly by nerve impulses.

mistakes.w: Heat damages enzymes so they die.
mistakes.r: High temperature denatures enzymes: the active site changes shape.

exam.q: Name the part of the brain that controls body temperature.
model: Hypothalamus
exam.tip: Spell it correctly.

exam.q: Name the layer of the skin that contains the sweat glands.
model: Dermis
exam.tip: Not epidermis.

exam.q: Describe how the hypothalamus detects a change in body temperature.
model: It has receptors that monitor the temperature of the blood
It receives nerve impulses from temperature receptors in the skin
exam.tip: Two sources of information = two marks.

exam.q: Explain how sweating helps to cool the body.
model: Sweat glands secrete (more) sweat onto the skin
water in sweat evaporates, transferring heat energy from the skin
exam.tip: The word 'evaporates' is essential.

exam.q: Explain how vasodilation helps to reduce body temperature.
model: Arterioles (supplying skin capillaries) widen / dilate
more blood flows through capillaries near the skin surface
more heat is lost (by radiation) to the surroundings
exam.tip: Never say the vessels move.

exam.q: Explain why a person's skin looks pale on a very cold day.
model: Vasoconstriction / arterioles narrow
less blood flows near the skin surface (to reduce heat loss)
exam.tip: Link the pale colour to reduced blood flow.

exam.q: Explain how shivering helps to raise body temperature.
model: Muscles contract rapidly, increasing (the rate of) respiration
respiration releases heat which warms the body / blood
exam.tip: Mention respiration explicitly.

exam.q: Give two differences between the body's response to being too hot and its response to being too cold.
model: Too hot: vasodilation; too cold: vasoconstriction
Too hot: more sweat; too cold: less sweat / shivering only when cold
exam.tip: Compare both sides in each point.

exam.q: Sweating is less effective at cooling the body in humid air. Suggest why.
model: The air already contains a lot of water vapour
so sweat evaporates more slowly, transferring less heat from the skin
exam.tip: Apply evaporation to the new situation.

exam.q: Explain how the body responds to a rise in core body temperature during exercise. Refer to the hypothalamus and the skin.
model: Respiration in muscles releases heat, raising blood temperature
Receptors in the hypothalamus detect the rise in blood temperature (and skin receptors send impulses)
Hypothalamus / thermoregulatory centre sends nerve impulses to effectors
Arterioles supplying skin capillaries dilate so more blood flows near the surface and more heat is lost by radiation
Sweat glands in the dermis secrete more sweat; evaporation transfers heat from the skin
Temperature falls back to 37 °C: negative feedback
exam.tip: Follow stimulus, receptor, coordination centre, effector, response.

exam.q: Explain how the body responds when core temperature falls below 37 °C.
model: Hypothalamus detects fall and sends impulses to effectors
Vasoconstriction: arterioles narrow, less blood near skin surface, less heat lost
Less sweat secreted so less heat lost by evaporation
Shivering: muscles contract, more respiration releases heat
exam.tip: Give the effect on heat loss or gain for each response.

worked.q: A student's core body temperature rose from 37.0 °C to 38.2 °C during a race and fell back to 37.0 °C 20 minutes after finishing. Calculate the rise in temperature and the mean rate of cooling after the race, then explain the cooling.
steps: Mean rate of cooling = 1.2 / 20 = 0.06 °C per minute.
The hypothalamus detected the raised blood temperature.
It caused vasodilation (more blood flowing near the skin, more heat lost by radiation) and more sweating (evaporation transfers heat).
Once at 37 °C, these responses decrease: negative feedback.
worked.ans: Rise of 1.2 °C; cooling at 0.06 °C per minute, due to vasodilation and sweating controlled by the hypothalamus.

worked.q: Model answer: A man falls into cold sea water. Explain the changes in his skin and muscles. (4 marks)
steps: Temperature receptors in the skin detect the cold and send impulses to the hypothalamus; the hypothalamus detects a fall in blood temperature.
Vasoconstriction: arterioles to skin capillaries narrow, so less blood flows near the surface and less heat is lost; his skin looks pale.
Sweat glands secrete little or no sweat, so less heat is lost by evaporation.
Skeletal muscles shiver, increasing respiration, which releases heat.
worked.ans: Vasoconstriction and reduced sweating cut heat loss; shivering increases heat released by respiration.

worked.q: Applied example: Explain why a person looks red and sweaty after a hot bath.
steps: The hot water raises skin and blood temperature (external change).
The hypothalamus causes vasodilation, so more blood flows through capillaries near the skin surface: the skin looks red.
Sweat glands secrete more sweat, which evaporates and cools the skin.
worked.ans: Vasodilation causes the red colour and increased sweating cools the body, both triggered by the hypothalamus.

bio_edx.6.8.summary: Blood glucose concentration is kept within a narrow range by **negative feedback** controlled by the **pancreas**. When blood glucose is too high the pancreas releases **insulin**, which makes body cells take up glucose and makes the **liver and muscle cells convert glucose into glycogen** for storage. (Higher tier) When blood glucose is too low the pancreas releases **glucagon**, which makes the **liver break down glycogen into glucose** and release it into the blood, so the level rises back to normal.

core.h: Why blood glucose must be controlled
core.p: Glucose is the main respiratory substrate: cells use it in **respiration** to release energy. It is absorbed into the blood from the small intestine after digestion of carbohydrates, so the amount in the blood changes all day. Controlling blood glucose is an example of **homeostasis**.
bullets: Cells need a steady supply of glucose for respiration; the **brain** relies especially heavily on glucose.
If blood glucose falls **too low**, cells cannot release enough energy (you feel tired, dizzy and may become unconscious).

If blood glucose rises **too high**, the blood becomes more concentrated than the cytoplasm of cells, so **water leaves cells by osmosis**; long-term high glucose damages blood vessels, eyes, kidneys and nerves.
Blood glucose **rises** after eating a carbohydrate-rich meal.
Blood glucose **falls** during exercise (muscles respire faster and use more glucose) and between meals or during fasting.

callouts.p: Maintaining a constant internal environment in the body, despite changes inside and outside the body.

core.p: The **pancreas** is an endocrine gland found just below the stomach. It **monitors the blood glucose concentration** as blood flows through it, and it secretes the hormones **insulin** and **glucagon** directly into the blood. The hormones are carried in the blood plasma to their **target organs**.
bullets: The pancreas acts as both the **receptor** (detects the change in glucose concentration) and the **coordinator** (releases the right hormone).
Insulin's main targets are the **liver** and **muscle cells**, but it also makes most body cells take up glucose.
Glucagon's main target is the **liver**.
Hormones are chemical messengers: slower and longer-lasting than nerve impulses, which suits a level that must be kept steady over hours.
The pancreas also makes digestive enzymes, but in this topic you only need its hormones.

callouts.p: Both insulin and glucagon are made by the pancreas. They have opposite effects on blood glucose concentration.

core.p: When blood glucose concentration is **too high** (for example after a meal) the pancreas detects this and **secretes insulin** into the blood. Insulin is carried to target cells, where it causes glucose to be removed from the blood.
bullets: Insulin causes **body cells to take up glucose** from the blood (it increases the permeability of cell membranes to glucose), so cells can use it for respiration.
Insulin causes **liver and muscle cells** to **convert glucose into glycogen**, which is stored inside the cells.
Both effects **lower the blood glucose concentration** back towards the normal level.
As glucose returns to normal, the pancreas **secretes less insulin**: this is negative feedback.

Full chain for 4-6 mark answers: glucose rises - detected by pancreas - insulin secreted into blood - travels to liver and muscles - glucose taken up and converted to glycogen - glucose falls to normal.

callouts.p: Say the liver and muscle cells store glycogen. Writing only 'the body stores it' does not get the mark.

core.p: **Glycogen** is an insoluble storage carbohydrate made from many glucose molecules joined together (a polymer of glucose). It is stored in **liver** and **muscle** cells. Because it is insoluble it does not affect the water potential of the cell, so it is a good way of storing glucose without water moving into cells by osmosis.
bullets: Glucose to glycogen is triggered by **insulin** (storage when glucose is high).
Glycogen to glucose is triggered by **glucagon** in the liver (release when glucose is low).
Muscle glycogen is mainly used by the muscle itself during exercise.
Liver glycogen can be broken down and released into the blood to supply the whole body.
Glycogen is the animal equivalent of **starch** in plants.

callouts.p: Glucose is the sugar, glycogen is the store, glucagon is the hormone. Spell them carefully: a misspelling that could be either word loses the mark.

core.p: When blood glucose concentration is **too low** (for example during exercise or after not eating for a long time) the pancreas detects this and **secretes glucagon** into the blood. Glucagon travels to the **liver**.
bullets: Glucagon causes **liver cells to convert glycogen into glucose**.
The glucose is **released into the blood**, so blood glucose concentration **rises** back to normal.
As glucose returns to normal, the pancreas **secretes less glucagon** (negative feedback).
While glucose is low, the pancreas also secretes **less insulin**, so less glucose is removed from the blood.
Insulin and glucagon are therefore **antagonistic hormones**: they have opposite effects on the same variable.

callouts.p: Explaining the role of glucagon in controlling blood glucose is Higher tier content (spec 7.14).

core.p: Many questions ask you to compare the two hormones. A table makes the contrast clear.
bullets: Same gland, same transport (blood), opposite triggers and opposite effects.
Both work by negative feedback.
Both act on the liver, but only insulin causes cells in general to take up glucose.

head: Feature
Insulin
Glucagon (HT)
rows: Liver and muscle (and most body cells)
Liver cells release glucose into blood

core.p: Blood glucose control is a classic **negative feedback** system: a change away from the normal level triggers a response that **reverses the change**, bringing the level back to normal. When the level is back to normal, the stimulus is removed and the response is switched off.
bullets: Rise in glucose - insulin released - glucose falls - insulin release reduced.
Fall in glucose - glucagon released - glucose rises - glucagon release reduced.
This keeps glucose fluctuating **within a narrow range** rather than at one exact value.
Having two hormones with opposite effects gives **finer, faster control** than one hormone alone, because the body can actively push the level both up and down.
Compare with thyroxine (7.3), which is also controlled by negative feedback.

callouts.p: A mechanism in which a change from the normal level causes a response that returns the level back to normal.

fig.cap: Negative feedback control of blood glucose. Red path: after a meal glucose rises, the pancreas secretes insulin, cells take up glucose and the liver and muscles store it as glycogen, so glucose returns to normal. Purple path (HT): when glucose is too low the pancreas secretes glucagon and the liver converts glycogen back to glucose.

core.p: Following the timeline after eating is a common data or graph question.
bullets: Carbohydrates are digested to glucose in the small intestine and **absorbed into the blood**, so blood glucose **rises**.
The pancreas detects the rise and **secretes insulin**; blood insulin concentration rises shortly **after** the glucose rise (there is a short delay).
Liver and muscle cells take up glucose and convert it to glycogen, so blood glucose **falls**.
Insulin secretion then falls as glucose returns to normal.
The level may dip slightly below normal (an **overshoot**); the pancreas then secretes glucagon to bring it back up (HT).

callouts.p: On a glucose and insulin graph, the insulin peak comes after the glucose peak. Explain this delay: the pancreas must first detect the rise, and hormones take time to travel and act.

core.p: During exercise muscle cells respire faster, so they take more glucose out of the blood. Blood glucose would fall, so the body responds.
bullets: Blood glucose falls as muscles use glucose for respiration.
The pancreas detects this and **secretes less insulin**, so less glucose is removed into storage.
(HT) The pancreas **secretes glucagon**; the liver converts glycogen into glucose and releases it into the blood.
Muscle glycogen is also broken down inside the muscles to supply their own respiration.
Result: blood glucose is kept near normal and working muscles still get enough glucose.

core.h: How the hormones travel and act
core.p: Hormones are secreted by endocrine glands **directly into the bloodstream** and carried in the **plasma** around the whole body. Only **target cells** with the correct receptors respond.
bullets: Insulin reaches every part of the body, but responds only in cells with insulin receptors.
The liver is ideally placed: blood from the gut flows to the liver, so it meets glucose soon after absorption.
Hormonal responses are **slower** than nervous responses but **last longer**, which suits a variable that changes over minutes to hours.
Hormones are eventually broken down (for example in the liver), so a response stops when secretion stops.

callouts.p: A chemical messenger secreted by an endocrine gland directly into the blood, which carries it to a target organ where it produces a response.

fig.cap: The pancreas detects blood glucose and secretes insulin (blue) and glucagon (purple) into the blood. The blood carries them to target organs: the liver, which stores glycogen, and muscle cells.
