core.p: If this control system fails, blood glucose cannot be regulated. This is covered fully in 7.15-7.16, but you should understand why it follows from this point.
bullets: If the pancreas **does not produce enough insulin**, glucose stays high after meals (type 1 diabetes).
If **body cells stop responding to insulin**, glucose also stays high (type 2 diabetes).
This shows that both the **hormone** and the **target cells' response** are needed for control.

core.p: Marks come from a clear, logical chain using exact keywords.
bullets: Always state **which direction** glucose has changed and **which hormone** is secreted.
Say the hormone is secreted **by the pancreas** and travels **in the blood**.
State the effect on the **target organ**: liver and muscle store glucose **as glycogen** (insulin); liver converts glycogen **to glucose** (glucagon).
Finish with the outcome: blood glucose **returns to normal**.
In 6-mark answers, mention **negative feedback** and both hormones (if Higher).

callouts.p: Insulin does not 'turn into glycogen' and glucagon does not 'turn into glucose'. Hormones trigger the liver cells to convert one substance into the other.

analogy.t: A bank account with a savings pot
analogy.p: Think of blood glucose as the money in your current account and glycogen as a savings account held by the liver. When too much money arrives (after a meal), **insulin** is the instruction to move the extra into savings (glucose to glycogen). When the current account runs low (exercise), **glucagon** is the instruction to withdraw from savings (glycogen to glucose). The bank manager watching the balance is the pancreas. Where it breaks down: a bank moves money instantly by one transfer, whereas hormones take time to travel in the blood and the control is never perfectly exact, so glucose fluctuates within a range. Also, insulin makes cells all over the body take up and use glucose, which is more like spending than saving.

terms.d: A simple sugar used by cells as the main substrate for respiration; carried dissolved in the blood plasma.
The amount of glucose dissolved in a given volume of blood; kept within a narrow range by homeostasis.
An endocrine gland that monitors blood glucose concentration and secretes insulin and glucagon.
A hormone secreted by the pancreas when blood glucose is too high; causes cells to take up glucose and the liver and muscles to convert glucose to glycogen, lowering blood glucose.
(HT) A hormone secreted by the pancreas when blood glucose is too low; causes the liver to convert glycogen into glucose and release it into the blood, raising blood glucose.
An insoluble storage carbohydrate made of many glucose molecules, stored in liver and muscle cells.
The main target organ for insulin and glucagon; stores glucose as glycogen and releases glucose into the blood when needed.
Target cells for insulin that take up glucose and store it as glycogen.
Maintaining a constant internal environment in the body, despite changes inside and outside the body.
A control mechanism in which a change from the normal level triggers a response that returns the level to normal.
A chemical messenger secreted by an endocrine gland into the blood and carried to a target organ.
A gland that secretes hormones directly into the bloodstream.
An organ whose cells have receptors for a particular hormone and respond to it.
A pair of hormones with opposite effects on the same variable, such as insulin and glucagon on blood glucose.
The chemical reaction in cells that releases energy from glucose; the reason cells need a constant glucose supply.

mistakes.w: Insulin is turned into glycogen.
mistakes.r: Insulin causes the liver and muscle cells to convert glucose into glycogen.

mistakes.w: Glucagon is made in the liver.
mistakes.r: Glucagon is secreted by the pancreas; its target organ is the liver.

mistakes.w: Glycogen is a hormone that raises blood sugar.
mistakes.r: Glycogen is a storage carbohydrate; glucagon is the hormone.

mistakes.w: The brain/hypothalamus detects blood glucose and releases insulin.
mistakes.r: The pancreas detects blood glucose concentration and secretes insulin.

mistakes.w: Insulin is released when blood glucose is low.
mistakes.r: Insulin is released when blood glucose is too high; glucagon when it is too low.

mistakes.w: Glucose is stored in the pancreas.
mistakes.r: Glucose is stored as glycogen in the liver and muscles.

mistakes.w: Insulin travels along nerves to the liver.
mistakes.r: Insulin is secreted into the blood and carried in the plasma to target organs.

mistakes.w: Blood sugar goes back to normal (without explaining how).
mistakes.r: State the mechanism: cells take up glucose and the liver and muscles convert it to glycogen, so blood glucose concentration decreases.

mistakes.w: Glucagon makes glucose turn into glycogen.
mistakes.r: Glucagon causes glycogen to be converted into glucose, which is released into the blood.

exam.q: Name the organ that secretes insulin.
model: Pancreas.
exam.tip: Spell pancreas correctly; this is a one-word recall mark.

exam.q: Name the substance that glucose is stored as in the liver.
model: Glycogen.
exam.tip: Not glucagon: check your spelling.

exam.q: State how insulin is transported from where it is made to its target organ.
model: In the blood (plasma) / bloodstream.
exam.tip: Hormones always travel in the blood.

exam.q: Give two effects of insulin that reduce blood glucose concentration.
model: Causes body cells to take up glucose from the blood.
Causes liver and muscle cells to convert glucose into glycogen (for storage).
exam.tip: Two distinct effects are needed; naming the liver and muscles helps.

exam.q: Explain why blood glucose concentration rises after a meal containing starch.
model: Starch is digested (by amylase) into sugars / glucose.
Glucose is absorbed (from the small intestine) into the blood.
exam.tip: Link digestion to absorption into the blood.

exam.q: A graph shows blood glucose and blood insulin concentration after a meal. Explain why the peak in insulin occurs after the peak in glucose.
model: The pancreas must first detect the rise in blood glucose before it secretes insulin.
Insulin takes time to be secreted, travel in the blood and act on target cells.
exam.tip: Describe the sequence: detection then secretion then action.

exam.q: (Higher) Explain how glucagon increases blood glucose concentration.
model: Glucagon is secreted by the pancreas when blood glucose is too low.
It travels in the blood to the liver.
It causes the liver to convert glycogen into glucose, which is released into the blood.
exam.tip: Three steps: release, transport, effect on the liver.

exam.q: (Higher) Explain why blood glucose control is described as negative feedback.
model: A change in blood glucose (rise or fall) triggers a response that reverses the change.
e.g. rise in glucose causes insulin release, which lowers glucose; once normal, insulin secretion falls.
exam.tip: Give the definition and apply it with an example.

exam.q: During a long run, a runner's blood glucose concentration stays almost constant. Explain how this happens.
model: Muscles respire faster and use glucose, so blood glucose starts to fall.
The pancreas detects the fall and secretes less insulin.
(HT) The pancreas secretes glucagon, which travels in the blood to the liver.
The liver converts glycogen into glucose and releases it into the blood, so glucose returns to normal.
exam.tip: Start with why glucose falls, then the pancreas response, then the liver.

exam.q: (Higher) Explain how insulin and glucagon interact to keep blood glucose concentration within a narrow range.
model: The pancreas monitors blood glucose concentration.
When glucose is too high (e.g. after a meal) the pancreas secretes insulin into the blood.
Insulin causes body cells to take up glucose and liver and muscle cells to convert glucose to glycogen, so blood glucose falls.
When glucose is too low (e.g. exercise/fasting) the pancreas secretes glucagon.
Glucagon causes the liver to convert glycogen into glucose, which is released into the blood, so blood glucose rises.
This is negative feedback: as the level returns to normal, secretion of the hormone decreases; the two hormones have opposite (antagonistic) effects.
exam.tip: Cover both hormones fully, use 'glycogen' accurately, and finish with negative feedback.

exam.q: Suggest why glucose is stored as glycogen rather than as glucose inside liver cells.
model: Glycogen is insoluble.
So it does not affect water movement / cause water to enter cells by osmosis (and does not leave the cell).
exam.tip: Link insolubility to osmosis.

worked.q: A student eats a sugary drink. Describe and explain the changes in their blood glucose and insulin concentrations over the next two hours.
steps: Sugar is absorbed into the blood, so blood glucose concentration rises quickly.
The pancreas detects the rise and secretes insulin, so blood insulin rises a short time after glucose.
Insulin causes cells to take up glucose and liver and muscle cells to convert glucose to glycogen.
Blood glucose falls back towards normal.
As glucose returns to normal, the pancreas secretes less insulin, so insulin concentration falls (negative feedback).
worked.ans: Glucose rises then falls back to normal; insulin rises after the glucose rise and falls once glucose is normal, because insulin causes glucose to be stored as glycogen.

worked.q: Blood glucose changed from 5.0 mmol/dm3 to 8.5 mmol/dm3 after a meal. Calculate the percentage increase and state which hormone would be secreted.
steps: Change = 8.5 - 5.0 = 3.5 mmol/dm3.
Percentage increase = (change / original) x 100 = (3.5 / 5.0) x 100.
Glucose has risen above normal, so the pancreas secretes insulin.
worked.ans: 70% increase; insulin is secreted by the pancreas.

worked.q: (Higher) A person has not eaten for 12 hours. Explain how their blood glucose concentration is maintained.
steps: Without food, no glucose is absorbed and cells keep using glucose for respiration, so blood glucose falls.
The pancreas detects the fall, secretes less insulin and secretes glucagon.
Glucagon travels in the blood to the liver.
Liver cells convert stored glycogen into glucose and release it into the blood.
Blood glucose rises back to normal; glucagon secretion then decreases (negative feedback).
worked.ans: Glucagon from the pancreas causes the liver to break down glycogen into glucose, which enters the blood and keeps blood glucose near normal.

bio_edx.6.9.summary: Diabetes is a condition in which the body cannot control its **blood glucose concentration**, so glucose stays too high. In **type 1 diabetes** the **pancreas does not produce enough insulin** (the insulin-secreting cells are destroyed), so it is controlled by **insulin injections** together with careful diet and glucose monitoring. In **type 2 diabetes** the **body cells no longer respond properly to insulin** (or not enough is made), so it is controlled mainly by **diet and exercise**, with medication if needed.

core.p: Normally the pancreas secretes **insulin** when blood glucose is high, and insulin makes cells take up glucose and the liver and muscles store it as **glycogen**. In diabetes this system fails, so blood glucose concentration can rise **too high** and stay high.
bullets: Diabetes is a **non-communicable disease**: it cannot be passed from person to person.
There are two types, with **different causes** and **different treatments**.
High blood glucose over many years damages **blood vessels**, the **eyes**, **kidneys** and **nerves**, and increases risk of heart disease and stroke.
Glucose may appear in the **urine** because the kidneys cannot reabsorb it all: a classic test for diabetes.
Symptoms include thirst, needing to urinate often, tiredness and weight loss.

callouts.p: A condition in which the body cannot control blood glucose concentration properly, so it can become too high.

core.p: In type 1 diabetes the **pancreas does not produce enough insulin** (or produces none). The insulin-secreting cells in the pancreas have been destroyed, usually by the person's **own immune system** attacking them.
bullets: Without insulin, body cells are **not signalled to take up glucose**, and the liver and muscles do **not convert glucose to glycogen**.
So after a meal blood glucose rises and **stays high** (hyperglycaemia).
Type 1 usually develops **in childhood or early adulthood**, and often appears quickly.
It is **not caused by lifestyle**; there is a genetic link.
It cannot currently be cured or prevented; it must be managed for life.

callouts.p: Type 1 diabetes is caused by the pancreas not producing (enough) insulin.

core.p: Because the missing factor is insulin, the main treatment is to **replace insulin** by **injection** (or an insulin pump). The person must balance insulin with what they eat and how active they are.
bullets: **Insulin injections**, usually several times a day, often just before meals, so the extra glucose absorbed from food can be taken into cells and stored.
**Monitoring blood glucose** regularly (finger-prick test or a sensor) so the dose can be adjusted.
Dose depends on **diet** (how much carbohydrate is eaten) and **exercise** (exercise uses glucose, so less insulin may be needed).
**Controlled diet**: limiting foods rich in simple sugars avoids sudden spikes; regular meals avoid big swings.
Insulin is a protein, so it must be **injected**: if swallowed it would be **digested** by protease enzymes in the gut.
Risk: too much insulin or too much exercise can make glucose **too low** (hypoglycaemia), so people carry sugary food.

callouts.p: A favourite 2-mark question: insulin is a protein so it would be digested (broken down by protease) in the stomach/intestine before it could be absorbed into the blood.

core.p: In type 2 diabetes the pancreas still makes insulin, but **body cells no longer respond to insulin** properly (**insulin resistance**), or the pancreas **does not produce enough insulin** to meet demand. Either way, glucose is not taken up from the blood efficiently.
bullets: Cells (especially liver, muscle and fat cells) become **less sensitive** to insulin.
Blood glucose stays **too high** after meals.
Type 2 usually develops **later in life** and comes on gradually.
It is far more common than type 1 (most cases of diabetes in the UK are type 2).

callouts.p: Type 2 diabetes is caused by body cells no longer responding to insulin (or the pancreas not producing enough insulin).

core.p: A **risk factor** increases the **chance** of getting a disease; it does not guarantee it. Type 2 is strongly linked to lifestyle, which means it can often be **prevented or delayed**.
bullets: **Obesity**: carrying excess body fat, especially **around the waist (abdomen)**, is the biggest risk factor.
**Lack of exercise** and a **diet high in sugar and fat**.
**Increasing age**.
**Family history / genetics** and ethnic background.
How obesity is measured (BMI and waist:hip ratio) is the next spec point (7.17).

callouts.p: Obesity is correlated with type 2 diabetes and is a risk factor; not every obese person develops it, and some people of healthy weight do.

core.p: Because the problem is how cells respond, treatment focuses on reducing the glucose load and improving the body's sensitivity to insulin.
bullets: **Controlled diet**: less sugar and refined carbohydrate, less fat, more fibre, so blood glucose rises less after meals.
**Regular exercise**: muscles use glucose for respiration, lowering blood glucose, and exercise helps cells respond to insulin.
**Losing weight**: reduces insulin resistance; some people can bring blood glucose back to normal this way.
**Medication** (tablets) may be prescribed if diet and exercise are not enough, e.g. drugs that help cells respond to insulin or reduce glucose release by the liver.
Some people eventually need **insulin injections** if the pancreas can no longer produce enough.

callouts.p: For full marks, link each treatment to blood glucose: e.g. exercise increases respiration in muscles, which uses up glucose, so blood glucose falls.

fig.cap: How each type is controlled. Type 1 (left): monitor glucose, inject insulin matched to food, plan diet and exercise. Type 2 (right): healthy diet, exercise and weight loss first, then medication or eventually insulin if needed.

core.p: Exams often show blood glucose after a meal or a glucose drink for a person with and without diabetes.
bullets: Without diabetes: glucose rises a little after the meal, then insulin brings it **back to normal within about 2 hours**.
With diabetes: glucose starts **higher**, rises **further** and falls back **much more slowly** (or not at all).
In a graph showing insulin, a person with **type 1** shows **little or no rise in insulin**; a person with **type 2** may show insulin rising but glucose still staying high.
Use data: quote values with units (e.g. mmol/dm3 or mg/100 cm3) and compare peaks and times.

core.h: Why glucose stays high: the mechanism
core.p: Linking the cause to the effect is where grade 9 marks are earned.
bullets: Type 1: no insulin secreted - no signal reaches target cells - cells do not take up glucose - liver and muscle do not convert glucose to glycogen - glucose stays high.
Type 2: insulin secreted - target cells do not respond (insulin resistance) - glucose not taken up or stored - glucose stays high.
In both cases, the **negative feedback** loop that should lower glucose is broken.

core.p: Good control matters both day to day and long term.
bullets: **Too high** (hyperglycaemia): thirst, frequent urination, tiredness; long-term damage to blood vessels, eyes (sight loss), kidneys and nerves (e.g. in the feet).
**Too low** (hypoglycaemia, usually from too much insulin or missing a meal): shaking, sweating, confusion, unconsciousness; treated by eating sugar.
Regular monitoring allows the person to keep glucose within a safe range.

callouts.p: Diabetes itself causes high glucose, but treatment with insulin can cause glucose to fall too low if the dose is too high for the food eaten or exercise done.

core.p: Diabetes questions usually test whether you can match cause to treatment with exact wording.
bullets: Type 1: write '**pancreas does not produce (enough) insulin**'. Treatment: '**insulin injections**'.
Type 2: write '**body cells no longer respond to insulin**' (or 'do not produce enough insulin'). Treatment: '**diet and exercise**' (then drugs).
Never write that type 2 is 'caused by eating sugar'; write that it is a **risk factor** linked to **obesity**.
In 6-mark compare questions, cover cause, treatment and the reason the treatment works for each type.

analogy.p: Think of insulin as a key and the body cell as a locked door that lets glucose in. In **type 1**, the key factory (pancreas) has been shut down, so there are no keys: the fix is to deliver keys from outside (insulin injections). In **type 2**, keys are made, but the locks have become stiff and the keys do not turn well (cells do not respond), so the best fix is to reduce the crowd waiting at the door (less sugar in the diet) and loosen the locks (exercise and weight loss). Where it breaks down: insulin does not physically open a door; it binds to receptors and triggers the cell to take in glucose and convert it to glycogen, and in type 2 the pancreas may also make too little insulin.

terms.d: A condition in which blood glucose concentration cannot be controlled properly and becomes too high.
Diabetes caused by the pancreas not producing (enough) insulin, because the insulin-secreting cells are destroyed.
Diabetes caused by body cells no longer responding to insulin, or the pancreas not producing enough insulin.
A hormone secreted by the pancreas that causes cells to take up glucose and the liver and muscles to store it as glycogen, lowering blood glucose.
When body cells do not respond properly to insulin, so glucose is not taken up from the blood.
The endocrine gland that monitors blood glucose and secretes insulin (and glucagon).
The amount of glucose dissolved in the blood, normally kept within a narrow range.
The main treatment for type 1 diabetes: insulin is injected under the skin because it would be digested if swallowed.
Something that increases the chance of developing a disease, such as obesity for type 2 diabetes.
Having a large excess of body fat; the main risk factor for type 2 diabetes.
A disease that cannot be passed from one person to another.
Blood glucose concentration that is too high.
Blood glucose concentration that is too low, e.g. after too much insulin or missing a meal.
An insoluble storage carbohydrate made from glucose, stored in liver and muscle cells when insulin is present.
Eating regular meals with limited simple sugars so blood glucose does not rise sharply.

mistakes.w: Type 1 diabetes is caused by eating too much sugar.
mistakes.r: Type 1 is caused by the pancreas not producing enough insulin; it is not caused by lifestyle.

mistakes.w: Type 2 diabetes means the body makes no insulin.
mistakes.r: In type 2, body cells no longer respond to insulin (or not enough insulin is made).

mistakes.w: People with type 2 diabetes must always inject insulin.
mistakes.r: Type 2 is usually controlled by diet and exercise first, then medication; insulin only if needed.

mistakes.w: Insulin can be taken as a tablet.
mistakes.r: Insulin is a protein, so it would be digested by protease in the gut; it must be injected.

mistakes.w: Exercise increases blood glucose.
mistakes.r: Exercise increases respiration in muscles, which uses glucose and lowers blood glucose.

mistakes.w: Diabetes is when you have too little sugar in the blood.
mistakes.r: Diabetes causes blood glucose concentration to be too high; low glucose is a risk of too much insulin.

mistakes.w: Obesity causes type 2 diabetes in everyone who is overweight.
mistakes.r: Obesity is a risk factor that increases the chance of type 2 diabetes; it is correlated, not certain.

mistakes.w: Insulin turns glucose into glucagon.
mistakes.r: Insulin causes glucose to be converted into glycogen in the liver and muscles.

mistakes.w: Type 1 diabetics should eat no carbohydrate.
mistakes.r: They should eat a controlled diet and match their insulin dose to their carbohydrate intake.

exam.q: State the cause of type 1 diabetes.
model: The pancreas does not produce (enough) insulin.
exam.tip: Mention the pancreas and insulin.

exam.q: State the cause of type 2 diabetes.
model: Body cells no longer respond to insulin / pancreas does not produce enough insulin.
exam.tip: 'Insulin resistance' is accepted if explained.

exam.q: Give the main treatment for type 1 diabetes.
model: Insulin injections.
exam.tip: 'Insulin' alone may not be enough; say injections.

exam.q: Explain why insulin is injected rather than taken by mouth.
model: Insulin is a protein.
It would be digested / broken down by protease enzymes in the stomach or small intestine (so would not reach the blood intact).
exam.tip: Two marks: protein, then digestion.

exam.q: Give two ways a person with type 2 diabetes can control their blood glucose without medication.
model: Eat a controlled diet low in sugar / refined carbohydrate (and fat).
Exercise regularly / lose weight.
exam.tip: Two different lifestyle changes.

exam.q: Explain why a person with type 1 diabetes may need to eat a sugary snack before exercise.
model: Exercise increases respiration in muscles, which uses up glucose.
So blood glucose could fall too low (especially with injected insulin); the snack raises blood glucose.
exam.tip: Link exercise to respiration and glucose use.

exam.q: Explain why regular exercise helps to control type 2 diabetes.
model: Muscle cells respire more and take up more glucose, lowering blood glucose.
Helps weight loss / reduces body fat.
This makes cells more responsive to insulin (reduces insulin resistance).
exam.tip: Give the mechanism, not just 'it is healthy'.

exam.q: A graph shows that after a glucose drink, person A's blood glucose returns to normal after 2 hours, but person B's stays high for 4 hours. Explain which person has diabetes.
model: Person B has diabetes.
B's blood glucose stays high for longer because insulin is not produced / cells do not respond to insulin.
So glucose is not taken up by cells or converted to glycogen (as quickly).
exam.tip: Identify, then explain using insulin's action.

exam.q: Suggest why the number of people with type 2 diabetes in the UK has increased.
model: Increase in obesity.
Due to diets high in sugar and fat / less exercise / ageing population.
exam.tip: Link to a named risk factor.

exam.q: Compare the causes and control of type 1 and type 2 diabetes.
model: Type 1: pancreas does not produce (enough) insulin (insulin-secreting cells destroyed).
Type 1 is controlled by insulin injections, usually around mealtimes.
Type 1 also needs regular blood glucose monitoring and a controlled diet/exercise to match the insulin dose.
Type 2: body cells no longer respond to insulin (or not enough insulin produced).
Type 2 is controlled by a controlled diet (low sugar), regular exercise and weight loss.
Type 2 may need medication or eventually insulin if lifestyle changes are not enough; type 2 is linked to obesity, type 1 is not.
exam.tip: Balance both types and give similarities and differences, not two separate lists.

worked.q: Blood glucose of a person rose from 5.0 to 12.0 mmol/dm3 after a meal and was still 11.0 mmol/dm3 two hours later. Calculate the percentage increase at the peak and explain what this suggests.
steps: Increase = 12.0 - 5.0 = 7.0 mmol/dm3.
Percentage increase = (7.0 / 5.0) x 100 = 140%.
After 2 hours glucose is still far above the starting level, whereas a person without diabetes would be back to normal.
This suggests the person has diabetes: insulin is not produced (type 1) or cells do not respond to it (type 2), so glucose is not taken up.
worked.ans: 140% increase; the slow fall suggests diabetes.

worked.q: Model answer: A 50-year-old man with a large waist is diagnosed with type 2 diabetes. Explain how his doctor would advise him to control it.
steps: Cause: his body cells no longer respond properly to insulin, so glucose stays high.
Eat a controlled diet with less sugar and refined carbohydrate, so less glucose enters the blood after meals.
Exercise regularly: muscles respire more and use glucose, lowering blood glucose.
Lose weight: reduces insulin resistance so cells respond better to insulin.
If this is not enough, take medication; insulin injections may be needed later.
worked.ans: Diet, exercise and weight loss first, then medication if needed, because the problem is cells not responding to insulin.

worked.q: Applied example: A teenager with type 1 diabetes eats a large pasta meal. Explain how they should manage their blood glucose.
steps: Pasta contains starch, which is digested to glucose and absorbed, so blood glucose will rise.
Their pancreas cannot produce enough insulin, so glucose would stay high.
They measure their blood glucose and inject a dose of insulin matched to the carbohydrate in the meal.
The insulin causes cells to take up glucose and the liver and muscles to store it as glycogen, so glucose returns to normal.
They keep monitoring, because too much insulin could make glucose fall too low.
worked.ans: Test glucose, inject insulin matched to the meal, and continue monitoring.

bio_edx.6.14.summary: Your body cannot store excess amino acids, so the liver breaks them down in a process called **deamination**. The amine group is removed and turned into **ammonia**, which is very toxic, so the liver quickly converts it into **urea**, which is much less toxic. Urea dissolves in the **blood plasma**, is carried to the **kidneys**, filtered out of the blood and excreted in **urine**. The rest of the amino acid is not wasted: it can be respired for energy or converted to carbohydrate or fat and stored.

core.p: Proteins in food are digested by **protease** enzymes in the stomach and small intestine into **amino acids**. These are absorbed into the blood in the small intestine and carried to the liver, then to body cells.
bullets: Protein → amino acids by **protease** enzymes (e.g. pepsin in the stomach)
Amino acids are absorbed by diffusion and active transport in the small intestine
They travel in the **blood plasma**, first to the liver in the hepatic portal vein
Cells use amino acids to build new **proteins** (enzymes, antibodies, muscle, haemoglobin)

callouts.p: Amino acids are the monomers of proteins. Cells need them for growth and repair.

core.h: Why excess amino acids are a problem
core.p: If you eat more protein than your cells need for growth and repair, the extra amino acids cannot be stored in the body. Unlike glucose (stored as glycogen) and fatty acids (stored as fat), there is **no store for amino acids**, so they must be broken down.
bullets: The body has **no way to store** excess amino acids
Glucose can be stored as **glycogen**; lipids as **fat** in adipose tissue; amino acids cannot
Excess amino acids would otherwise build up in the blood
So the liver breaks them down and the nitrogen-containing part is removed

head: Nutrient
Can it be stored?
How?
rows: As glycogen in liver and muscle
Excess is deaminated in the liver

callouts.p: Do not write that excess amino acids are stored as protein. Excess amino acids are broken down in the liver.

core.p: **Deamination** means removing the amine group (the part containing nitrogen, NH2) from an amino acid. It happens only in **liver cells**, using enzymes.
bullets: Takes place in the **liver**, not the kidneys
The **amine group (NH2)** is removed from each excess amino acid
The amine group is converted into **ammonia (NH3)**
The remaining carbon-containing part of the amino acid is kept and used
Deamination is controlled by **enzymes** inside liver cells

callouts.p: The removal of the amine group from excess amino acids in the liver, forming ammonia.

core.h: Ammonia: why it must be changed
core.p: Ammonia is **highly toxic**. Even a low concentration in the blood can damage cells, especially in the brain, and it changes the pH of body fluids, which can disturb enzymes. The body cannot let it build up.
bullets: Ammonia is **very toxic** to cells
It is very soluble and alkaline, so it can upset the **pH** of the blood and tissue fluid
A change in pH can **denature enzymes** and stop reactions working
Getting rid of ammonia directly would need huge volumes of water
So the liver converts it **immediately** into a safer substance: urea

callouts.p: Ammonia is very toxic; urea is much less toxic, so it can be safely carried in the blood.

core.p: In liver cells, ammonia is combined with **carbon dioxide** in a series of enzyme-controlled reactions to make **urea**. This uses energy from respiration (ATP).
bullets: Ammonia + carbon dioxide → urea (+ water), in the **liver**
Urea is **less toxic** than ammonia
Urea is **soluble in water**, so it dissolves in blood plasma
Making urea needs energy, so liver cells have many **mitochondria**
Urea is the main **nitrogenous waste** product in humans

callouts.p: A less toxic waste product made in the liver from ammonia produced by the deamination of excess amino acids.
You only need the idea: ammonia (from amino acids) is converted to urea in the liver. You do not need the detailed reaction steps.

core.h: What happens to the rest of the amino acid
core.p: After the amine group is removed, the remaining part of the molecule contains carbon, hydrogen and oxygen. The body uses it rather than wasting it.
bullets: It can be **respired** to release energy
It can be converted into **glucose** and stored as **glycogen**
It can be converted into **fat** and stored
So only the nitrogen part becomes waste

core.h: Transport of urea in the blood
core.p: Urea leaves liver cells and diffuses into the blood. Because it is soluble, it travels dissolved in the **plasma** to the kidneys.
bullets: Urea diffuses out of liver cells into the blood
Carried **dissolved in plasma**, not in red blood cells
Reaches the kidneys in the **renal artery**
Blood leaving the kidney in the **renal vein** contains much less urea

callouts.p: Red blood cells carry oxygen. Urea, glucose, carbon dioxide and hormones are carried in the plasma.

core.h: Removal of urea by the kidneys
core.p: In each nephron, urea is **filtered** out of the blood in the glomerulus into the Bowman's capsule because it is a small molecule. Unlike glucose, it is **not reabsorbed** (or only a little), so it stays in the filtrate and leaves in urine.
bullets: **Ultrafiltration** at the glomerulus: small molecules including urea, water, glucose and ions enter the filtrate
Glucose is **selectively reabsorbed**; urea is not
Water is reabsorbed, so urea becomes more **concentrated** in the urine
Urine travels down the **ureter** to the **bladder**, then out through the urethra

callouts.p: Removing urea in urine is excretion: getting rid of waste made by the body's own metabolism.

core.p: Urea is made by your cells' chemical reactions, so removing it counts as **excretion**. Faeces are mostly undigested food that never entered cells, so getting rid of them is **egestion**.
bullets: **Excretion**: removal of metabolic waste (urea, carbon dioxide, excess water)
**Egestion**: removal of undigested food as faeces
Lungs excrete carbon dioxide; kidneys excrete urea
Urea is also lost in small amounts in **sweat**

core.p: The more protein you eat beyond your needs, the more amino acids are deaminated, so **more urea** is produced and appears in urine.
bullets: High-protein diet → more excess amino acids → more deamination → **more urea**
More urea needs more water to remove it, so urine volume or concentration rises
People with **kidney failure** are often put on a **low-protein diet** to reduce urea build-up
Urea builds up in the blood if kidneys fail, which is why dialysis removes it

callouts.p: Exam questions often link urea to kidney failure and dialysis: dialysis fluid contains no urea so urea diffuses out of the blood.

core.p: Making urea is one of many homeostatic jobs of the liver. It keeps the concentration of toxic nitrogen waste in the blood low, helping maintain a constant internal environment.
bullets: Deamination of excess amino acids and **urea production**
Stores glucose as **glycogen** (with insulin) and releases it (with glucagon)
Breaks down old red blood cells and some toxins such as alcohol
Releases heat from its many reactions

core.p: Exam answers on this point usually want the steps in order, using the correct words.
bullets: 1. Protein digested to **amino acids**, absorbed into blood
2. Excess amino acids cannot be stored, taken to the **liver**
3. **Deamination**: amine group removed
4. Amine group forms **ammonia**, which is toxic
5. Ammonia converted to **urea**, which is less toxic
6. Urea carried in **blood plasma** to the kidneys
7. Urea **filtered** in the glomerulus and not reabsorbed
8. Urea excreted in **urine**, stored in the bladder

callouts.p: In a 4 to 6 mark answer, put the steps in a logical order and name the organ at each stage.

analogy.t: Recycling a parcel with a dangerous label
analogy.p: Imagine a delivery depot (the liver) receives more parcels (amino acids) than anyone ordered, and there is no warehouse to keep them. Workers cut off a dangerous chemical label (the amine group) and recycle the cardboard (the carbon part, used for energy or stored). The label turns into a toxic gas (ammonia), so it is sealed into a safer tub (urea) and sent by van (blood plasma) to the waste plant (kidneys), which flushes it away (urine). Where it breaks down: in the body there are no workers choosing; enzymes do it automatically, and the sealing step needs energy from respiration, not just packaging.

terms.d: The monomer (building block) of proteins, containing an amine group with nitrogen.
An enzyme that breaks down proteins into amino acids.
Amino acids beyond what cells need for making proteins; they cannot be stored.
Removal of the amine group from excess amino acids in the liver.
The nitrogen-containing NH2 part of an amino acid.
A highly toxic, alkaline substance formed from the amine group during deamination.
A less toxic, soluble nitrogenous waste made in the liver from ammonia and carbon dioxide.
The organ where deamination and urea production take place.
The liquid part of blood that carries dissolved substances such as urea.
Organ that filters the blood, removing urea, excess water and ions as urine.
Liquid containing urea, water and ions, made by the kidneys and stored in the bladder.
Removal of waste products made by the body's metabolism, such as urea and carbon dioxide.
Removal of undigested food from the gut as faeces.
Filtering of small molecules such as urea out of the blood under high pressure in the glomerulus.
Taking useful substances such as glucose back into the blood from the nephron; urea is not reabsorbed.
Waste containing nitrogen, made from the breakdown of amino acids; urea in humans.

mistakes.w: Urea is made in the kidneys.
mistakes.r: Urea is made in the **liver**; the kidneys only remove it from the blood.

mistakes.w: Excess amino acids are stored as protein or in the liver.
mistakes.r: Excess amino acids **cannot be stored**, so they are deaminated in the liver.

mistakes.w: Excess proteins are deaminated.
mistakes.r: Excess **amino acids** are deaminated.

mistakes.w: Urea is made directly from amino acids.
mistakes.r: The amine group is removed to form **ammonia**, which is then converted to urea.

mistakes.w: Ammonia is converted to urea because urea is not toxic.
mistakes.r: Urea is **less toxic** than ammonia (not completely harmless).

mistakes.w: Urea is carried by red blood cells.
mistakes.r: Urea is carried **dissolved in the plasma**.

mistakes.w: Urea is reabsorbed like glucose.
mistakes.r: Glucose is selectively reabsorbed; urea is **not reabsorbed** and stays in the filtrate.

mistakes.w: Getting rid of urea is egestion.
mistakes.r: Urea is a metabolic waste, so removing it is **excretion**.

mistakes.w: The whole amino acid is excreted.
mistakes.r: Only the nitrogen part becomes urea; the rest is **respired** or stored as glycogen or fat.

exam.q: Name the organ where urea is produced.
model: Liver
exam.tip: Do not write kidney.

exam.q: State the name of the process that removes the amine group from amino acids.
model: Deamination
exam.tip: Spell it carefully: de-amin-ation.

exam.q: Name the toxic substance produced when amino acids are deaminated.
model: Ammonia
exam.tip: One word answer.

exam.q: Explain why ammonia is converted into urea in the liver.
model: Ammonia is (highly) toxic
Urea is less toxic so it can be transported safely in the blood
exam.tip: Use the comparison word less toxic.

exam.q: Explain why excess amino acids must be broken down rather than kept in the body.
model: Amino acids cannot be stored in the body
So they are deaminated / broken down in the liver
exam.tip: Contrast with glucose stored as glycogen.

exam.q: Describe how urea is transported from where it is made to where it is removed from the body.
model: Dissolved in (blood) plasma
From the liver to the kidneys
exam.tip: Name both organs and the plasma.

exam.q: A person changes to a high-protein diet. Explain why the amount of urea in their urine increases.
model: More amino acids are absorbed than needed / more excess amino acids
More deamination in the liver / more ammonia produced
More ammonia converted to urea, which is filtered by the kidneys into the urine
exam.tip: Follow the chain of cause and effect step by step.

exam.q: Explain why the concentration of urea in the renal vein is lower than in the renal artery.
model: Urea is filtered out of the blood in the glomerulus / kidney
Urea is not reabsorbed so it leaves in urine
exam.tip: Remember the renal vein carries blood away from the kidney.

exam.q: Describe what happens to excess amino acids in the body.
model: They are taken to the liver
Deamination: the amine group is removed
Ammonia is formed
Ammonia is converted to urea
The remaining part is used for respiration / stored as glycogen or fat
exam.tip: Any four of these points; use correct terms.

exam.q: Explain how the body produces and removes urea after a protein-rich meal.
model: Protein digested by protease into amino acids
Amino acids absorbed into the blood in the small intestine
Excess amino acids cannot be stored
Deaminated in the liver: amine group removed forming ammonia
Ammonia is toxic so is converted to urea, which is less toxic
Urea dissolves in plasma and is carried to the kidneys
Urea filtered from blood at the glomerulus and not reabsorbed
Excreted in urine, stored in the bladder
exam.tip: 6 markers reward a logical sequence that covers production AND removal.

worked.q: Model answer: Explain why patients with kidney failure are advised to eat a low-protein diet.
steps: Kidney failure means urea is not removed from the blood efficiently
A high-protein diet gives more excess amino acids
More excess amino acids are deaminated in the liver, making more urea
Urea would build up to harmful levels in the blood
So eating less protein means less urea is produced between dialysis sessions
worked.ans: Less protein → fewer excess amino acids → less deamination → less urea made, so urea does not build up in the blood when the kidneys cannot remove it.

worked.q: Applied example: A student says, 'Ammonia goes to the kidneys and is turned into urea there.' Correct this statement.
steps: Identify the error: urea is not made in the kidneys
Ammonia is produced by deamination in the liver
It is converted to urea in the liver immediately because it is toxic
Urea, not ammonia, travels in the plasma to the kidneys
worked.ans: Ammonia is converted to urea in the liver; only urea is carried in the blood plasma to the kidneys to be excreted.

worked.q: Data example: Blood entering a kidney contains 0.30 g of urea per litre; blood leaving contains 0.25 g per litre. Calculate the percentage decrease and explain it.
steps: Decrease = 0.30 - 0.25 = 0.05 g per litre
Percentage decrease = (0.05 / 0.30) x 100
Explanation: urea is filtered into the nephron and not reabsorbed, so it leaves in urine
worked.ans: 16.7% decrease, because the kidney filters urea out of the blood and excretes it in urine.

svg.cap: Deamination: liver enzymes remove the amine group (NH2) from an excess amino acid. The carbon-containing remainder is respired or stored; the amine group becomes ammonia, which combines with carbon dioxide to form urea.
